source: Odyssey_Almanacs_English.zip - English translations of Taiyi’s 119 《奥德赛》(Odyssey) character almanacs, supplied by djclocktower.
note: Full almanac import: every section of every almanac is carried onto the wiki. Rule Details -> summaryBullets, How to Run -> howToRun, Examples -> examples, Playing Tips -> tips, "Bluffing as the X" -> bluffing, and the reminder-token detail and Design Notes go into custom sidebar boxes. Icons come from the image URLs in each almanac’s Script Tool JSON block, normalized onto the site’s 591x591 frame with the same algorithm as assets/art-normalize.js. Translation credited to DJ_DJ_DJ on every row. Licence on all 119: "Open (may be used in any script; do not modify the ability)".
nightOrder: Taiyi’s almanacs number the night order on their own scale (7510, 11010, ...). Each entry names an official reference character, so each row is anchored to that character’s standard script-tool night order and offset by 0.1 (before/after). Characters sharing an anchor are ordered by the almanac’s own sub-value. 86 of 102 entries resolve against the standard table; the 16 listed in "estimatedNightAnchors" below hang off characters the standard table does not carry, and were placed by hand - worth spot-checking.

characters.name: Tango
characters.ability: During initial setup, the Storyteller publicly designates a character: if that character is in play, an Outsider is added or removed.
characters.lede: Tango makes certain characters add or remove an Outsider.
characters.quote: Tonight's lead dancer is — the Scarlet Woman! Let's give a warm round of applause as the Scarlet Woman takes the stage to lead the dance! What? She's not here?
summaryBullets: The Storyteller may publicly designate any one Townsfolk, Outsider, Minion, or Demon character — but cannot designate Fabled, Loric, or Traveller characters.
If the Storyteller designates an Outsider character, Tango cannot remove that Outsider character — that wouldn't satisfy the "if that character is in play" condition.

Optional rule: The Storyteller may publicly designate two characters — if one of them is in play, an Outsider is added; if the other is in play, an Outsider is removed. The Storyteller doesn't say which character adds an Outsider and which removes one.
howToRun: When the game begins, announce that Tango has been added to the game, and publicly designate one character as the "lead dancer".
During game setup, if the "lead dancer" character is put into the bag, add an Outsider and remove a Townsfolk — or remove an Outsider and add a Townsfolk.
examples: Before the game begins, the Storyteller publicly designates the Poisoner as the "lead dancer". This game, the Poisoner is in play — so there's one more Outsider than normal.
Before the game begins, the Storyteller publicly designates the Imp as the "lead dancer". This game, the Imp is in play — so there's one fewer Outsider than normal.
Before the game begins, the Storyteller publicly designates the Fortune Teller as the "lead dancer". This game, the Fortune Teller is not in play — so the Outsider count doesn't change.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: For scripts without Outsider-count logic, Tango provides Outsider-count variation logic — and helps the evil team bluff as Outsiders, or makes the in-play Outsiders look more suspicious.

characters.name: Ward Surveillance
characters.ability: The Storyteller might tell Demon & Minion players anything about the Lunatic. The Lunatic might learn other players are the Lunatic.
characters.lede: Ward Surveillance makes the Lunatic unable to pull free.
characters.quote: Lunatic #1 had Stargazy Pie tonight, and Lunatic #2 had a three-minute private meeting with his 'Minion' today! Report complete!
summaryBullets: You'd best also give the Lunatic some "Ward Surveillance"-like information to deceive him — otherwise the neglected Lunatic easily realizes he isn't actually the Demon.

The Storyteller decides what information to give the Demon or Minions through Ward Surveillance. You don't need to provide every detail about the Lunatic to the Demon every time — because if the Lunatic doesn't receive similarly detailed information next time, they'll immediately conclude they're the Lunatic.

You can use Ward Surveillance to tell the Demon what character the Lunatic thinks he is — but in this script there's no great need, because the Pukka acts on the first night and the Imp doesn't; the Demon can judge what character the Lunatic thinks he is by whether the Lunatic acted on the first night.
howToRun: When the game begins, announce that Ward Surveillance has been added to the game.

At any point during the game (usually the first night), you may tell Demon and Minion players anything you want to tell them about the Lunatic. The timing can be any point at night, or during the day. The information can be: who the Lunatic is, the Minions and not-in-play characters the Lunatic learned, who the Lunatic learned is the Lunatic — anything about the Lunatic. The form can be gestures, notes, typing on an electronic screen, face-to-face communication, etc.
examples: Momo is the Demon; Yaya is the Lunatic. On the first night, Momo learns that Yaya is the Lunatic, learns that the Minion Yaya learned of is himself, learns that the bluffs Yaya learned are the Ravenkeeper, the Monk, and the Magician, and learns that Yaya learned player #1 is the Lunatic.

Momo is the Lunatic; Yaya is the Exorcist. On the first night, Momo learns that Yaya is the Lunatic, learns that the Minion Yaya learned of is himself, learns that the bluffs Yaya learned are the Ravenkeeper, the Monk, and the Magician, and learns that Yaya learned player #1 is the Lunatic. Some of what Momo learns is right and some is wrong — because he's the Lunatic.
Momo is the Pukka; Yaya is the Lunatic. On the first night, Momo learns that Yaya is the Lunatic, and that Yaya thinks he's the Pukka and chose player #1.
Momo is the Demon; Yaya is the Lunatic. On the first night, Momo learns that Yaya is the Lunatic but learns nothing else about the Lunatic — because the Storyteller doesn't want to tell him.

Momo is the Mastermind; Yaya is the Lunatic. On the first night, Momo learns that Yaya is the Lunatic, learns that the Minions Yaya learned of are himself and player #1 (the Storyteller is deceiving the Lunatic that the Magician is in play), and learns that the bluffs Yaya learned are the Ravenkeeper, the Monk, and the Minstrel.
characters.creator: Taiyi

characters.name: Lethe
characters.ability: Evil players might think they are good characters: the Storyteller acts for them. The game only ends when all evils die, then everyone wins.
characters.lede: The Demon and Minions might forget their true characters.
characters.quote: The world fears me, saying I wash away all past lives. But they don't know — to forget one's sins is also to forget one's innocence. The deepest punishment here is not remembering what you did wrong, but never again remembering what you ever did.
summaryBullets: Optional rule: If all players are willing to experience it, you may announce before the game begins that Lethe will definitely be activated this game.
Under normal circumstances, don't activate Lethe every game. Occasionally slipping one or two games into a normal session for an element of surprise works best.

The Storyteller must decide whether to activate Lethe before setup begins. Players cannot learn in any form whether Lethe is activated. If Lethe isn't activated, it has no effect on the game — all details below assume Lethe is activated.
The Demon's and Minions' abilities all work normally (including setup-adjusting abilities); actively-used abilities are operated by the Storyteller in their place.
The Demon and Minions don't learn the Demon info or Minion info, or any other information gained through Demon or Minion abilities.
Minions and the Demon always think they're a Townsfolk or Outsider character — regardless of death, poisoning, drunkenness, etc.
Minions and the Demon are still treated as their true Minion or Demon characters by other players' abilities.

The Storyteller cannot break the rules — Minion and Demon abilities must be used within the rules. If the Minions and Demon die or otherwise lose their abilities, the Storyteller can no longer use those abilities.
The game only ends when all evil players are dead — announce that all players win.
If the Demon dies first and Minions remain alive, multiple safe nights may occur, exposing that Lethe is active. That's fine — keep playing and let the players try to find the last evil player.

Generally, as long as any evil player survives, the game continues. But to avoid excessive game length and players losing patience: if only two players remain alive and one of them is evil, you may declare the game over with all players losing. They've been given plenty of chances.
Lethe's purpose isn't "the Storyteller defeats the players" — it provides a puzzle-solving experience for everyone together. Don't aim to beat the players; aim to provide a fun puzzle experience.
howToRun: Before setup begins, tell everyone that this game may be affected by Lethe — or may not be. Then secretly decide whether to activate Lethe. If you decide to activate Lethe, don't reveal it in any form. Replace the Demon's and Minions' character tokens with Townsfolk or Outsider character tokens and put them into the bag (the original Demon's and Minions' setup-adjusting abilities still take effect).

After collecting all character tokens, secretly decide who is the Demon and who are the Minions. Place the Demon's and Minions' character tokens beside the character tokens those players think they have, to remind yourself. For this game, run the Demon and Minions as the characters they think they are.

Each night or day, if the Demon or Minions need to act, you act in their place. If the Demon or Minions die, or become poisoned or drunk through other characters' abilities, they lose their abilities — and you can no longer act in their place.
When all evil players are dead, announce the game is over — all players win.
examples: The Storyteller secretly decides to activate Lethe. The Imp, the Baron, and the Poisoner all think they're good characters. Because of the Baron's ability, there are two more Outsiders than default. Each night, the Storyteller uses the Imp's and the Poisoner's abilities in their place. On the fourth day, the Imp, the Baron, and the Poisoner all die by execution. The Storyteller announces that all players win together.
The Storyteller secretly decides not to activate Lethe. The game proceeds normally — Lethe has no effect on the game.
tips: If you drew a good character, whether Lethe is activated doesn't much affect your goal — as always, find the suspicious evil players and execute them.
If you drew a good character and suspect your ability isn't working properly, you can ask to be executed yourself — because you might be an evil player under Lethe's influence.

If you drew a Minion or Demon character, Lethe definitely wasn't activated this game. But you can use this to fabricate logic suggesting Lethe was activated — even trick good players into executing themselves, helping you win.
characters.creator: Taiyi, Saki (homage to the designer of the colliding design)

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content: [[Is the Demon" ×1, "Is a Minion" ×3]]

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A puzzle-solving gameplay style.

Everyone deduces, deduces, deduces.

customBoxes.title: Running It as the Storyteller
customBoxes.content:
Early in the game, disguise the situation as a normal game as much as possible.

If Lethe is exposed, that's fine — proceed normally and wait for the players to execute all evil players.

If the players make no progress at all, you may appropriately "help" them within the rules — e.g., giving poisoned, drunk, or Demon-and-Minion-deluded players fairly "outrageous" information, or using the Demon's ability at night to kill an evil player. But no matter what, you must follow the rules — none of your actions may break the game rules.

characters.name: Lucky Star
characters.ability: The player who draws this token receives some "benefits" and draws another token. [This token is added to the setup as an extra]
characters.lede: The player who draws the Lucky Star harvests good fortune.
characters.quote: Ding-dong! The doorbell rings, and you open the door to find a box of chocolates labeled 'For today's luckiest person'. Have one — sweetness till tomorrow, and good luck after you finish!
summaryBullets: The "benefits" are decided by the Storyteller.
If the "benefits" relate to the game, you must publicly explain them in advance to avoid affecting players' deductions.
howToRun: After setup is complete, add the Lucky Star's character token to the bag as an extra.
Publicly tell all players that the Lucky Star has been put into the bag, and what reward the lucky player who draws it will receive.
When a player draws the Lucky Star, take it back, congratulate them, and have them draw again.
examples: The Storyteller announces that the player who draws the Lucky Star gets today's treat for free. Xiaobai draws the Lucky Star and hands it to the Storyteller, then draws again — the Fortune Teller.

The Storyteller announces that the player who draws the Lucky Star gets a small gift the Storyteller prepared. Xiaobai draws the Lucky Star and hands it to the Storyteller, then draws again — the Fortune Teller. Xiaobai gets the gift.

The Storyteller announces that the player who draws the Lucky Star may get the character they want in the next game. Xiaobai draws the Lucky Star and hands it to the Storyteller, then draws again — the Fortune Teller. In the next game, Xiaobai gets the Tinker they wanted to play.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: A functional character prepared for Storytellers — for hosting events and warming up the atmosphere.

characters.name: Hell's Roulette
characters.ability: After nominating, a player rolls a 6-sided die: if its number already exists, they die, and all rolled dice are removed.
characters.lede: Nominating players bear a huge risk of death.
characters.quote: The rules are simple — take a deep breath, then pull the trigger.
summaryBullets: Hell's Roulette requires preparing 1 or 6 six-sided dice in advance.
If a player dies to Hell's Roulette after making a nomination, the nomination still proceeds normally.
If necessary, you can switch to dice with more or fewer faces based on player count.
howToRun: Whenever a player makes a nomination, that player must roll a 6-sided die into a designated container. If no other die in the container shows the same number, keep that die. If another die in the container shows the same number, remove all dice from the container — that player dies. The nomination still proceeds normally.
If you only have one die, the Storyteller records each rolled number. If a rolled number duplicates an already-recorded number, that player dies, and all records are cleared.
examples: On the first day, the Fortune Teller makes a nomination and rolls a 1. The Saint makes a nomination and rolls a 1 — the Saint dies. Remove these two dice.

On the first day, the Fortune Teller makes a nomination and rolls a 1. The Saint makes a nomination and rolls a 6. The Butler makes a nomination and rolls a 5. The Baron makes a nomination and rolls a 1 — the Baron dies. Remove these 4 dice.
With only one six-sided die, the Storyteller records the number each nominating player rolls. If a rolled number duplicates a recorded number, the nominating player dies, and the record is cleared.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A game-accelerating Loric character. Suitable for slower-paced scripts, or to speed up games featuring very large player counts. While reducing unnecessary nominations, it causes extra deaths — controlling nomination counts while causing 1–3 player deaths. Very effective at speeding up the game.

The dying players are player-controlled — avoiding the negative experience of important information or the Demon dying.

Incorporates tense, thrilling elements — stimulating players' senses and adding fun.

characters.name: Painter
characters.ability: On your 1st night, learn an in-play character. Each night, choose a player: if they are the character recently learned, learn another.
characters.lede: The Painter must guess which players are the characters they learn.
characters.quote: You all say to paint skin with 'flesh color,' but what flesh color is there? Your face holds the white of flour drifting from the mill next door; his carries the orange of the iron foundry; a child's cheeks are rose red with a dab of lemon yellow. Before I paint a person, I smell them, and mix my pigments by scent. The virtue of oils is that colors can be compounded fresh, like a prescription. When this face is done, you'll find the sitter by following the smell.
summaryBullets: If the Painter chooses a player who is not their most recently learned character, they are woken to choose again the next night as normal.
If, for any reason, the player whose character the Painter learned becomes a different character mid-game, the Painter still learns a new character upon choosing that player.
If the Painter is created mid-game, that night they learn an in-play character and are not asked to choose a player. From the next night on, the Painter chooses a player each night.
The Painter may learn Townsfolk or Outsider characters, and may also learn Minion or Demon characters—but never Travellers or other types.

Manage the Painter's power carefully: do not give them easily guessed characters several times in a row. From the Painter's second character onward, consider giving Minion or Demon characters, which are harder to guess, to keep their information in check.

If the Vortox is in play, or the Painter otherwise receives false information, a player is still marked "Most Recently Learned." As long as the Painter chooses that player, they learn a new character.
The Painter cannot learn Traveller characters (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: a character, e.g. Fortune Teller, Imp.
False information format: a character that is not in play.
howToRun: On the first night, wake the Painter and tell them an in-play character, and place the "Most Recently Learned" reminder by that character token.

Each night except the first, wake the Painter. They choose a player. If the Painter chose the player marked "Most Recently Learned," tell them a new in-play character and move the "Most Recently Learned" reminder to that player's character token. Put the Painter to sleep. If the Painter chose a different player, put the Painter to sleep.
examples: On the first night, the Painter learns the Noble. On the second night, the Painter chooses the Saint player; the Painter learns no new character. On the third night, the Painter chooses the Noble player and learns the Baron.

On the first night, the Painter learns the Noble. On the second night, the Painter chooses the Noble player and learns the Baron. On the third night, the Painter chooses the Baron player and learns the Imp.
tips: If you are the Painter, you can publicly hunt for your learned character early to chain into new characters quickly—but this is very dangerous, since it exposes you as the Painter and paints a target on your back.
If you are the Painter, you can lie low early. You may guess wrong once or twice, but given enough time, players will eventually reveal their characters publicly.
If you are the Demon, a player hunting for a specific character on the first day is very likely the Painter. If you don't want them snowballing information, attack them at night.
If you are the Demon, a Painter who survives to the late game may hold two, three, or more in-play characters—devastating for evil. If you find the Painter, deal with them early.
bluffing: The Painter is a solid bluff. You can use its ability to excuse never revealing your character. If you want to survive to the end, "confirm" one or two good players' characters so they trust you.

If you are a Minion unafraid of death, you can publicly claim to have learned several good characters—mixing your evil teammates among them to improve their odds of survival. Or go aggressive: claim your correct guesses were evil characters and accuse specific players. This is risky but high-reward: whether you are executed or your targets are, the Demon buys a great deal of time.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Tell them an in-play character, and place the 'Most Recently Learned' reminder by that player's character token.
characters.otherNightReminder: Let them choose a player. If they chose the player marked 'Most Recently Learned,' tell them a new in-play character.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Most Recently Learned]]
Placed when: While preparing the first night, and whenever the Painter guesses correctly.
Placed where: Beside a player's character token.
Removed/moved when: When the Painter leaves play or dies; moved when the Painter guesses correctly.

characters.name: Witcher
characters.ability: Once per game, at night*, choose a player: they die & the Demon cannot attack tonight. If you kill the Demon, swap characters & alignments.
characters.lede: The Witcher can strike in the Demon's stead.
characters.quote: Every Demon head I sever twists my shadow a little more. The townsfolk keep telling me to be careful not to get hurt, but they don't know—the real danger is hearing my own heartbeat grow more and more like Its. I've begun to like the taste of raw meat, to relish their screams as they flee. The hunt? It's just pressing my other self into the mud. When the day comes that I can't draw this sword and there's no light left in my eyes—find me, and kill me with it.
summaryBullets: Attack: when a player with a Demon ability, or the Storyteller, selects a player with the Demon's killing ability. Attacks usually kill an alive player; sometimes they don't, such as attacking a player who cannot die or a dead player. Cannot attack: a player with a Demon ability is woken for their ability, is told they cannot attack, and is put back to sleep.
As long as the Witcher successfully kills a player, the Demon cannot attack that night.

If the Witcher kills the Demon and becomes the new Demon, the new Demon is not restricted by the Witcher ability—because the original Witcher has left play and the current Witcher is dead—so they may kill normally that same night.
If the Witcher chooses a player but that player does not die (such as choosing a dead player or a protected player), the Demon may attack as normal.
Demon abilities unrelated to attacking still function normally and are unaffected by the Witcher.
If the Witcher chooses the Heiress and the Heiress's ability makes the Demon die in her place (not recommended), this counts as the Witcher having killed the Demon.

When the Po is told it cannot attack, this does not count as the Po "choosing no players." If the Po cannot attack on a night when it could have chosen 3 players, the Po may still choose 3 players the following night.
The Witcher cannot choose Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Witcher. The Witcher either shakes their head no or points at a player. If the Witcher chooses a non-Demon player who can die, place the "Dead" reminder by that player's character token. Tonight, wake the Demon as usual to make a choice, but shake your head to tell them they cannot attack, and put the Demon to sleep.

If the Witcher chose the Demon, and the Demon can die, place the "Dead" reminder by the Demon's character token. Then tell the Witcher that they have become the evil Demon, and put them to sleep. Then wake the Demon and tell them they have become the good Witcher. The new Demon wakes at their own point in the night order and may kill as normal.
examples: On the second night, the Witcher chooses the Widow; the Widow dies. The Imp is woken and learns that they cannot attack tonight.

On the second night, the Witcher chooses the Vortox. The Vortox dies and becomes the good Witcher, while the Witcher becomes the evil Vortox. That same night, the new Vortox chooses a player, who dies.
On the second night, the Witcher uses their ability and chooses the already-dead Widow. The Vortox chooses the Chambermaid. The Chambermaid dies.
tips: If you are the Witcher, your ability is extremely powerful: you can take over the Demon's shift for a night and kill anyone you wish. Choosing whom to kill is your first question—a suspected Minion? Or the Demon themself, to become every player's new nightmare?

If you are the Witcher, you can reveal early and kill a player everyone believes is evil, so the town trusts you really are the Witcher. But beware: if your target was the Demon, you become the new Demon—and since you already claimed Witcher, the old Demon will certainly expose you. That all but hands you a loss.

If you are the Witcher, you can hide your character until after you've used your ability and confirmed you didn't become the Demon, then reveal. Safer, but less convincing—any evil player can claim to be the Witcher who killed last night's victim.
If you are the Witcher, never choose a dead player: if you kill no one, your ability does nothing.
If you are the Demon and you spot the Witcher, kill them before they use their ability, so they can't interfere with your plans.

If you are the Demon and you want to win fast by any means, baiting the Witcher into killing you is a "clever" ploy: if they do, you—as a dead player—become extremely persuasive, and you can almost certainly rally the town to execute the new Demon tomorrow, winning quickly as good... though you'll have thrown your evil teammates away.

If you are the Demon, don't fear the Witcher too much. At most they cover your shift for one night. If you are the Po and you suspect the Witcher will act tonight, hold your blade—the Witcher's ability then accelerates the game in your favor.
bluffing: Have the Demon kill a player most of the town believes is evil, then step forward as the Witcher claiming you killed them. You will be highly credible.
characters.creator: Taiyi

characters.otherNightReminder: Wake them and let them choose a player; mark the chosen player with the 'Dead' reminder.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: After the Witcher acts at night and chooses a player.
Placed where: If the chosen player is alive, can be killed by the Witcher, and the Witcher is sober and healthy, place it by that player's character token, reminding the Storyteller to announce the night's dead at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead at dawn, at the Storyteller's convenience.

[[No Ability]]
Placed when: After the Witcher chooses to use their ability at night and chooses a player.
Placed where: Beside the Witcher's character token as long as they chose a player, whether or not the Witcher was drunk or poisoned.
Removed when: When the Witcher dies or leaves play.

characters.name: Constable
characters.ability: On your 1st night, learn an Outsider or Minion player. If you die at night, learn one of the other type. [+1 Outsider]
characters.lede: The Constable learns Minions and Outsiders.
characters.quote: Footprints. Mud stains. Scratches on the windowsill. Every detail you overlook speaks to me. I've worked one hundred and thirty-two cases and convicted ninety-seven people—not one wrongful verdict, not one that got away. You think you can be number one hundred and thirty-three? I'll be watching.
summaryBullets: Do not tell the Constable whether the learned player is a Minion or an Outsider—the Constable must work that out for themself.
If the Constable is due to learn a player of a type but no qualifying player is in play, wake the Constable and shake your head, meaning no qualifying player exists.

If the Vortox is in play, on the first night the Constable learns a Townsfolk or Demon player instead. If the Constable dies at night, they learn another Townsfolk or Demon player, of a different character type to the first—e.g. if they learned a Townsfolk on the first night, they learn a Demon upon death.
Information format: a player, e.g. Xiaomei, player 1.
False information format: a player who is neither a Minion nor an Outsider.
howToRun: During setup, before putting character tokens in the bag, replace one Townsfolk token with an Outsider token.

On the first night, wake the Constable and tell them a Minion or Outsider player. On the night the Constable dies, wake them and tell them a Minion or Outsider player (of a different character type to the player given on the first night, and still an Outsider or Minion player).
examples: Player 1 is the Baron, and player 2 is the Damsel. On the first night, the Constable learns player 1. On the second night, the Constable dies; they are woken and learn player 2.
Player 1 is the Saint, and player 2 is the Poisoner. On the first night, the Constable learns player 1. On the second night, the Constable dies; they are woken and learn player 2.
tips: If you are the Constable, you can reveal your learned player early and let everyone analyze whether they are the Minion or the Outsider.

If you are the Constable, you can stay hidden until you die at night. You will then know one Outsider and one Minion—crucial information. Whoever among them claims not to be an Outsider is almost certainly the Minion. Even if you can't tell which is which, neither of them is the Demon.
If you are the Demon, steer clear of the Constable. Attacking them is not a good idea.
If you are the Demon and you notice there seem to be more Outsiders than the default, watch out—a Constable is very likely in play.
bluffing: The Constable is not an easy bluff, because its ability adds an Outsider. You usually need a teammate to coordinate an Outsider claim with you, or your team must have its own Outsider-adding ability, before you can wear this disguise perfectly. Otherwise you'll quickly fall under suspicion when the Outsider count doesn't add up.
If you are a Minion, you can name the Demon as the player you learned. If the other players trust you enough, they'll conclude that player definitely isn't the Demon.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Tell them a Minion or Outsider character.
characters.otherNightReminder: If they died tonight, wake them and tell them a Minion or Outsider character (of a different type to last time).

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Knows]]
Placed when: While preparing the first night, or when the Constable enters play.
Placed where: Beside a Minion or Outsider player's character token.
Removed when: When the Constable dies or leaves play.

characters.name: Herald
characters.ability: Once per game, at night, choose another player: learn 2 players. All 3 of you are different character types. [+1 Outsider]
characters.lede: The Herald learns many players of differing character types.
characters.quote: This book records the heraldry of seventeen families of the town. When one house marries another's daughter, the crest gains a border. When a branch splits off, it gains a dividing line. When a house breeds a traitor, the whole shield is cloven in two—see this page. I do not paint patterns; I paint bloodlines. Every stroke is a covenant, every color block a verdict.
summaryBullets: The Herald cannot choose or learn themself, and does not learn duplicate players.
The Herald may choose or learn alive or dead players.
The chosen player and the two learned players must all be of different character types—the three players must cover three of the four types: Demon, Minion, Outsider, Townsfolk.
The Herald cannot choose or learn Travellers (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: 2 players, e.g. Xiaomei and Xiaozhang, or players 1 and 2.
False information format: 2 players, but among the chosen and learned players, several share one character type—e.g. Townsfolk-Townsfolk-Townsfolk, Townsfolk-Townsfolk-Outsider, Minion-Minion-Demon.
howToRun: During setup, before putting character tokens in the bag, replace one Townsfolk token with an Outsider token.

Each night, wake the Herald. They either shake their head no or point at another player. If they shake their head no, nothing happens; put the Herald to sleep. If they point at another player, tell them two players—these three players must all be of different character types. After the Herald uses their ability, mark them with the "No Ability" reminder. Do not wake them on future nights.
examples: Because the Herald is in play, there is one more Outsider than the default.
On the first night, the Herald chooses the Hatter player (an Outsider) and learns the Fortune Teller player (a Townsfolk) and the Poisoner player (a Minion).

On the first night, the Herald does not use their ability. On the second night, the Herald chooses the Poisoner player (a Minion) and learns the Imp player (the Demon) and the Saint player (an Outsider).
tips: If you are the Herald, among your three players there is usually at least one Demon or Minion—sometimes both!
If you are the Herald, share your information and work out quickly who among the three is the Townsfolk, the Outsider, the Minion, or the Demon!
If you are the Herald, since your ability adds an Outsider, finding out who that Outsider is matters enormously.
If you are the Herald and at least two of your three players claim to be Townsfolk or Outsiders, someone is lying!

If you are the Herald, you can wait a few days before using your ability. Risky—you might die in the meantime—but with time you'll understand the board: what everyone claims, who seems suspicious. You can then choose based on a confirmed Outsider or Townsfolk, making your information much stronger!
If you are the Herald, use your ability soon! You only get one chance, and if you die before using it, you'll never forgive yourself.
bluffing: Declare that three players are of three different character types—which means at least one of them is evil (a Minion or the Demon)! This sparks enormous discussion and redirects the town's attention.
Remember, the Herald's ability adds an Outsider, so bluffing as an Outsider usually requires a teammate to also claim Outsider.

If a teammate of yours is widely believed to be evil, you can pretend to have chosen them, then name another teammate (whom you're helping bluff as an Outsider) and a Townsfolk as your learned pair. This nicely supports that teammate's Outsider bluff.
Remember, the Herald cannot choose themself.
characters.creator: Taiyi, Aa
characters.firstNightReminder: Let them choose another player, then tell them two players.
characters.otherNightReminder: Let them choose another player, then tell them two players.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[No Ability]]
Placed when: After the Herald chooses to use their ability at night and chooses a player other than themself.
Placed where: Beside the Herald's character token as long as they chose another player, whether or not the Herald was drunk or poisoned.
Removed when: When the Herald dies or leaves play.

characters.name: Bard
characters.ability: Each day, publicly choose any players: Townsfolk among them are drunk until you choose again. Tonight, learn how many you made drunk.
characters.lede: The Bard can make Townsfolk drunk to learn how many Townsfolk there are.
characters.quote: Every soul my fingertips touch falls into dream. While you stagger in your cups, I count the trembling strings... three? five? Those numbers will tell me how many 'honest men' betray the shape of lies within their sweet dreams.
summaryBullets: The Bard learns the number of the Bard's "Drunk" reminders in play at the moment the information is given.
The Bard's drunkenness lasts from the moment the Bard publicly chooses until the next time the Bard publicly chooses.
The Bard may publicly choose only once per day.
If the Bard chooses themself, they are drunk until they publicly choose again, this choice makes no other player drunk, and you may give them false information.
A drunk or poisoned Bard cannot make Townsfolk drunk, and you may give them false information.
If the Bard becomes sober and healthy again mid-effect, the Townsfolk they chose that day immediately become drunk.
The Bard may only choose alive players. If a chosen Townsfolk dies at night, this does not affect the Bard counting them as drunk (alive/dead status and drunk status are independent).
If a Townsfolk drunk due to the Bard becomes a non-Townsfolk character, that player immediately becomes sober.
A player who was not a Townsfolk when publicly chosen by the Bard does not become drunk due to the Bard even if they later become a Townsfolk.
If a player who is not the Bard publicly claims to be the Bard during the day and chooses players, no player becomes drunk due to them even if they become the Bard that night.
The Bard cannot choose Travellers (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: a number, e.g. 1, 2, 3.
False information format: a number different from the actual number of players drunk due to the Bard.
howToRun: At any point during the day, the Bard may publicly choose any number of players. After the Bard chooses, place "Drunk" reminders by the Townsfolk they chose, and remove any previously placed "Drunk" reminders. Those players are drunk from now until the Bard publicly chooses again. At night, wake the Bard and tell them the number of "Drunk" reminders in play.
examples: On the first day, the Bard publicly chooses 3 players, 2 of whom are Townsfolk. Those 2 Townsfolk immediately become drunk. That night, the Bard is woken and learns a "2".

On the first day, the Bard publicly chooses 3 players, 2 of whom are Townsfolk, who immediately become drunk. That night, the Demon kills the Bard. Because the Bard died, the 2 Townsfolk become sober again and use their abilities normally that night.

On the first day, with the Vortox in play, the Bard publicly chooses 3 players, 2 of whom are Townsfolk, who immediately become drunk. That night, the Bard is woken and learns a "0". The next day, the Bard publicly chooses an Outsider; the 2 previously chosen Townsfolk become sober.

On the first day, the Witch claims to be the Bard and publicly chooses 3 Townsfolk. That night, the Witch turns themself into the Bard—but still nobody is drunk due to them, because they were not the Bard when they publicly claimed to be.

On the first day, the Bard publicly chooses the Gambler, who immediately becomes drunk. At night, the Gambler chooses the Leper Gnome and immediately becomes the Leper Gnome. Because the former Gambler is now a Minion, not a Townsfolk, they immediately become sober.
tips: If you are the Bard, talk to the players you intend to choose before choosing publicly, so you don't drunk an important Townsfolk. Or don't—but you may risk being executed on the spot.
If you are the Bard and you want to choose Townsfolk who act during the day (like the Fisherman), let them use their abilities first—otherwise your choice makes them drunk immediately.
If you are the Bard, encourage other players to also claim to be the Bard, so the Demon can't tell early who the real one is.
If you are the Bard, you can choose only Townsfolk who have already used their abilities—verifying they are Townsfolk without drunking anyone important.
If you are the Bard, you can choose only players claiming Outsider. If you learn they are Townsfolk, your information must be wrong.
If you are the Bard, never choose yourself—if you're drunk, your information becomes meaningless.
If you are the Bard, think carefully before choosing too many players. Drunking a crowd of Townsfolk is rarely good for the good team, and you'll struggle to tell which of them are Townsfolk.
bluffing: If you are a Minion ready to charge, recklessly publicly choose important Townsfolk. If they don't execute you, when they later share information you can argue it's drunk information and can't be trusted.
If you are the Demon, choose carefully and report believable information. This helps you survive to the late game.
You can claim Bard for the first few days, then pivot to another character if the bluff fails. Claiming Bard to help hide the real Bard is something good players often do—so it reads as good.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Tell them how many players are currently drunk due to their ability.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Drunk" ×5]]
Placed when: When the Bard publicly chooses.
Placed where: Beside the character tokens of chosen Townsfolk. Place this token even if the Bard is drunk or poisoned—you may place the Drunk reminders upside-down to remind yourself the drunkenness isn't actually in effect.
Removed when: When the Bard publicly chooses again, or when the Bard dies or leaves play.

characters.name: Aerialist
characters.ability: On the night you die, learn one player of each character type. If a good player's execution or ability killed you, you are drunk.
characters.lede: After dying, the Aerialist learns players of different character types.
characters.quote: Hahahaha! Can you smell it? The sulfur wind is tearing at my parachute! Listen! The rhythm of snapping shinbones beats any death metal! Among the audience my brains are about to splatter—the most embarrassed one is the Demon!
summaryBullets: If a character type has no players in play when the information is given, skip that type.

A "good player's ability" means the character ability held by a good player, whether that ability comes from an evil or a good character. It includes good evil characters (a good Imp), and excludes evil good characters (an evil Gossip).
If the Aerialist is nominated and executed due to the Sphinx's ability, this counts as being nominated and executed by the Sphinx.
The Aerialist's "all character types" does not include Travellers, and the Aerialist never learns Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: several players, e.g. players 1, 2, 3, 4 or Xiaomei, Xiaoshuai, Xiaozhang.

False information format: several players, but not one of every character type—e.g. Townsfolk-Townsfolk-Townsfolk-Outsider, Townsfolk-Outsider-Minion-Minion, or Townsfolk-Minion-Demon (when an Outsider is in play).
howToRun: When the Aerialist dies, if they died by an execution resulting from a good player's nomination, or by a good player's ability, place the "Drunk" reminder by their character token. That night, wake the Aerialist and tell them one player each of the Minion, Demon, Townsfolk, and Outsider types (skip any type with no players in play; provide only the types that exist). If they are marked "Drunk," you may give them true or false information.
examples: Player 1 (the Demon) nominates and executes the Aerialist. That night, the Aerialist is woken and learns player 1 (the Demon), player 2 (a Minion), player 3 (an Outsider), and player 4 (a Townsfolk).

Player 1 (a good Townsfolk) nominates and executes the Aerialist; the Aerialist is drunk. That night, the Aerialist is woken and learns player 1 (a Townsfolk), player 2 (a Townsfolk), player 3 (an Outsider), and player 4 (a Townsfolk).
There are no Outsiders in play. On the second night, the Demon kills the Aerialist. That night, the Aerialist is woken and learns one Demon, one Minion, and one Townsfolk player.
The Lycanthrope kills the Aerialist on the second night; the Aerialist is drunk. That night, the Aerialist is woken and learns four Townsfolk players.
tips: If you are the Aerialist, bluff as an important Townsfolk to bait the Demon into killing you at night.

If you are the Aerialist, and the town doesn't know whom to execute—or you're about to be executed anyway—reveal your character before nominations, choose a player you believe is evil, and ask them to nominate and execute you. Most players will support this, and good players will happily execute you. If they refuse, they are very likely evil.
If you are the Aerialist, you can hide your character and deliberately provoke a player you suspect into nominating and executing you. Catch them off guard.
If you are the Aerialist and you gained your information via execution, think hard about whether it is true or false.
If you are the Aerialist and you died at night, your information is very likely true.
If you are the Aerialist, analyze your information well and share it. Identify the most likely Demon and push for their execution.

If you are the Aerialist and the Vortox is in play, your information will be false—its only value is that it is definitely wrong. Think carefully: the Storyteller may have just ruled out a crucial possibility for you!
bluffing: The Aerialist works as a backup bluff. When your bluff as an important Townsfolk collapses, you can claim you were actually the Aerialist all along, confusing evil and baiting the Demon into killing you to help the good team.

If you are a less-important Minion, you can publicly claim Aerialist and ask a player (anyone—even a teammate) to nominate and execute you, then use your "information" to attack other players or protect your teammates.

characters.otherNightReminder: If they died, wake them and tell them one player each of the Minion, Demon, Townsfolk, and Outsider types.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Drunk]]
Placed when: When the Aerialist dies.
Placed where: When the Aerialist died by an execution resulting from a good player's nomination, or by a good player's ability. Place this token even if the Aerialist was already drunk or poisoned.
Removed when: When the Aerialist leaves play.

characters.name: Heiress
characters.ability: The 1st time you are about to die, 2 alive players might die instead of you.
characters.lede: Other players may die in the Heiress's place.
characters.quote: Call me 'my Lady,' not 'miss,' and certainly not 'girl.' Anyone can be a miss — there is only one Lady. My father has three hundred servants, fifty estates, and twelve titles — do you know which ones? No? Then hold your tongue and mind how you address me. 'My Lady' — that is the only thing you need remember.
summaryBullets: Trigger the Heiress's ability at fitting moments to keep the situation mysterious.

The players who die instead of the Heiress may be good or evil, but they cannot be already-dead players. As an Outsider, the Heiress's ability should generally harm the good team, so the Storyteller should carefully weigh whether to trigger the substitution and which players die.
A player cannot die instead of themself. So if you decide to trigger the Heiress's ability, the Heiress cannot be one of the two dead players.

Substitute players die as substitutes — the death is not caused by the Heiress. For example, if the Demon kills the Heiress at night and the Storyteller decides the Aerialist and another player die instead, treat it as the Demon killing the Aerialist, so the Aerialist gets correct information. Or if the Duke chooses the Heiress and the Storyteller decides the Plague Doctor and another player die instead, the Plague Doctor dies outright without triggering their ability — because in this context the Plague Doctor dies directly rather than being chosen (nobody chose the Plague Doctor, so naturally their ability doesn't trigger).
If an evil player nominates and executes the Heiress (or uses the Sphinx's ability), and the Storyteller decides the Aerialist dies instead, the Aerialist gets correct information.
It's not recommended to use the Heiress's ability to create complex, hard-to-understand situations.
The two substitute deaths technically have an order, decided by the Storyteller.
Traveller players never die instead of the Heiress (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: The first time the Heiress is about to die: if it is daytime, you may spare the Heiress from death and declare two other players dead. If it is nighttime, you may spare the Heiress from death, choose two other players, place the "Die Instead" reminder by their character tokens, and declare them dead at an appropriate time.
If players died instead of the Heiress, place the "No Ability" reminder by the Heiress's character token.
examples: On the first day, the Heiress is executed but does not die; the Saint and the Noble die.
On the first day, the Heiress is executed, and she dies.
On the second night, the Heiress is attacked by the Imp at night but does not die; the Baron and the Fortune Teller die.
tips: If you're the Heiress and don't want important Townsfolk dying early, don't reveal your character too soon — the Demon may well kill you, and the Storyteller may let important Townsfolk die in your place.

If you're the Heiress and want to prove your character, you can try accepting execution: if the Storyteller lets other players die instead of you, it confirms you're the Heiress. Though it may come at a heavy price — the deaths of important characters. Better others dead than me: as a noble Lady, what matters more than your vindication? Let the lowly ants die if they must.
If you're the Demon and you know who the Heiress is, attacking her may cause multiple players to die.
If you're the Demon and you attacked a player who didn't die while two others did, that player is very likely the Heiress.
bluffing: Publicly claiming to be the Heiress has a certain deterrent effect — people may not dare execute you, especially early in the game.

If several players died, you can step forward as the Heiress and suggest the multiple deaths might be your doing. This gives the night's many deaths a plausible explanation, keeping the good team from seeing the real cause.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.content:
[[Die Instead" ×2]]
Placed when: When the Heiress is about to die.
Condition: At night, if you decide to let other players die instead of the Heiress, place this reminder by the character tokens of the substitute players.
Removed when: The Heiress dies or leaves play.

[[No Ability]]
Placed when: When the Heiress is about to die.
Condition: If you let other players die instead of the Heiress, place this reminder by the Heiress's character token.
Removed when: The Heiress dies or leaves play.

characters.name: Sphinx
characters.ability: Each night, choose a character: tomorrow, if in play, they are publicly asked a yes/no question. A wrong answer might get them executed.
characters.lede: The Sphinx questions a specific character — a player who fails to answer correctly is executed.
characters.quote: The eyes of mortals are forever blinded by lies, but my gaze pierces every disguise. When fate's interrogation descends, only those who see the truth shall survive.
summaryBullets: If the Sphinx chose a character that isn't in play, nobody is questioned. If multiple players are the character the Sphinx chose, the Storyteller decides which of them is questioned.

The Sphinx's question can happen at any point in the day before an execution occurs; the exact timing is up to the Storyteller. It's recommended to question after all players have finished nominating — this lets the Storyteller better judge how to use the Sphinx's ability based on the vote counts.
The precondition for carrying out an execution is "did not answer correctly" — refusing to answer or otherwise refusing to cooperate also counts as "did not answer correctly."

If you decide to execute a player who didn't answer correctly, do it immediately when they answer wrong. After executing a player with the Sphinx's ability, you may tell the player "Unfortunately, you answered wrong — face the Sphinx's punishment," or another mood-setting line, to make clear they were executed by the Sphinx's ability.

If the player answered correctly, or you decide to spare a player who answered wrong, do not reveal in any form whether they answered correctly. You can say something like "You narrowly escaped, young one — you won't be so lucky next time."
Questions should revolve around in-game information. Try not to ask questions unrelated to the current game.
Before questioning, first ask all players to stay quiet. Other players may not blurt out answers, give hints, or interject during the questioning — players who do so are considered to be cheating.
If possible, communicate with the Sphinx appropriately and listen to his views on the question and whether to execute. If he has already designed a question, you can use it directly.

If a player answered wrong, should they be executed? Understand the following: 1) Using the Sphinx's ability to execute a player means an absolutely true piece of information is thrown out. In the vast majority of cases, you should not expose information unfavorable to the evil team — e.g. "Is player #1 the Demon?" The player answers no and is executed; this tells everyone the Demon is #1. 2) If executing would end the game that day, be careful — the Storyteller should keep the game going to the final day whenever possible. On the final day, if the evil team is ahead, even if the questioned player didn't answer correctly, it's best not to execute. If the evil team has been behind, and this question is the evil team's last chance to turn the game around, you may consider carrying out the execution to help evil achieve the reversal (answering wrong is, after all, the player's own responsibility). 3) Even without executing, the Sphinx's question can have a misleading effect — ask a question the good team is currently puzzling over, and even if the answer is wrong, don't execute, which may make the good team believe no execution happened because the answer was right. 4) If executing is more harmful than helpful to evil, best not to execute — e.g., executing an already-dead player while the Demon is still safe, or executing would expose information extremely unfavorable to evil. 5) If the evil team has a huge lead and the good team is clueless, you can also execute appropriately to leak some useful clues to the good team — but know when to stop.

Advanced techniques: 1) If the evil team urgently needs an execution, you can build questions around "good players' lies." For example, if the Fortune Teller is claiming to be the Soldier, you can ask "Is this player the Soldier?" Other players often answer wrong — this way you successfully execute, don't expose information unfavorable to evil, and increase the good team's suspicion of the Fortune Teller. 2) Whether you're questioning a good player or an evil player, your questioning style should stay consistent — no perceptible differences. If your style varies too much, it won't help evil players bluff and instead easily exposes your intent. 3) If you want to execute but don't want to expose information unfavorable to evil, ask detailed, easily-overlooked questions (e.g., whether certain players were or weren't all woken by their own abilities last night, whether more than 1 player was drunk or poisoned yesterday, whether all of three certain players are Townsfolk, etc.). 4) If players especially love to second-guess the Storyteller's psychology, you can use that psychology against them. For example, you often question around "good players' lies" (asking whether a player is the character they're claiming, when they often aren't). After a few executions, players will take for granted that the player in your question definitely isn't their claimed character. At that point, do the opposite — ask whether players who are claiming their real character are that character. Players will often answer wrong, and you can execute them with ease.
Jinx: When the Sphinx chooses the Damsel, the Damsel immediately loses her ability.
The Sphinx cannot choose Traveller characters (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night, wake the Sphinx and have him choose a character. If the character he chose is in play, place the "Question" reminder by that character. At any point the next day, you may first ask all players to stay quiet, then publicly ask the player with the "Question" reminder a yes-or-no question. If that player gives the correct answer, nothing happens. If that player does not give the correct answer, you may execute them immediately — or pretend nothing happened.
examples: On the first night, the Sphinx chooses the Slayer. The Slayer is not in play. The next day, nobody is questioned.

On the first night, the Sphinx chooses the Slayer, and the Slayer is Fangfang. The next day, after all nominations have ended, the Storyteller asks all players to stay quiet and asks Fangfang: "Is the Gambler in play?" Fangfang answers "yes." The Gambler is in play — nothing happens.

On the first night, the Sphinx chooses the Slayer, and the Slayer is Fangfang. The next day, after all nominations have ended, the Storyteller asks all players to stay quiet and asks Fangfang: "Is the Gambler in play?" Fangfang answers "yes." The Gambler is not in play, and the Storyteller decides Fangfang is executed immediately. The Storyteller then announces nightfall.

On the first night, the Sphinx chooses the Slayer, and the Slayer is Fangfang. The next day, before nominations begin, the Storyteller asks all players to stay quiet and asks Fangfang: "Is the Gambler in play?" Fangfang answers "yes." The Gambler is not in play, but the Storyteller decides not to execute Fangfang — nothing happens.

On the third night, the Sphinx chooses the Sphinx. The next day, after all nominations have ended, the Storyteller asks all players to stay quiet and asks the Sphinx: "Are you the Demon?" The Sphinx answers "yes" — the Sphinx is executed immediately. The Storyteller then announces nightfall.
tips: One of the Sphinx's uses is finding any character you want to find. If you deeply fear the Fortune Teller, choose the Fortune Teller — if nobody is questioned by the Storyteller the next day, the Fortune Teller isn't in play. If a player is questioned, that player must be the Fortune Teller.
Good players usually reveal their character after being questioned. Choosing your teammates' characters helps them bluff and makes them look more credible.
You can deliberately choose not-in-play characters at specific moments to pretend the Sphinx isn't in play or is already dead, confusing the good team.

If you'd rather the Storyteller execute after a questioned player answers wrong, you can signal the Storyteller at night or during the day — the Storyteller will take your opinion into account as much as possible (not absolutely).

If you've devised some brilliant questions, you can communicate with the Storyteller in any form during the day or night — the Storyteller will take your opinion into account as much as possible (not absolutely).
If you're a good player, best to reveal your character after being questioned by the Sphinx — the Sphinx already knows who is his chosen character based on who was questioned.
If you're a good player and you survived a questioning, your answer wasn't necessarily right. But conversely, if you were executed, you definitely answered wrong.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake the Sphinx and have him choose a character.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake the Sphinx and have him choose a character.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Question]]
Placed when: After the Sphinx chooses a character at night.
Condition: The character the Sphinx chose is in play.
Removed when: After the questioning is complete, or when the Sphinx dies or leaves play.

jinxes.name: Damsel
jinxes.text: When the Sphinx chooses the Damsel, the Damsel immediately loses her ability.

characters.name: Leper Gnome
characters.ability: A Townsfolk choosing you with their ability becomes the Leper Gnome. You lose all abilities. You win & lose with evil, even if dead.
characters.quote: Come here! Embrace me! What on earth are you afraid of!
summaryBullets: The Leper Gnome's ability may create multiple Leper Gnomes within one day (e.g., Townsfolk 2 chooses Leper 1 and becomes Leper 2; Townsfolk 3 chooses Leper 2 and becomes Leper 3; Townsfolk 4 chooses Leper 3 and becomes Leper 4).

A Townsfolk player who chooses the Leper Gnome with their own ability immediately becomes the Leper Gnome — they no longer receive information or use their ability normally (e.g., if the Witch Hunter chooses a sober and healthy Leper Gnome, the Witch Hunter becomes the Leper Gnome, and the Leper Gnome is not killed by the Witch Hunter — because before the Witch Hunter's ability takes effect, he is no longer the Witch Hunter).
Whether the choosing Townsfolk acts by day (the Minstrel) or by night (the Innkeeper, the Servant), as long as they choose the Leper Gnome, they immediately become the Leper Gnome.
Becoming the Leper Gnome only changes the character — it does not change the player's team.
After a Townsfolk player becomes a new Leper Gnome, the original Leper Gnome loses all abilities, including the ability "Your win condition is the same as the evil players', even if you are dead."
A Leper Gnome who has not lost all abilities due to his own ability keeps the ability "Your win condition is the same as the evil players'" even after death.
Do not tell the Leper Gnome whether he has lost his ability — he must judge for himself.
Special rule: a Leper Gnome created from a Townsfolk is not treated as a Minion by other characters' abilities (the Damsel, the Hatter, Cerberus).
howToRun: If a Townsfolk player chooses the Leper Gnome with their own ability — whether it's day or night at that moment — immediately replace that Townsfolk's character token with the Leper Gnome, then mark the chosen Leper Gnome with "No Ability". If it's night, tell the new Leper Gnome they became the Leper Gnome. If it's day, tell the new Leper Gnome they became the Leper Gnome at the earliest opportunity after nightfall.
When the game ends, a Leper Gnome who still has his ability wins or loses together with the evil team.
examples: On the first night, the Seamstress chooses the Leper Gnome; the Seamstress becomes the Leper Gnome, and the original Leper Gnome loses his ability. When the game ends, evil wins — the new Leper Gnome (the former Seamstress) also wins.

On the first day, the Minstrel publicly chooses several players including the Leper Gnome; the Minstrel becomes the Leper Gnome, and the original Leper Gnome loses his ability. When the game ends, good wins — the new Leper Gnome (the former Minstrel) loses due to his own ability.

On the second night, the Innkeeper chooses the original Leper Gnome; the Innkeeper becomes the Leper Gnome, and the original Leper Gnome loses his ability. Then the Seamstress chooses the Leper Gnome (the former Innkeeper); the Seamstress also becomes the Leper Gnome, and the Leper Gnome (the former Innkeeper) also loses his ability. Then the Servant chooses the Leper Gnome (the former Seamstress) and also becomes the Leper Gnome; the Leper Gnome (the former Seamstress) also loses his ability. When the game ends, evil wins — the Leper Gnome (the former Servant) also wins thanks to his ability. The Leper Gnome (the former Innkeeper) and the Leper Gnome (the former Seamstress) lose.
tips: If you're an evil Leper Gnome, do everything you can to lure other Townsfolk players into choosing you with their abilities! Spread your leprosy! That's how you realize your value!

If you're a good Leper Gnome, you need to understand this first — becoming the Leper Gnome doesn't change your team! You are still good. But the Leper Gnome's ability may require you to stand with the evil team.

If you became the Leper Gnome from a Townsfolk, now you must seriously consider who you should fight for. If you can be sure no other Townsfolk has chosen you — meaning you still have your ability — you can win together with evil through the Leper Gnome's ability. But if another Townsfolk has chosen you — that makes you lose your ability, and you still need to serve the good team! Unfortunately, you don't know whether you still have your ability. Think hard! Judge carefully!
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.tags: Character Change, Even If Dead, Loss Condition, Win Condition

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[No Ability]]
Placed when: When a Townsfolk player chooses the Leper Gnome with their own ability.
Condition: Place it by the chosen Leper Gnome's character token.
Removed when: The Leper Gnome leaves play.

characters.name: Cerberus
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a player: if they are evil, also choose another player. Your choices die. Minions you kill keep their ability.
characters.lede: Cerberus can kill Minions while preserving their abilities.
characters.quote: I gnaw upon your flesh, ferry your soul across, and then — wander with me at the gates of Hell.
summaryBullets: As long as Cerberus's chosen player is evil, he must choose again — this may repeat many times in one night until he chooses a good player. All chosen players are killed by him.

Only Minions killed by Cerberus keep their ability. If Cerberus chooses an already-dead Minion, they don't regain their ability. If Cerberus chooses a Minion but fails to kill him for some reason, and that Minion later dies from another cause, they don't keep their ability either.
A Minion killed by Cerberus keeps their ability. If their character type stops being Minion, they no longer keep their ability — even if they become a Minion again later.
If a player marked with "Ferry" is no longer a Minion, remove their "Ferry" reminder — Cerberus's ability-preservation effect no longer applies to that player.
Jinx: If Cerberus kills the Mastermind, the Mastermind keeps his ability even if Cerberus dies by execution.
Cerberus's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake Cerberus and have him choose a player. If the chosen player is good, place the "Dead" reminder by that player. If the chosen player is evil, signal Cerberus to choose again. Repeat until Cerberus chooses a good player. Place "Dead" reminders by all chosen players. Place "Ferry" reminders by the Minion players among them.
examples: On the second night, Cerberus chooses the Servant. The Servant dies.

On the second night, Cerberus chooses the Mastermind; the Storyteller signals Cerberus to choose again. Cerberus chooses the Servant. The Mastermind and the Servant die — the Mastermind, though dead, keeps his ability. The next day, Cerberus is executed, but the game continues because of the Mastermind's ability. The day after that, a good player is executed; the Mastermind's ability triggers — evil wins.

On the second night, Cerberus chooses the evil Ogre; the Storyteller signals Cerberus to choose again. Cerberus chooses the Godfather; the Storyteller signals Cerberus to choose again. Cerberus chooses the Servant. The Ogre, the Godfather, and the Servant die — the Godfather, though dead, keeps his ability.
tips: Your ability is crucial for the evil team — many tactics revolve around it. For example, creating extra deaths to help the evil team bluff as the Gambler, the Gossip, the Lady, or the Wish Fairy.
Killing Minions early preserves them from losing their abilities to death, ensuring important Minion abilities survive into the mid-to-late game.
Killing all Minions in one go late in the game to end it early is also a fine tactic.
If you're a good player: if Cerberus is in play, Minions may be among the players who die at night. Figure out who that Minion is and what abilities they've kept.

If you're a good player who suspects Cerberus is in play and you believe Cerberus hasn't killed his Minions, he's very likely secretly building up power, plotting to kill all Minions at once to end the game early. Find the Demon quickly — otherwise the game may suddenly end on a night with 5–6 alive players.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him and have him choose a player; if he chooses an evil player, have him keep choosing.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead" ×3]]
Placed when: After Cerberus acts at night and chooses players.
Condition: The player Cerberus chose is currently alive, can be killed by Cerberus, and Cerberus is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead players at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead players at dawn; the Storyteller may remove them at their convenience.

[[Ferry" ×2]]
Placed when: After Cerberus kills a Minion.
Condition: If a player successfully killed by Cerberus is a Minion character, place it by that player's character token.
Removed when: Cerberus dies or leaves play, or when the marked player's character is no longer a Minion.

jinxes.name: Mastermind
jinxes.text: If Cerberus kills the Mastermind, the Mastermind keeps his ability even if Cerberus dies by execution.

characters.name: Truelove
characters.ability: On your 1st day, you may have the Storyteller witness you swap characters with another player, then privately learn if anyone lied.
characters.lede: The Truelove learns whether another player is lying.
characters.quote: Your eyes are avoiding me. That's all right—take your time. Let me take out my true heart first so you can inspect the goods. Once you're satisfied it isn't fake, you can decide whether to take out yours. No need to decide now—I can wait. A true heart can't be rushed, and it can't be faked.
summaryBullets: "Exchange characters": two players telling each other their characters. Either may tell the truth or lie. You must "witness" the whole exchange, whether in public or in private.

"Privately learn": the Storyteller tells the Truelove without other players learning it. In a private setting with no other players, the Storyteller may say it directly. In a public setting, whisper it.

The Truelove detects whether the player lied, not their actual character. If the exchanging player is a character-misregistering character like the Doll or the Drunk, as long as they say the character they believe they are, they do not count as lying to the Truelove.
The Truelove's ability is unaffected by the Recluse or other characters' misregistration abilities, because misregistration cannot change whether a player "lied."
The Truelove's ability can be used only once.
Other players may refuse to exchange characters with the Truelove.
If the Truelove does not honestly state that their character is the "Truelove," then regardless of whether the other player lied, the result is "someone lied."
For a player who is not the Truelove but is bluffing as one, play along exactly as you would for a real Truelove.
The Truelove cannot exchange characters with Travellers (Traveller Exclusion Principle).

Information format: yes/no, or "someone lied" / "nobody lied"—just make sure the Truelove understands you. For an evil player bluffing as the Truelove, remind them how to phrase their result so they don't slip up.
False information format: the opposite result—"someone lied" becomes "nobody lied," and vice versa.
howToRun: On the Truelove's first day, the Truelove may invite the Storyteller to witness them exchanging characters with another player. Accompany them to the location the Truelove designates (it may be private or public). The Truelove and the other player each state their character, then you "secretly" tell the Truelove whether anyone lied. After the Truelove uses their ability, mark them with the "No Ability" reminder.
examples: On the first day, the Truelove invites the Storyteller into a small room to witness them and the Goblin player exchanging characters. The Truelove says they are the Truelove; the Goblin player says they are the Ascetic. After the Goblin player leaves, the Storyteller tells the Truelove "someone lied."

On the first day, the Vortox is in play. The Truelove invites the Storyteller to witness them and the Vortox player exchanging characters. In front of all players, the Truelove says they are the Truelove and the Vortox player says they are the Ascetic. The Storyteller then quietly whispers to the Truelove: "nobody lied."

On the first day, the Goblin player invites the Storyteller to witness them and the Ascetic player exchanging characters. In front of all players, the Goblin says they are the Truelove, and the Ascetic player says they are the Ascetic. The Storyteller then pretends to whisper something to the Goblin—while actually saying nothing at all.
tips: If you are the Truelove, publicly declare yourself on the first day and choose a suitable player for your ability. The town needs your information to form an initial guess about which Demon is in play.
If you are the Truelove, among players willing to visit the Storyteller with you, choose the more important characters—confirming them matters more to the town.

If you are the Truelove, clearly tell the other player they are taking part in your ability and get their consent first. Otherwise, if they refuse to cooperate once you've invited the Storyteller over, you've wasted your ability.
If you are the Truelove and you learn "someone lied," think hard about what went wrong: did your exchange partner deceive you, is the Demon this game a Vortox, or are you the Drunk?
If you are the Truelove and you learn "nobody lied," you can usually trust that your exchange partner is the character they claimed.

If you are the Truelove, remember your ability detects lying, not true characters: a player who believes they are a character but is actually the Drunk or the Doll counts as not lying if they tell you what they believe—so you cannot identify the Drunk or the Doll.
If you are an evil player, think twice before accepting the Truelove's invitation. If the Truelove learns you lied, you'll fall under immediate suspicion.
If you are an evil player and you know the Truelove is drunk or poisoned, or a character like the Vortox is in play, you can exchange characters with the Truelove boldly and safely.
bluffing: If you are a Minion, you can claim Truelove and coax as many players as possible into revealing their characters, gathering information to report to the Demon so they can prioritize killing the more important players at night.

If you are the Goblin or the Baron, you can play aggressively: announce that someone lied—attack your exchange partner outright, or make the town believe the Demon is a Vortox. This does raise your risk of execution, of course.
If you are the Demon or the Scarlet Woman, play it safe: announce that nobody lied, earning the town's approval and trust.
