characters.otherNightReminder: If an Ettin died today, the other Ettin dies too.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Die Tonight]]
Placed when: When an Ettin dies due to the Ettin's ability.
Condition: If an Ettin died today, place this reminder for all other Ettins to remind the Storyteller to kill the Ettins at night.
Removed when: After announcing the dead players at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

jinxes.name: Hell's Outcast
jinxes.text: If the total number of evil players in play already exceeds the initial setup by one (not counting evil Travellers), the Hellspawn's ability "you immediately turn evil and swap characters with the Demon" is changed to "you immediately swap characters and teams with the Demon".

characters.name: Archlich
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. Each dead player, when first chosen by you, chooses 2 players: they die.
characters.lede: The Archlich infuses corpses with energy, granting them mighty killing power.
characters.quote: I hear it. The unwillingness toward death in your soul, the hunger for power. The world fears you — but I admire you. Accept this gift. Your corpse shall become my first masterpiece; your will shall become the law that judges all living things. Breathe — this sweet terror... it shall be the first meal of your rebirth.
summaryBullets: Each player can trigger the Archlich's ability at most once, so the Archlich can't trigger the ability multiple times by repeatedly choosing the same dead player — even if that dead player is resurrected and dies again.

All Archliches and players with the Archlich's ability share the dead players' quota, even if the original Archlich dies or leaves play. So even if a new Archlich enters play, they cannot trigger the Archlich ability again on a dead player who already triggered it. For example: the Chimera can't repeatedly trigger the ability on the same dead player by repeatedly gaining the Archlich's ability; a Hellspawn turned into a new Archlich also can't re-trigger the ability on a dead player who already triggered it. If a player attempts this, remind them.

The Archlich may first choose an alive player and kill them, then choose that same player now dead — the ability still triggers, because this is the first time that player is chosen by the Archlich while dead.
Players who die from the choices of a dead player chosen by the Archlich are also treated as killed by the Archlich — but they aren't treated as "chosen by the Archlich's ability for the first time".
Don Quixote only affects Townsfolk abilities, so he can't affect the Archlich ability's judgment of whether a player is the Demon.
If the Archlich is drunk or poisoned, a dead player he chose is not woken.
The Archlich's ability cannot choose Traveller players, and a dead player chosen by the Archlich cannot choose Traveller players either (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Archlich. Have the Archlich point to any player. Put the Archlich back to sleep. If he chose an alive player, mark them "Dead". If he chose a dead player and that player doesn't have a "Triggered" reminder, wake them and show them in turn the "This character's ability applies to you" info token and the Archlich's character token, place the "Triggered" reminder by their character token, then have them choose two players — mark those two players "Dead".
At dawn, announce which players died during the night.
examples: On the second night, the Archlich chooses the alive Poisoner — the Poisoner dies. The next night, the Archlich chooses the dead Poisoner; the Poisoner chooses the Noble and the Fortune Teller — the Noble and the Fortune Teller die.

On the second night, the Archlich chooses the dead Poisoner; the Poisoner chooses the Noble and the Fortune Teller — they die. The next day, the Poisoner publicly supports the Hellspawn; the Hellspawn swaps characters with the Archlich and becomes the new Archlich. That night, the new Archlich chooses the dead Poisoner — nobody dies that night, because each player can only trigger the Archlich's ability once, no matter which Archlich it is.

On the first day, the Noble dies by execution. That night, the Archlich chooses the dead Noble; the Noble chooses the Poisoner and the Archlich — the Poisoner and the Archlich die. The game ends. The good team wins.

On the first day, the Noble dies by execution. That night, the Archlich chooses the dead Noble; the Noble chooses two dead players — nobody dies. The next night, the Archlich chooses the dead Noble again; the Noble is not woken, because each player can only trigger the Archlich's ability once.
tips: As the Archlich, you must learn to make use of corpses. If you only choose alive players and never dead ones, you're just an ordinary Demon with no special ability. Every dead player is your material — think about how to use corpses to paint a beautiful killing masterpiece.
Choosing dead evil players is a smart choice — they'll kill from your standpoint as much as possible and won't proactively reveal your existence — but dead evil players are always limited in number.

Dead good players are inexhaustible; you can hardly choose them all. But choosing dead good players may come with costs. First, the good team learns of your existence — a good player chosen by you will almost certainly publicly announce they were chosen by the Archlich. Second, they may choose players you'd rather not choose — such as evil players or dead players. They might even kill you outright. So unless you have a particularly wicked complete plan, best choose dead good players with caution.

If you suspect multiple players' deaths in play were caused by the Archlich and no player claims to have been touched by the Archlich, then evil players must be among the previous dead — most likely players who died by execution!

Don't firmly believe dead players who claim they were chosen by the Archlich. Evil players can deliberately use this tactic to lead the good team into misjudging the Demon type — or to lead you into executing a good player.

If you're a dead good player and you're woken by the Archlich's ability tonight, best make your choices carefully. Whether to choose 2 dead players to avoid unnecessary deaths as much as possible, or to choose the players you believe are evil to cut down the evil count — it's all up to you.
If you're a dead good player chosen by the Archlich, make your choices the players you suspect of being the Archlich! Let the audacious Demon reap what he sowed!
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead" ×2]]
Placed when: After the Archlich, or a dead player chosen by the Archlich, acts at night and chooses players.
Condition: If the player the Archlich chose is currently alive, can be killed by the Archlich, and the Archlich is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token. For players chosen by a dead player marked "Triggered": place it by the character tokens of those among the two chosen players who are currently alive and can be killed by the Archlich.
Removed when: After announcing the dead players at dawn; the Storyteller may remove them at their convenience.

[[Triggered" ×3]]
Placed when: After the Archlich acts at night and chooses a dead player.
Condition: If the dead player the Archlich chose doesn't have a "Triggered" reminder, place it by that player's character token.
Removed when: This reminder is never removed for any reason.

characters.callout: Each player can trigger the Archlich's ability at most once. The [[TRIGGERED]] token is never removed for any reason. All Archliches and players with the Archlich's ability share a single pool of already-triggered dead players — even if the original Archlich dies or is replaced.
fighting: If multiple deaths seem Archlich-caused but no player has claimed to have been chosen, at least one previously dead player must be evil — most likely one who died by execution.
If a player claims they were chosen by the Archlich and the living player they chose did not die, that player who didn't die is almost certainly the Demon.

Do not blindly trust dead players who claim they were chosen by the Archlich. Evil players can use this tactic to steer the good team into incorrect assumptions or lead the town to execute a good player.

If you are a dead good player woken by the Archlich, choose carefully. You could pick 2 dead players to minimise further deaths, or choose players you believe to be evil to reduce the evil team's numbers. The choice is yours.
If you were previously woken by the Archlich and the living player you chose did not die, that player is almost certainly the Demon. Announce this publicly.

characters.name: Hydra
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. If you are executed before the final day, a good & an evil player become the Hydra.
characters.lede: Execution makes the Hydra "split and multiply".
characters.quote: What you call 'the end' is nothing but life's basest, laughable illusion. My existence is life's own blind, greedy, endlessly replicating ugly truth. Execution? When every corner of your town writhes with my form, you will finally understand — you were never slaying a Demon; you were only helping me... evolve.
summaryBullets: "The final day": the first day of the game with fewer than 5 alive players (not counting Travellers). On the final day, the Storyteller publicly announces at the earliest opportunity that today is the final day. A game has at most one "final day" — if the game doesn't end on the final day, later days with fewer than 5 alive players are not treated as the "final day". If the game ends early (e.g. special victory or the Demon's death), that game may have no "final day". Before the final day arrives: the game period before the final day comes. When the final day arrives: the moment the final day comes (usually the first dawn with fewer than 5 alive non-Traveller players). After the final day arrives: the final day and the game period after it.

Attention!! The Hydra is a unique Demon requiring heavy Storyteller involvement — if the Storyteller or players misunderstand the Hydra's ability, the game experience may be terrible. Storytellers, carefully review the following points and brief the players in advance: 1) Becoming the Hydra only changes the character, not the team — players still serve their original team. 2) As long as a Demon is alive — even a good Demon — the good team cannot win. 3) A good Hydra being executed also makes 2 players become Hydras. The Storyteller must brief players on these points in advance, especially in games with new players — otherwise players easily misunderstand, leading the good team to make wrong judgments.

The Hydra is a Demon the Storyteller must firmly control based on the situation (similar to the Shabaloth). Turning two alive players into Hydras at an inappropriate time puts the good team in a no-win position. For example: with only 5 alive players left, the Hydra is executed, and the Storyteller turns two alive players into Hydras (one evil, one good) — after nightfall, 2 of the 4 players are Demons; unless one Demon kills the other and nobody else dies that night, the good team is certain to lose, because at least one of the remaining 2 players is a Demon. So Storytellers, remember: never use the Hydra's ability in a way that puts good in a no-win position.

If the Hydra dies by execution: in the early-to-mid game, it's recommended to choose 2 alive players to become Hydras (one evil, one good). In the mid-to-late game, it's recommended to turn an alive evil player into the Hydra and a dead good player into the Hydra — this both extends the game, keeping a Demon alive, and informs the good team that the Demon's position has moved. Of course, the final decision rests with the Storyteller — making the game more interesting is the most important consideration, so adapt freely to the actual situation.

If the Hydra dies by execution before the final day and he was the only alive evil player, it's not recommended to turn an alive good player into the Hydra to force the game to continue — in this case, just turn 2 dead players into Hydras and announce the game is over.

If multiple alive Hydras exist, the Storyteller decides the waking order. Generally the evil Hydra acts first, with the good Hydra right after. If you as the Storyteller have a more interesting idea, handle it your own way.
Traveller players cannot become the Hydra, and the Hydra's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Hydra. Have the Hydra point to any player. Put the Hydra back to sleep. The chosen player dies — place the Hydra's "Dead" reminder by that player's character token. If multiple alive Hydras are in play, the Storyteller decides the waking order. If the Hydra dies by execution and the final day hasn't arrived yet, choose one good player and one evil player (alive or dead), replace their character tokens with the Hydra (or mark them with "Is Hydra"), then at the earliest opportunity after nightfall, wake these players and tell them their new character.
examples: On the game's first day, the Hydra dies by execution; the Fortune Teller becomes the Hydra (good), and the Baron becomes the Hydra (evil). That night, each of them kills a player.
With 5 players left alive, the Hydra dies by execution; the dead Noble becomes the Hydra (a dead, good Hydra), and the alive Baron becomes the Hydra (an alive, evil Hydra).
On the final day, the Hydra dies by execution — the game ends, and the good team wins.
tips: If you're the Hydra — a Demon with unmatched survivability — you don't fear death much. You can boldly attack other players or do other high-risk things. So what if you get executed? As long as the evil team still has anyone alive, the game won't end.

If you're an alive evil player told you've become the Hydra, a good player in play has definitely also become the Hydra — though whether they're now dead or alive is unknown. Generally a dead Hydra poses little threat — they only tell everyone their character changed. But an alive good Hydra is a huge unstable factor — they might kill other good players, your teammates, even you. Whether to let them rampage to help end the game sooner, or to kill them quickly to remove the unstable factor, is up to you based on the situation.

If you're a dead evil player, claiming at the right moment that you became the Hydra is a very interesting tactic. Good players can't tell if you're telling the truth — if they choose to believe you, that means they accept that yesterday's executed player was the Hydra, leading good players into wrong judgments or even defeat.

If you're an alive evil player, you can also claim at the right moment that you were turned into the Hydra. This means you need to explain whom you chose last night as the Hydra — prepare your story in advance. The good team may demand you kill yourself at night; if you keep not dying, they can hardly keep believing you.

If you're an alive good player told you've become the Hydra — how interesting. You can kill yourself that night and tell everyone immediately at dawn — this neither adds chaos to the situation nor hides that yesterday's executed player was the Hydra. Of course, you can also keep quiet and secretly kill any player you want at night. Just remember to kill yourself before the final day — otherwise, because of your existence, the good team can't win. Please don't try to execute yourself — that would spawn even more Hydras.

If you're a dead good player told you've become the Hydra, best tell everyone about your change immediately at dawn — the Demon having moved is important information. Also, the Storyteller choosing a dead good player to become the Hydra may mean the game is nearly over — the good team is running out of time.

If an alive player claims they're good and became the Hydra, executing them may not be a good idea — executing a Hydra outside the final day triggers their splitting ability, even if the executed Hydra is good. A better approach: have them kill themselves at night before evil wins, because as long as a Demon is alive, the good team can't win.

In the vast majority of cases, only by executing the Hydra on the final day can the good team win immediately. But that doesn't mean executing the Hydra early is a bad idea — the good team might get an alive good Demon! That's a huge temptation — the good team can kill any player it wants. So if you find the Hydra early in the game, executing her immediately or saving him for the final day are both viable choices.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a player.

characters.name: Chimera
characters.ability: Each night*, gain the ability of a non-Chimera Demon, different to your last 2 choices, until dusk. [-1 Outsider]
characters.lede: The mighty hybrid Chimera can use the abilities of all other Demons in the script.
characters.quote: Three heads, six eyes — all watching you. My lion fangs crave your throat, my goat horns aim at your heart, my serpent's venom is ready on my tongue. Still standing there trembling? Good — I don't like prey that falls too quickly. Struggle, and give all three of my heads something to do.
summaryBullets: A simplified description of the Chimera's ability acquisition order: if the script contains the Chimera and 3 other Demons — 1, 2, 3 — then on the game's second night the Chimera may choose any of 1, 2, 3; suppose he chooses 1. On the third night he may choose 2 or 3; suppose he chooses 2. On the fourth night he can only choose 3 (the cycle is now fixed). On the fifth night he can only choose 1. On the sixth night he can only choose 2. And so on.

Because the Chimera only briefly holds other Demons' abilities, note that some abilities won't fully play out — for example, Townsfolk information is only wrong on the day the Chimera chose the Vortox.
A Chimera with the Hydra's ability who dies by execution outside the final day causes a good player and an evil player to become the Hydra — not the Chimera. Take note.
howToRun: During initial setup, before putting character tokens into the bag, replace one Outsider character token with one Townsfolk character token. (If there's no Outsider token that can be removed, don't add a Townsfolk token.)

Each night except the first, wake the Chimera and have him choose a Demon character; this choice must differ from both of his previous two choices. If his choice repeats either of the previous two, shake your head and have him choose again. Once a Demon character is chosen, wake him at that Demon's point in the night order that night and have him act.
examples: On the 2nd night, the Chimera chooses the Vortox — all Townsfolk information is wrong that night. On the 3rd night, the Chimera chooses the Archlich; that night he chooses a dead Minion, who chooses 2 other players and causes their deaths. On the 4th night, the Chimera chooses the Hydra; after dawn he is executed — a good player and an evil player become Hydras.

On the 2nd night, the Chimera chooses the Vortox. On the 3rd night, the Chimera wants to choose the Vortox again, but his choice must differ from both previous two — so he chooses the Archlich. On the 4th night, the Chimera wants to choose the Archlich, but his choice must differ from both previous two — so he can only choose the Hydra. On the 5th night, the Chimera can only choose the Vortox. On the 6th night, the Chimera can only choose the Archlich.
Because the Chimera is in play, there is one fewer Outsider than default.
tips: The Chimera is extremely powerful — he can use the abilities of all other Demons in the script. But he can only hold one ability per day, and once the Chimera's ability cycle is fixed it can't be changed — think carefully about how to properly choose and use your abilities.
If you foresee you'll be executed tomorrow, choosing the Hydra's ability that night is an excellent move — it helps the Demon line continue.
Because of your existence, there's one fewer Outsider than default — so whether to have a teammate claim to be an Outsider is a very important decision.

If you're a good player: assuming the Demon is the Chimera, then among nights two through four, the Chimera must have chosen the Vortox on one night — meaning on some night all Townsfolk information is guaranteed wrong. If Townsfolk information suddenly goes wrong collectively on some night, consider the Chimera as the in-play Demon.

Once formed, the Chimera's ability cycle is fixed. If you can confirm the Chimera chose the Vortox ability on the second night, then on the fifth and eighth nights the Chimera can only choose the Vortox ability. (Unless the Demon's position changed due to the Hellspawn — the Chimera re-entering play resets the cycle.)
If you're a good player and you find the Outsider count in play is one below default, the in-play Demon is very likely the Chimera.
If the Chimera and the Cyclops are both in play, the Outsider count doesn't decrease. You can't conclude the Demon isn't the Chimera just because the Outsider count is correct.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a Demon character other than the Chimera.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Is Chimera]]
Placed when: When the Chimera gains another Demon's ability.
Condition: When the Chimera chooses a Demon character, replace the Chimera's character token with the Demon character he chose and place the "Is Chimera" reminder. If that Demon character is in play, instead place "Is Chimera" by that player's character token, keeping the Chimera's token.
Removed when: This reminder is never removed for any reason.

characters.name: Hanged Man
characters.ability: When the game ends, if you voted with your vote token, whoever wins, loses & whoever loses, wins.
characters.lede: The Hanged Man can reverse the outcome after his death.
characters.quote: Habit teaches you to look downward; I hang upside down to teach you to look upward. When the blood rushes to your brain, common sense turns inside out. Once you learn to see the world inverted, the world gives you a new perspective.
summaryBullets: Vote token: the voting indicator a player gains upon death. A dead player gains one vote token and may only vote by using it. Whether each player has vote tokens, and how many, is public knowledge.

Using a vote token: the act of a dead player voting by spending their vote token. Losing a vote token through non-voting means does not count as using it. This act is public and visible to all players.
The Hanged Man has no ability before death.
The Hanged Man's ability triggers when the game ends, not when he votes with his vote token.
The Hanged Man's ability is designed for after death, so he does not lose his ability by dying — even though his ability text contains no "keep/gain ability after death" wording.

Normally each player gets only one vote after death (one vote token). If for some special reason (such as certain Fabled) the Hanged Man uses two vote tokens, his ability does not trigger twice to "reverse the reversal."
Resolve the Hanged Man's ability before the Skeleton King's, because before the Hanged Man's ability takes effect, the Skeleton King has not "won."
If several Hanged Man abilities are in effect at once, the result is reversed once for each ability.
As long as the Hanged Man is not poisoned or drunk when the game ends, his ability works normally — even if he was poisoned or drunk when he used his vote token.
Jinx: Puck cannot turn an evil player into the Hanged Man. If Puck creates an evil Philosopher who chooses the Hanged Man, that Philosopher immediately loses their ability.
howToRun: When the game ends, if the Hanged Man voted with his vote token this game, declare that the team that should have won loses, and the team that should have lost wins.
examples: The only Demon dies by execution; the game ends and good wins. Since the Hanged Man voted with his vote token that day, the result is reversed — evil wins.
A player dies by execution, leaving two alive players including the Demon; the game ends and evil wins. Since the Hanged Man previously voted with his vote token, the result is reversed — good wins.
The only Demon kills themself; the game ends and good wins. Since the Hanged Man previously voted with his vote token, the result is reversed — evil wins.
tips: If you're the Hanged Man, don't reveal your true character lightly. If evil learns you're the Hanged Man, they can watch whether you've used your vote token to shape their voting and killing strategy.

If you're the Hanged Man, you don't fear death — you should actively seek it. Only dead do you have an ability. You can bluff as an important character, hoping the Demon kills you at night: you get your death without wasting an execution.
If you're the Hanged Man and the player you believe is the Demon is about to be executed, don't use your vote token. Otherwise you'll very likely sabotage your own team.

If you're the Hanged Man and you've already spent your vote token, your job from then on is "make evil win" — by any means, such as rallying everyone to execute the remaining good players. But don't be too obvious: once the Demon learns your ability has triggered, they may kill themself to end the game.
If you're a good player, after death you can claim to be the Hanged Man and spend your vote token. With good enough acting, the Demon may be fooled into killing themself.
If you're the Demon, until a good player has used a vote token, the Hanged Man's ability definitely hasn't triggered. Don't worry about the Hanged Man too much.

If you're the Demon and think the Hanged Man might be in play, find him quickly and watch his death and voting closely. If he uses his vote token, "kill yourself" as soon as possible — by execution or any other means.

If you're the Demon with only four alive players including you, and you believe the Hanged Man has used his vote token, find a way to get yourself executed. If they execute another player instead, kill yourself after nightfall — then you win immediately via the Hanged Man's ability.

If you're the Demon with only three alive players including you, and you believe the Hanged Man has used his vote token, do everything you can to die by execution today. Once they execute another alive player, you instantly "win" from "only two players alive" — but since the Hanged Man's ability has triggered, you lose instead.
bluffing: If you're a Minion, you can bluff as the Hanged Man after death. On the final day, urge everyone to execute good players "to trigger the Hanged Man's ability." Of course, there is no Hanged Man, so you win by the Demon surviving to the end.

If you realize the Hanged Man's ability has triggered and the situation is spiraling out of control, you can claim that you are the Hanged Man. Since your ability hasn't triggered, the result won't reverse — use this to steer players into executing whoever you want.

The Hanged Man works as a backup bluff after your first bluff fails. The Hanged Man rarely reveals himself, so it's fairly feasible: in the mid-to-late game, especially on the final day, you can claim you were the Hanged Man all along and steer players toward the wrong execution.

characters.name: Joker
characters.ability: Each night, choose another player: you learn their suit. The 4 suits secretly correspond to the 4 character types.
characters.lede: The Joker can probe other players' card suits, but the meaning of the suits must be cracked.
characters.quote: I hear the spades conspiring, the hearts trembling, the clubs snickering, the diamonds standing firm. Don't be nervous — I'm just a harmless clown.
summaryBullets: The suit-to-character-type mapping in the Joker's ability is not fixed; it is decided by the Storyteller.
When first giving the Joker information, you must determine which character types the four suits correspond to, and this cannot be changed arbitrarily during the game.
If several Jokers or players with the Joker ability appear in a game, each has an independent suit mapping — they may be the same or different.
The Joker cannot choose Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades.

False information format: a suit that does not correspond to the chosen player. For example: if Demons correspond to diamonds in the Joker's ability and the Joker chose the Demon, false information is spades/hearts/clubs.
howToRun: When the Joker enters play, determine which character types the four suits correspond to in this Joker's ability; this cannot be changed arbitrarily during the game.
Each night, wake the Joker. Let them point at any player other than themself. Then show the Joker the suit (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades) corresponding to that player's character type.
examples: On the first night, the Joker chooses the Imp and learns diamonds. On the second night, the Joker chooses the Exorcist and learns spades. On the third night, the Joker chooses the Washerwoman and learns spades. This game, in this Joker's ability, spades correspond to Townsfolk, hearts to Outsiders, clubs to Minions, and diamonds to Demons.

On the first night, the Joker chooses the Saint and learns hearts. On the second night, the Joker chooses the Butler and learns hearts. On the third night, the Joker chooses the Widow and learns spades. On the fourth night, the Joker chooses the Baron and learns spades. This game, in this Joker's ability, spades correspond to Minions, hearts to Outsiders, clubs to Demons, and diamonds to Townsfolk.
tips: Do everything you can to figure out what your four suits represent — discuss it with everyone, or use other players' information as corroboration.
If two players you learned have different suits but both claim to be Townsfolk, at least one of them is not a Townsfolk! Maybe neither is!
If you've learned all four different suits, one of them is definitely the Demon!

If you've already checked two players claiming to be Townsfolk and they share a suit, be doubly vigilant about later players of a different suit claiming Townsfolk — they're very likely not Townsfolk! Of course, there's a tiny chance the first two are both Minions, which would also give them the same suit.
With only one night of information, your info is useless. Whatever happens, survive to the second night.

Early on, your information is worth little or nothing. But its value grows over time. If you survive to the mid-to-late game having cracked your suits, your information becomes decisive. Staying alive is your first goal.
If you're an evil player, you can bluff as an Outsider and steer the Joker into choosing you — this will badly confuse his attempts to decode his information.

If you're the Demon, the Joker is your number-one target. The longer he lives, the more threatening his information. Once his info clicks together, it hugely helps good map the game. You don't want him alive at the end — deal with him quickly.
bluffing: Before weaving your story, talk first with the players who seem good, gathering the identity claims they've made publicly or privately. Use this intelligence to construct your narrative so your "information" slots cleverly into the existing identity landscape, greatly boosting its credibility.

Keenly observe the trust chains inside the good team. A clever move: target your "checks" at players who already distrust each other. For example, if you notice someone strongly questioning another's identity, include both in your "information" report. This effectively inflames their existing conflict, plunging them into mutual accusations and creating room for you to survive.

Absolutely do not rush to publish your "intelligence" early in the game. At the start you hold almost zero information; the more you say, the more you slip. The hardest part of this bluff is the early game. Patiently observe for a few days, then gradually release your carefully scripted "information" once the board is clearer. Absolute accuracy isn't the priority — the key is that your logic must fit the current situation and sound reasonable.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake him to choose another player, and tell him that player's suit.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him to choose another player, and tell him that player's suit.

customBoxes.content:
[[Hearts" / "Diamonds" / "Spades" / "Clubs]]
Placed when: At any time.
Condition: For the Storyteller's own reminder use only.
Removed when: At any time.

characters.name: Mummy
characters.ability: If you die by an execution an evil player nominated, or from an evil player's ability, you rise on the final day.
characters.lede: If the Mummy dies at evil hands, he rises on the final day.
characters.quote: Anubis weighed my soul and granted me return to the mortal world. Beneath my shroud there is no selfishness — only the cold answers I brought back from the underworld.
summaryBullets: "The final day": the first day on which fewer than 5 players are alive (Travellers not counted). On the final day, the Storyteller publicly announces at the first opportunity that today is the final day. A game has at most one "final day"; if the game doesn't end on the final day, later days with fewer than 5 alive players are not treated as the "final day". If the game ends early (e.g., a special victory or the Demon's death), the game may have no "final day" at all. Before the final day arrives: the period before the final day. When the final day arrives: the moment the final day begins (usually the first dawn with fewer than 5 non-Traveller alive players). After the final day arrives: the final day and everything after.
Rising from death: a dead player becoming alive again. Life and death are public; the Storyteller publicly announces which player rose.
If the Mummy dies from a nomination-execution started by a good player or from a good player's ability, the Mummy does not rise.
The Mummy rises at most once per game (there is at most one "final day").
If the Mummy had not used or given up his vote token when he died, he loses the vote token he previously received after rising.
Traveller players are not treated as evil players by the Mummy's ability: if an evil Traveller nominates and executes the Mummy, the Mummy does not rise (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: When the Mummy dies, if he died from an ability owned by an evil player or from a nomination-execution started by an evil player, place the "Awaiting Revival" reminder by the Mummy's character token.
Immediately after announcing that the final day has arrived, if the Mummy is dead and marked "Awaiting Revival," remove the Mummy's shroud token and announce that the Mummy rises.
examples: On the first day, the Mummy dies from a nomination started by the Demon. On the final day, the Storyteller announces the Mummy rises.
On the first day, the Mummy dies from a nomination started by a good player. This game, the Mummy's rising ability never triggers.
On the second night, the Demon kills the Mummy. On the final day, the Storyteller announces the Mummy rises.
On the second night, the Gossip kills the Mummy. This game, the Mummy's rising ability never triggers.
tips: If you're the Mummy, your best destiny is to die before the final day arrives — by whatever means.
If you're the Mummy and you died by execution and then rose, the player who nominated you is definitely evil.
If you're the Mummy, you can hide your character and then rise on the final day, badly disrupting the evil team's plans.
If you're the Demon, the Mummy's existence may increase the number of execution rounds good can use — beware of that.
If you're the Demon, try not to attack or nominate the Mummy. If he stays alive, he does nothing at all.
bluffing: Mummies tend to actively seek death. If you want to bluff as the Mummy, your best bet is asking other players to nominate and execute you — but that usually means a very real risk of death.
You can use your failure to rise on the final day to "prove" the player who nominated you is good.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Awaiting Revival]]
Placed when: When the Mummy dies.
Condition: The Mummy died from a nomination-execution started by an evil player or from an evil player's ability.
Removed when: The Mummy leaves play or rises.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Combining rising from death with information design.

Increasing pressure on the evil team in the endgame circle.

characters.name: Cat Chorus
characters.ability: A player is drunk. At dusk, the Storyteller might name a song: if everyone sings it together, all Townsfolk are sober & healthy until dusk.
characters.lede: The Cat Chorus brings powerful music that briefly restores Townsfolk to sober health.
characters.quote: Attention! Attention! The Cat Chorus is officially taking over tonight, meow! Repeat — the Cat Chorus is officially taking over tonight, meow! Our mission: lead everyone partying until dawn, meow! Stay sharp, meow! Follow the beat and stomp together! One, two, three, four! Meow! Meow! Meow! Meow!
summaryBullets: In the vast majority of cases, the Cat Chorus makes a Townsfolk drunk.
In rare cases, the Cat Chorus makes themself drunk. Then, even if the players sing successfully, poisoned and drunk Townsfolk do not recover, because the Cat Chorus has no ability.
Even if the Cat Chorus isn't in play, or the Cat Chorus in play is poisoned, drunk, dead, or has no ability, you may still name songs — especially when a player claims to be the Cat Chorus.

The Cat Chorus's ability temporarily restores poisoned/drunk Townsfolk to sober health; it doesn't remove those effects outright. After the Cat Chorus's effect ends, players who temporarily recovered re-enter their original poisoned/drunk state. You may flip poison/drunk reminders face-down to show they're temporarily suppressed.
Even with a successful chorus, the Cat Chorus cannot restore poisoned/drunk non-Townsfolk characters to sober health.
The Cat Chorus's ability doesn't affect negative effects other than poison and drunkenness, such as the Vortox's false information or interaction interference.
After naming a song, give the players a few minutes to sing. Resolve night actions only after the singing ends and you've announced the result.
The Cat Chorus loses all ability upon death. The Townsfolk made drunk by them sobers up.

Don't fuss too much over whether every player sang or how good the singing was — some players are naturally shy. If you consider it a "success," declare it a success. As the Storyteller, if the atmosphere is too cold, you should actively stir up everyone's enthusiasm.
Having everyone close their eyes at night makes players braver about singing.
Name familiar songs whenever possible, and prepare accompaniment if you can.
The Storyteller decides at which dusk to name a song.
Generally name a song at the first day's dusk or later dusks — not on the first night.
For balance, generally stop naming songs after one successful chorus per game. If the chorus failed, you may name songs again at later dusks.

If the atmosphere is great and players are eager to sing, you may keep naming songs at later dusks even after a success — but tell players in advance that later choruses no longer trigger the Cat Chorus's ability (restoring poisoned/drunk Townsfolk).
howToRun: While preparing for the first night, choose any player and place the Cat Chorus's "Hammered!" reminder by their character token. That player is drunk.

At any dusk, you may publicly name a song, then give the players a few minutes and judge their singing. If you judge the chorus a success, publicly declare "Tonight's concert was a huge success!" or similar, then place the "Hyped Up!" reminder in the center of the Grimoire — all Townsfolk's poison and drunkenness effects are temporarily suppressed until the next dusk. If you judge the chorus a failure, publicly declare "The performance failed!" or similar. You may name songs again at later dusks.
examples: The Fortune Teller is drunk because of the Cat Chorus. On the first night, the Fortune Teller gets false information. After the first day's execution (dusk), the Storyteller says: "Night is falling — tonight we're holding a concert! I want to hear 'Blue Lotus-ha'!" Most players join the chorus and sing well; the Storyteller declares "The concert was a huge success!" All poisoned and drunk Townsfolk temporarily become sober and healthy: that night, the Monk — poisoned by the Widow — successfully protects a player attacked by the Demon, and the Fortune Teller — drunk from the Cat Chorus — gets correct information. At the next dusk, the Monk's and the Fortune Teller's poison/drunkenness take effect again.

The Cat Chorus is in play. After the second day's execution (dusk), the Storyteller declares night falls and names the song "Teens in Times, We Love You"; the singing is terrible and the Storyteller declares "The performance failed!" At the next dusk, the Storyteller names "Qi Li Xiang"; most players join and sing well, and the Storyteller declares "The concert was a huge success!" All poisoned and drunk Townsfolk temporarily become sober and healthy.

After the third day's execution (dusk), the Storyteller declares night falls and names "The Furry Song"; most players join and sing well, and the Storyteller declares "The concert was a huge success!" But the Cat Chorus isn't actually in play, so poisoned and drunk Townsfolk do not recover.
tips: If you're the Cat Chorus, remember: one player is drunk because of you.
If you're the Cat Chorus, on the night of your successful chorus, no Townsfolk will be poisoned or drunk (unless you are) — that night's information is highly credible!
If you're the Cat Chorus — get hyped! Your mission is leading everyone through one carnival night after another! Close your eyes and lead the singing! Don't be shy — nobody can see anyone anyway!
If you're the Demon, kill the Cat Chorus: even a successful chorus then restores nobody. But that also means the player drunk from the Cat Chorus sobers up upon their death.
bluffing: Lead everyone in partying every night — it makes other players believe you're the Cat Chorus.
Bluffing as the Cat Chorus lets you explain why a Townsfolk's information was "off" on the first night — they were drunk because of you.
