But this doesn't mean using extreme measures to win — such as deliberately including no information characters in the setup, or using Minion or Townsfolk abilities to rapidly kill all Townsfolk in the first few days. A meticulously planned, brilliant "battle of wits" is far more fun than an unscrupulous, despicable win — and the good team will accept their defeat wholeheartedly. So create brilliant games whenever possible. Win fairly, generously, and with grace.

You may communicate with the Sea-born in any form at any time, day or night — that's your fatherly love, and he deserves it. But we don't recommend revealing too much information to the Sea-born, such as showing him the Grimoire directly or briefing him on every player's character. There's no need to go that far — he is your son; you are not his son. Helping him doesn't mean reporting every detail of your work to him; just do as much as you see fit.

You may not break the rules — use Minion abilities reasonably and within the rules. For example, you can't use a once-per-game ability multiple times, or arbitrarily change an already-confirmed choice — e.g., you used the Poisoner to choose the Noble, but then the Fortune Teller chose the Sea-born; you can't retroactively change the Poisoner ability's choice — that's considered cheating.
The Sea-born's ability may increase or decrease the initial Outsiders. All Outsiders may be in play, or none at all, or one more or one fewer, or the default Outsider count.
The Sea-born's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: During game setup, before putting character tokens into the bag, remove all Minion character tokens and add an equal number of Townsfolk tokens. Then you may replace any number of Townsfolk tokens with Outsider tokens.
Before the game begins, decide which Minion abilities you have this game. During the game, you must use your Minion abilities reasonably and within the rules.
While the game is in progress, help or favor the Sea-born as much as possible within the rules.
Each night except the first, wake the Sea-born. Have him point to a player. Place the "Dead" reminder by that player.
examples: On the first night, the Sea-born is woken by the Storyteller and learns three bluffs. The Storyteller uses the Poisoner's ability to choose the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller gets false information. On the second night, the Sea-born points to the Noble; the Storyteller shakes their head and points to the Fortune Teller — the Sea-born takes the advice and chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller dies. On the third day, the Sea-born quietly visits the Storyteller in private and gets some advice.

On the first night, the Storyteller uses the Poisoner's and the Cerenovus's abilities to choose one player each. On the second night, the Storyteller uses the Poisoner's, the Cerenovus's, and the Assassin's abilities to choose one player each.
On the first day, the Sea-born quietly visits the Storyteller in private; the Storyteller gives him some advice about bluffs and gameplay.
The Sea-born is in play — the initial Outsider count in play is one more than default.
tips: If you're the Sea-born, the Storyteller is your only teammate — he'll help you as much as possible. When you get the chance, try communicating with him at night or during the day and listen to his advice. This will help you win.
If you're a good player, the Sea-born has no Minions — remember this. If you find you seemingly can't locate any evil players in play, consider the possibility of the Sea-born.

If you're a good player and you find important Townsfolk always dying early in the game, or more Minion abilities being used than there are Minions, you should be alert to the possibility that the Demon is the Sea-born.

If the Demon is the Sea-born, the vast majority of players in play are good. An evil Storyteller is manipulating Minion abilities trying to deceive you. You'll have enough days to find that single evil player.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: After the Sea-born acts at night and chooses a player.
Condition: The player the Sea-born chose is currently alive, can be killed by the Sea-born, and the Sea-born is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

characters.name: Gargoyle
characters.ability: The 1st time another player nominates you, they die. If you killed an evil player, you become their character & alignment.
characters.lede: The Gargoyle kills players who dare offend him, but he is easily assimilated by evil.
characters.quote: The wind between the stone cracks is the sleep-talk of my thousand-year slumber. The moon on the eave's corner is my poem line mottled across eternity. I hold ancient secrets and watch over the long night's end. When the bell tolls, the stubborn stone opens its eyes — all who gaze upon me shall be devoured by hell.
summaryBullets: When the Gargoyle is first nominated by another player, that player dies immediately. The nomination process proceeds normally.

When the Gargoyle is first nominated by another player, if the Gargoyle is poisoned or drunk, the nominating player does not die. Even if the Gargoyle later becomes sober and healthy, being nominated again cannot trigger the ability — the Gargoyle's ability has been wasted.

Only when the Gargoyle's ability kills an evil player does the Gargoyle change character and team. If the nominating player doesn't die for some reason, the Gargoyle's character and team do not change.
If the Gargoyle asks during the day after killing a player to confirm their current character and team, do not answer.

The Gargoyle's character and team change happens immediately after they kill another player. So if the Gargoyle kills the Demon, the game doesn't end — the Gargoyle becomes the new Demon. But you tell the Gargoyle how their character and team changed only after nightfall.
The Gargoyle nominating themself does not trigger the ability to kill themself.
A Traveller nominating the Gargoyle does not trigger the Gargoyle's ability (they are not treated as "the first other player to nominate you") (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: When the Gargoyle is nominated, if this is the first time the Gargoyle has been nominated by a player other than themself, the nominating player dies, and the vote proceeds normally. Place "No Ability" by the Gargoyle's character token.

When the Gargoyle's ability successfully causes a death, if the killed player is evil, immediately swap the Gargoyle's character token for the dead player's character token, and the Gargoyle turns evil. At the first opportunity after nightfall, wake the Gargoyle and tell them how their character and team changed. Place "Former Gargoyle" as a reminder if needed.
examples: On the first day, the Fortune Teller nominates the Gargoyle. This is the first time the Gargoyle has been nominated by another player; the Fortune Teller dies.

On the second day, the Poisoner nominates the Gargoyle. This is the first time the Gargoyle has been nominated by another player; the Poisoner dies, and the Gargoyle becomes the evil Poisoner. That night, the Gargoyle is woken and learns he has become the evil Poisoner.

On a day with only 3 alive players, the Imp nominates the Gargoyle. This is the first time the Gargoyle has been nominated by another player; the Imp dies, and the Gargoyle becomes the evil Imp. Only 2 players remain alive; the game ends; evil wins.
tips: If you're the Gargoyle and you don't want other players dropping dead to your ability, it's best to go public as the Gargoyle and warn everyone to be careful about nominating you. You can also nominate yourself first to prevent others from nominating you.

If you're the Gargoyle and your team and character didn't change on the night after you killed a player, that player was good! You can announce this immediately at dawn. Of course, people may not believe you — you'd say the same thing even if you'd turned evil!

If you're the Gargoyle and you've turned evil, the player you killed was definitely evil! You're no longer on the good team and you have a new character and ability — think hard about how to serve evil!
If you're on the evil team and want to add a new member to evil, nominating the Gargoyle is a fine choice. You'll be killed by them, but they inherit your character and ability and stay in play.
If you're the Demon and you think you're about to be exposed, nominate the Gargoyle — let them kill you and become the new Demon! It's one effective way to extend Demon survival.

If you're a Minion and everyone suspects you of being the Demon, deliberately nominate the Gargoyle and let them kill you. This turns everyone's attention to executing the Gargoyle. You still died, but at least evil gained a teammate.
bluffing: Bluffing as the Gargoyle is usually difficult, since you don't have the Gargoyle's ability. But if the script has characters like the Yaggababble or the Witch that can help you fake a Gargoyle, you can try posing as one.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.tags: Alignment Change, Character Change, Death, Nominations, Once Per Game

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[No Ability]]
Placed when: When the Gargoyle is first nominated by another player.
Condition: As long as the Gargoyle is first nominated by another player, place this token by the Gargoyle's character token, whether or not the Gargoyle is drunk or poisoned.
Removed when: The Gargoyle dies or leaves play.

[[Former Gargoyle]]
Placed when: When the Gargoyle becomes another character.
Condition: The Storyteller places or removes it as needed.
Removed when: The Storyteller places or removes it as needed.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Gargoyle is designed as the counterpart to the Golem — both are strong self-proof characters. One "attacks," the other "defends"; one is "active," the other "passive." The Golem's negative shows up as the good team losing multiple nomination rights, while the Gargoyle's negative shows up as possibly increasing the evil player count — even relocating the Demon.

The Gargoyle looks like a strong self-proof character, but at the moment of self-proof he may already no longer be the Gargoyle. The player he killed really died, yet there's no telling whether the killed player was the Demon. And the good team concretely lost rounds and execution chances.

The Gargoyle is a further bold exploration of turn-evil, Demon-relocating Outsiders.

The Gargoyle's design resembles Hell's Outcast — a strategic card for the evil team. Evil can build all kinds of plays around the Gargoyle's ability, conceiving deeper strategies.

The Gargoyle carries the huge negative effect of possibly relocating the Demon, but with fairly visible traces.

characters.name: Onmyoji
characters.ability: Each night, you learn a player: they are of a different alignment to the player you learned last night.
characters.lede: The Onmyoji learns good and evil players in alternation each night.
characters.quote: Heaven and earth, mountain and lake — thunder, wind, water, fire, the eight trigrams interlock... Complete!
summaryBullets: It is not recommended to let the Onmyoji learn himself.
The Onmyoji may learn the same player more than once.
When first giving the Onmyoji information, you may tell him either a good player or an evil player.
The Onmyoji does not learn Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: one player (e.g., "player #1" or "May").
False information format: a player on the same team as the player the Onmyoji learned last night. When the Onmyoji first learns information, it may be any player.
howToRun: Each night, wake the Onmyoji. Tell him one player who must be on a different team to the player he learned last night.
The first time you wake the Onmyoji, you may tell him any player.
examples: On the first night, the Onmyoji learns May. On the second night, he learns Sean. On the third night, he learns Zach. On the fourth night, he learns Leo. May and Zach are good; Sean and Leo are evil.
On the first night, the Onmyoji learns May. On the second night, he learns Sean. On the third night, he learns Zach. On the fourth night, he learns Leo. May and Zach are evil; Sean and Leo are good.
tips: With only one night of information, your info is useless — that player could be good or evil. Whatever happens, survive to the second night.
If you've learned two players, exactly one of them is evil!
bluffing: Report several good players to ignite conflict between them — make them attack each other!
Weave real evil players into your information; it makes you look more like a genuine Onmyoji.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake him and tell him any one player.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him and tell him any one player.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: A benchmark-template character.

characters.name: Venomtail
characters.ability: The 1+X Townsfolk nearest to you clockwise are poisoned. [No Outsiders in play. X is the number of Outsiders removed by you]
characters.lede: Venomtail converts Outsiders into poisoned Townsfolk, dragging a "poison" tail behind him.
characters.quote: See this beautiful tail behind me? Bought it from an outlander at a steep price. Every segment is one of your poisoned, blackening neighbors; every segment is silently rotting. It grows longer and heavier as it drags. Don't fret — once the venom crawls through your bones, you'll be pinned onto it too, swaying behind me forever.
summaryBullets: The Townsfolk players nearest clockwise to Venomtail are poisoned, whether those Townsfolk are alive or dead. If Venomtail dies or otherwise loses his ability, those Townsfolk recover.
Venomtail's effect skips non-Townsfolk characters in the clockwise direction.
If a player becomes a new Venomtail, or a poisoned Townsfolk becomes a non-Townsfolk character, the poisoned players change immediately based on the new positional relationships.

As long as you add Venomtail during initial setup, you definitely cannot add any Outsiders. If other Outsider-adding/removing characters exist, first count their Outsider adjustments, then remove all Outsiders. The number of Outsiders actually removed due to Venomtail's ability determines how many Townsfolk are poisoned by Venomtail.
Detailed formula for Venomtail's X value: X is fixed at initial setup and never changes for any reason. If Venomtail is created mid-game, that Venomtail's X value is definitely 0.
howToRun: During initial setup, before putting character tokens into the bag, replace all Outsider character tokens with Townsfolk character tokens.

While preparing for the first night, count how many Outsiders Venomtail removed. For each Outsider removed, one more Townsfolk player nearest clockwise to Venomtail is poisoned (continuing down the line) — place "Poisoned" reminders by their character tokens.

If a Townsfolk poisoned by Venomtail becomes a non-Townsfolk character, immediately remove their "Poisoned" reminder — they are no longer poisoned by Venomtail from now on. Find the next nearest Townsfolk clockwise from Venomtail who isn't already poisoned by Venomtail, and poison them.
examples: 12-player game. Venomtail removed 2 Outsiders, so 1+2 = 3 Townsfolk are poisoned. Venomtail is player #1 — so player #2 (the Fortune Teller), player #3 (the Innkeeper), and player #4 (the Ravenkeeper) are all poisoned.

12-player game. Venomtail and the Fang Gu (+1 Outsider) are in play. Venomtail removed 3 Outsiders, so 1+3 = 4 Townsfolk are poisoned. Venomtail is player #1; the Fang Gu is player #2 — so player #3 (the Fortune Teller), player #4 (the Innkeeper), player #5 (the Ravenkeeper), and player #6 (the Washerwoman) are all poisoned.

12-player game. Venomtail and the Vigormortis (-1 Outsider) are in play. Venomtail removed 1 Outsider, so 1+1 = 2 Townsfolk are poisoned. Venomtail is player #1; the Vigormortis is player #2 — so player #3 (the Fortune Teller) and player #4 (the Innkeeper) are poisoned.

10-player game. Venomtail removed no Outsiders, so 1+0 = 1 Townsfolk is poisoned. Venomtail is player #1; the Imp is player #2; the Scarlet Woman is player #3. Player #4 (the Fortune Teller) is poisoned.

10-player game. Venomtail removed no Outsiders, so 1+0 = 1 Townsfolk is poisoned. Venomtail is player #1. Player #2 (the Fortune Teller) is poisoned. On the second night, the Pit-Hag turns player #2 into an Outsider — since #2 is no longer a Townsfolk, from now on player #3 (the Empath) is poisoned instead.
tips: If you're Venomtail, no Outsiders are in play — which means you're born with every Outsider as a bluff!

If you're Venomtail, try your best to disguise the Outsider count as normal — that's your most important job! If nobody claims to be an Outsider, players will quickly conclude Venomtail is in play. If you don't want to bluff as an Outsider yourself (once players confirm Venomtail is in play, you must be an evil player — very likely the Venomtail — and they'll trace all the poisoned Townsfolk from you), have your teammates bluff as Outsiders instead. That way, even if Venomtail's presence is exposed, players can't quickly locate all the poisoned Townsfolk from the fake Outsiders' positions.

If you're Venomtail, your death lets all Townsfolk poisoned by you recover — watch out for this. If your teammates are mixed among the players poisoned by you — especially the Demon — they can fake being poisoned by you, or fake recovering upon your death, to win other players' trust.
If you're an Outsider, Venomtail definitely isn't in play! Don't consider any possibility of Venomtail existing — at least at game start, Venomtail definitely doesn't exist.
If you're a Townsfolk and you believe Venomtail is in play, players claiming to be Outsiders are definitely evil! Try to execute them, and look for signs of poisoning in their clockwise direction.
If you're a Townsfolk and you and several Townsfolk near you seem poisoned, Venomtail may be causing trouble "upstream" of you — try to find and execute him, and you'll recover.
If you're a Townsfolk and you've found Venomtail, the players "downstream" of him aren't necessarily all good! Other evil players may be mixed in among them as cover — distinguish carefully.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.tags: Information, Neighbor, Poison, Setup, You Start Knowing

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Poisoned]]
Placed when: While preparing for the first night, or when a Townsfolk poisoned by Venomtail stops being a Townsfolk.
Condition: Place it by the character tokens of the Townsfolk players nearest clockwise to Venomtail.
Special note: Continuous detection checks which players are Venomtail and the Townsfolk players nearest to him clockwise. Whenever the seating or characters of Venomtail or the Townsfolk nearest to him clockwise change, move the "Poisoned" reminders to the character tokens of players who meet the condition.
Removed when: Venomtail dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The no-Outsiders setup adjustment is an unprecedented, innovative, and bold design. It inevitably brings many problems — e.g., Outsiders definitely know Venomtail isn't in play, the evil team must usually arrange Outsider claims, Venomtail gets every Outsider as a bluff, etc. Innovation always comes with problems, and good design needs the test of time.

Venomtail converting Outsiders into poisoned Townsfolk is, in a sense, equivalent to turning Townsfolk into "Drunks". So which has the bigger negative effect — the original Outsiders, or a pile of "Drunks"? What Outsiders should a script include to create interesting, wonderful chemistry with Venomtail? The design space left for script authors is vast.

Venomtail's ability seems powerful — many Townsfolk are poisoned by it. But it also leaves considerable "traces": confirming no Outsiders are in play almost confirms Venomtail, Venomtail's poison concentrates in one area with a strong positional signature, and players can trace the poison chain back to Venomtail. So Venomtail is a Minion designed with a strong "traceable poison" philosophy.

characters.name: Yuki-onna
characters.ability: On your 1st night alive & your 1st night dead, choose a player: they are poisoned.
characters.lede: Yuki-onna's obsession crosses life and death, delivering deadly poison at every stage.
characters.quote: Love severed, incense spent, the moon a hook; the infatuated soul chases snow toward the netherworld. Icy winds mourn her shadow, her heart unsettled; freezing rain soaks her robes, her hatred unspent. Resentment frosts through flesh and bone; hatred becomes a long rope binding guilt. Life and death entwined without end; love and hate imprisoned, never ceasing.
summaryBullets: Distinguish Yuki-onna's two poisons. When Yuki-onna dies, players previously poisoned by Yuki-onna (Living Venom) recover immediately because Yuki-onna loses her ability upon death.

Yuki-onna's post-death poisoning ability (Death Venom) doesn't fail just because Yuki-onna is dead — this ability is a death-triggered ability. As long as the dead Yuki-onna remains in play, the poisoning persists.
If Yuki-onna dies during the day, she is woken at her place in the night order to use her ability.

If Yuki-onna dies at night, she is woken immediately after the character ability that killed her finishes resolving, and uses her ability. Yuki-onna's "other nights" position only serves as her action order when she dies during the day.
If an alive player is turned into Yuki-onna, she is woken and uses her ability that night (Living Venom).
If a dead player is turned into Yuki-onna, she is woken and uses her ability that night (Death Venom).
Yuki-onna's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: On the first night, wake Yuki-onna and have her point to a player. Mark that player with Yuki-onna's "Living Venom" — they become poisoned. Put Yuki-onna back to sleep. When Yuki-onna dies or leaves play, remove her "Living Venom" reminder — they recover.

If Yuki-onna dies during the day, wake Yuki-onna at her place in the night order that night and have her point to a player. Mark that player with Yuki-onna's "Death Venom" — they become poisoned. Put Yuki-onna back to sleep.

If Yuki-onna dies at night, immediately after the character ability that caused her death finishes resolving, wake Yuki-onna and have her point to a player. Mark that player with Yuki-onna's "Death Venom" — they become poisoned. Put Yuki-onna back to sleep.
examples: On the first night, Yuki-onna chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller is poisoned. On the third day, Yuki-onna dies by execution; the Fortune Teller recovers. That night, Yuki-onna chooses the Fortune Teller again; the Fortune Teller is poisoned.

On the first night, Yuki-onna chooses the Noble; the Noble is poisoned. On the second night, Yuki-onna is killed by the Demon; the Noble recovers. Yuki-onna chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller is poisoned.

On the first night, Yuki-onna chooses the Noble; the Noble is poisoned. On the second night, Yuki-onna dies because of the Gossip's ability; the Noble recovers. Yuki-onna chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller is poisoned.
On the first night, Yuki-onna chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller is poisoned. Yuki-onna stays alive the whole game, and the Fortune Teller remains poisoned throughout.
tips: If you're Yuki-onna, on the first night, choose players who seem to have powerful characters! Or players you think are highly skilled! Since you have no game information to go on, choose boldly — it takes a bit of luck.

If you're Yuki-onna and you discover you poisoned an important player on the first night with a big impact, try not to die, to keep them poisoned. Of course, if you die by accident, you can keep choosing them to keep them poisoned — but then you can't poison any other player for the rest of the game.

If you're Yuki-onna and you discover you poisoned an unimportant player while a more important player urgently needs your poison, find a way to die — ideally by execution. If all else fails, have the Demon kill you.

If you're a good player, remember: only a dead Yuki-onna can poison a new player. So you don't need to worry like with the Poisoner about a different player being poisoned each day. At most 2 players can be poisoned by Yuki-onna — and only if Yuki-onna has died.

If you're a good player, Yuki-onna's first-night choice has little reference to go on — it's mostly a blind choice. So the probability of an important player being poisoned on night one isn't high. If you find an important player seemingly poisoned by Yuki-onna, it's likely Yuki-onna chose them again after dying — try to find who Yuki-onna is among the dead players.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.tags: On Death, Poison, You Start Knowing
characters.firstNightReminder: Have her choose a player.
characters.otherNightReminder: Have her choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Living Venom]]
Placed when: After Yuki-onna chooses a player on the first night.
Condition: If Yuki-onna is sober and healthy when choosing, place it by the character token of the player she chose.
Removed when: Yuki-onna dies or leaves play.

[[Death Venom]]
Placed when: After Yuki-onna chooses a player on the first night after her death.
Condition: If Yuki-onna is sober and healthy when choosing, place it by the character token of the player she chose.
Removed when: Yuki-onna leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
As a pure poisoning Minion, Yuki-onna can't avoid comparison with the Poisoner, the official game's only pure poisoning Minion: 1) Yuki-onna and the Poisoner's ability effects are consistent — "at any given moment, only one player is poisoned"; 2) Although Yuki-onna's ability while alive is far weaker than the Poisoner's, the death-refresh ability form is something the death-fearing Poisoner can't do. Yuki-onna doesn't fear death — she even seeks it out. This differentiates her from other "Poisoner-like" pure-poison Minions; rather than simply being a weakened Poisoner, she differs in other respects — achieving "each has its strengths" against the Poisoner, with an extremely concise, easy-to-understand ability description.

"On your first night alive and your first night dead" — a simple, innovative, easy-to-understand ability description that naturally and briefly specifies the timing for one character's two abilities. One sentence covers both an entry ability and a death-triggered ability.

Yuki-onna's death-switches-the-poison design brings "execution deterrence" to scripts. Executing evil is no longer always beneficial for good, making players think more deeply about whom to execute. The Yuki-onna player also needs strategy — how to die at the right time to switch the poison target. Yuki-onna alone can even establish the latent logic that "a player killed at night is a Minion", because Yuki-onna can be killed by the Demon to trigger her ability.

characters.name: Dretch
characters.ability: Each night*, a player dies. When nominated, you may declare you are the Dretch: if good players outnumber evil, a Minion becomes the Dretch.
characters.lede: Push a Dretch too hard and it will call in more Dretches!
characters.quote: K'zhak! K'zhak! Dretch! Dretch! (Abyssal: Come! Dretches!)
summaryBullets: Declaring you are the Dretch: after being nominated, any speech expressing that he's trying to trigger the Dretch's ability — it can be strange shrieks, a cry for help, or directly publicly claiming to be the Dretch. Upon receiving this, the Storyteller must clearly announce to everyone "this player has declared they are the Dretch". Make sure all players correctly understand the player's action. If the Storyteller doesn't publicly express "this player has declared they are the Dretch", no player becomes a Dretch.

After the Dretch declares he is the Dretch, if there are more good players than evil players alive, a Minion immediately becomes the Dretch. In most cases, an alive Minion should be prioritized for becoming the Dretch.

The same Dretch, no matter how many times he declares in one day, can only trigger the ability once — turning one evil player into the Dretch. If multiple Dretches declare on the same day (including a new Dretch created that day immediately declaring), you turn multiple Minions into Dretches.

As a lowly Demon, the Dretch cannot control his attack target — the Storyteller decides whom he attacks. If multiple Dretches are alive, you kill multiple players. It's not recommended to deliberately attack dead players with the Dretch's ability to reduce the death count — that violates the Dretch's design intent; the point of multiple Dretches is to accelerate the game. Although you can't kill fewer, you CAN kill evil players! Go kill Minions — even other Dretches. In Dretch games, especially with multiple Dretches alive, the Storyteller often needs to moderately kill evil players to control the situation and avoid a guaranteed-loss position for good.

Once multiple alive Dretches exist in play, nights get very bloody. If you kill multiple good players with the Dretch's ability, good can hardly win. In that situation, you need to appropriately kill evil players — even Dretches. Understand this: killing evil players isn't all bad for the evil team. Even killing evil players, even Dretches — as long as the game doesn't end, it accelerates the game, shrinks good's execution rounds, and helps the Demon reach the final day faster.
The Dretch's ability cannot choose Traveller players, and evil Travellers are not counted as evil players by the Dretch's ability (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, you decide which player dies. If multiple Dretches are alive, you kill multiple players. Don't kill like an omniscient Demon — on the contrary, if multiple Dretches exist, at times you need to make decisions that help the team at a disadvantage.

If the Dretch, after being nominated and before voting begins, "declares he is the Dretch" (any speech expressing that he's triggering the Dretch's ability — see Rule Details), announce to all players that the nominated player has declared he is the Dretch, so everyone clearly hears it. If there are more good players than evil players among the alive players at that moment, turn one evil player into the Dretch. At the earliest opportunity after nightfall, wake the new Dretch player and tell him his character is now the Dretch.
examples: On the first day, the Dretch is nominated. The Dretch speaks: "Coo-coo-coo gah-gah-gah! Save me, save me!" The Storyteller responds: "Someone has declared they are the Dretch!" Among the alive players there are 9 good players and 3 evil players — evil is fewer — the Baron becomes the Dretch.

On the third day, the Dretch is nominated. The Dretch speaks: "K'zhak! K'zhak! Dretch! Dretch!" The Storyteller responds: "He has declared he is the Dretch!!" Among the alive players there are 5 good players and 3 evil players — evil is fewer — the Baron becomes the Dretch. That day the Butler dies by execution. That night, a good player and an evil player are killed by the Dretches.

On the fifth day, the Dretch is nominated. The Dretch speaks: "I am the Dretch!" The Storyteller responds: "Received — you declared you are the Dretch." Among the alive players there are 2 good players and 2 evil players — since evil players do not outnumber good players, nobody becomes a Dretch. That day the Dretch dies by execution — the game ends, and the good team wins.
tips: If you're the Dretch and you think you'll be executed today, declare you are the Dretch! This amounts to "turning yourself in" — admitting you're an evil player — but at least it beats losing the game outright.
If you're the Dretch, watch the balance of remaining players — if evil players aren't fewer than good players, you can't create more Dretches!

If you're the Dretch, declaring with 3–4 alive players left is pointless. With 2 evil players alive, good players can't possibly outnumber evil players. And if you're the only evil player left, there's no alive Minion to take your place either. Of course, if your goal is to bluff — playing yourself as a Minion begging to be executed in the Demon's place — this might work.

If you're the Dretch and you're sure you won't be executed today, nominating yourself and declaring is a radical, bold plan. Multiple alive Demons in play give evil a huge advantage — multiple players die each night, bringing the game to its final day faster.

If you're a Minion and the Demon has already declared today, consider declaring immediately! If you're the new Dretch created by the declaration, your declaration creates yet another new Dretch! Multiple alive Dretches bring the evil team a huge advantage. But be careful — the Storyteller may kill some evil players with the Dretch's ability at night.
If you're a Minion and your Demon boss is in mortal danger, you can deliberately declare to force the other players to execute you! That keeps your Demon boss safe — for today, at least.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Choose a player: they die.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: When the Dretch acts on nights other than the first.
Condition: The Storyteller decides which player the Dretch attacks. If that player is currently alive and can be killed by the Dretch, place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

[[Is Dretch" ×2]]
Placed when: For the Storyteller's own reference only.
Condition: For the Storyteller's own reference only.
Removed when: For the Storyteller's own reference only.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Dretch is a swarming, low-rank, small Demon — matching the ability design elements of not choosing its attack target and declaring itself.

The Dretch's design intent is to help new players adapt to the game quickly, making the Demon seat less stressful for beginners. The Dretch's kills are Storyteller-controlled, and when executed, a simple public declaration can relocate the Demon — very low skill required, so the player can focus on their character bluff.

The Dretch is a public-declaration-type evil character. Such characters often have extremely high ability payoffs, because publicly declaring is itself a huge cost — exposing an evil player's position. How to balance these two is the design challenge of public-declaration evil characters.

characters.name: Illus
characters.ability: If your neighbors live, Townsfolk players' abilities yield false information.
characters.lede: Illus makes all Townsfolk get false information.
characters.quote: Tonight you will have a dream. In the dream you'll meet someone you deeply love. You'll kiss her, you'll embrace her, you'll smell the reassuring scent in her hair. Then you'll wake. But in the waking world, her scent will become carrion and bile. Every breath will make you vomit. Yet she'll still smile at you. She'll say, 'What's wrong, darling?' And then you'll forget you ever loved anything that wasn't her. And I — I am the thing that isn't her.
summaryBullets: False information: objectively wrong, untrue information. Whether information is false is not affected by any ability.
Whenever players whose character is a Townsfolk gain information through an ability, they get false information — even if they're drunk or poisoned, the information is guaranteed false.
Illus doesn't affect information others gain by other means, such as rules the Storyteller explains or changes to a player's character or team.
If Illus dies, leaves play, is drunk or poisoned, or loses his ability, Townsfolk no longer get false information.
If a player neighboring Illus dies, Townsfolk no longer get false information.
Illus's ability ignores Travellers — the death of a Traveller neighboring Illus doesn't affect Illus's ability (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: As long as Illus and the two players neighboring him are all alive, whenever a Townsfolk's ability requires you to give them information, you must give false information.
examples: Illus is in play. On the first night, the Chambermaid learns of an evil player, the Fortune Teller chooses two non-Demon players but learns one of them is the Demon, and the Seamstress chooses two players of the same team but learns they're on different teams.
Illus is in play. On the first night, all Townsfolk get false information. On the second night, Illus is killed by the Demon — all Townsfolk no longer get false information.

Illus is in play. On the first night, all Townsfolk get false information. On the second night, all Townsfolk get false information. The next day, the Seamstress neighboring Illus dies by execution. That night, all Townsfolk no longer get false information.
tips: If you're Illus, tell your teammates you're Illus — this makes it easier for everyone to decide whether to produce "true information" or "false information".

If you're Illus, report "true information" together with your teammates to mask Illus's existence! If the good team doesn't realize Illus is in play, the false information produced by other Townsfolk will massively disrupt the good team's judgment!

If you're Illus, don't fear the good team confirming Illus is in play and using that as a logical base to sort out information. Even if the good team realizes Illus is in play, they can only get true information by flipping binary information — non-binary information becomes nearly worthless.

If you're Illus, proactively seek execution when necessary — or even let the Demon kill you. This returns Townsfolk information to true, and if the good team doesn't correctly realize which day Illus died, it causes massive information disruption.
If you're an evil player and Illus isn't in play, try to convince everyone Illus is in play! This discredits most information in play as "false information" — massive disruption.

If you're a good player, don't over-fear Illus — if you can confirm Illus is in play, just read information in reverse! What you should really watch is whether Illus died on some day — that would turn information true partway through.

If you're a good player, in scripts with Illus, get in the habit of thinking along two logic lines — one where Illus is in play and information is false, one where Illus isn't in play and information is true.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Info Always False]]
Placed when: When Illus enters play.
Condition: When Illus enters play, place it by Illus's character token.
Removed when: Illus dies or leaves play, or when a player neighboring Illus dies.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Vortox's ability is strong and cool! But not every script suits the Vortox! Illus is the Minion version of the Vortox. Simple! Powerful! Convenient! Easy to understand!

Illus causes even greater disruption than the Vortox, because Illus can die partway through, returning information to true — something the Vortox can hardly do.

A Vortox-type Minion — I'd been thinking about how to design such a Minion for a very, very long time. Were there flashier schemes? Like binding information truth to adding/removing Outsiders and the Outsider count? Like binding information truth to the Minion's own life or death? Even associating positional information? Or triggering on the first night alive and dead? I considered all of them — not just considered, I wrote piles of drafts — but in the end I rejected them all. I found that script creation doesn't need such fancy stuff; what it truly needs is the simplest, most fundamental false-information Minion. Adding even a single word would be gilding the lily. So the final Illus is this fundamental, this utterly plain.

Illus's original ability: "Townsfolk players' abilities yield false information." Didn't I say adding a single word would be gilding the lily? So why add another sentence? There was nothing wrong with Illus's original ability — but to shut certain people up, adding one sentence does no harm.

characters.name: Tzeentch
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. You have extra Demon bluffs. Choose one: you have that character's ability.
characters.lede: Tzeentch has the perfect disguise.
characters.quote: There's no need to strain to discern my outline — the shape standing before you now will melt and twist the next second. I am master of every disguise; I have buried countless false avatars among the crowds. So-called loyalty, alignment, good and evil — all are shells to blind the mortal. I never conquer by brute force; with cunning I turn allies against each other and bring convictions crashing down. Ceaseless change is the only truth, and I am the Lord of Change.
summaryBullets: On the first night, when learning the Demon info, Tzeentch gets extra bluff characters — and he must choose one from all the bluff characters. The Storyteller decides how many extra bluffs he gets. Bluff characters can only be not-in-play Townsfolk or Outsider characters.
If Tzeentch is drunk or poisoned, he loses not only Tzeentch's own ability but also the ability of the character gained through Tzeentch's ability.
If the ability Tzeentch has is one that triggers or is retained after death, and Tzeentch dies, Tzeentch keeps that gained ability — for example, the Puzzle Master.
If Tzeentch chooses an ability that changes the initial setup (e.g., the Balloonist), the setup-changing part of that character's ability doesn't take effect.
At night, Tzeentch is additionally woken at the times that character would be woken.
If Tzeentch is created mid-game, since Tzeentch doesn't learn the Demon info, he also can't gain a bluff or its ability.
Tzeentch's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: On the first night, give Tzeentch more bluff characters than a normal Demon and have him choose one of them. Then place that character token next to Tzeentch's character token to remind yourself that Tzeentch also has that character's ability. Run the game as if Tzeentch has that character's ability.
Each night except the first, wake Tzeentch. Have him point to any player. That player dies — mark them with the "Dead" reminder. Put Tzeentch back to sleep.
examples: On the first night, Tzeentch learns 4 bluffs: the Gossip, the Dreamwalker, the Innkeeper, and the Saint. Tzeentch chooses and gains the Dreamwalker's ability. That night, Tzeentch is woken by the Dreamwalker's ability and chooses the Fortune Teller player — Tzeentch learns "Fortune Teller, Baron".

On the first night, Tzeentch learns 6 bluffs: the Gossip, the Dreamwalker, the Innkeeper, the Saint, the Golem, and the Washerwoman. Tzeentch chooses and gains the Gossip's ability. On the first day, Tzeentch publicly makes a true statement (the Gossip's ability). That night, Tzeentch is woken and attacks a player. Then, another player dies because of the Gossip's ability.

On the first night, Tzeentch learns 5 bluffs: the Gossip, the Dreamwalker, the Golem, the King, and the Choirboy. Tzeentch chooses and gains the Golem's ability. On the first day, Tzeentch nominates the Baron player — the Baron dies. Due to the Golem's ability restriction, Tzeentch cannot nominate again for the rest of the game.
tips: If you're Tzeentch, you get extra bluffs! That gives you more room to operate. Don't be stingy — share these bluffs with your Minions.

If you're Tzeentch, you can perfectly disguise yourself as your bluff character — a superb advantage. You can learn other players' characters like a real Dreamwalker, or cause extra deaths like a real Gossip. Prioritize bluff characters that let you "prove yourself"! After you "prove yourself", everyone believes you more easily!

If you're Tzeentch, you can avoid claiming to be the bluff you chose, and instead secretly sabotage with its ability — causing drunkenness with the Innkeeper's ability, or extra deaths with the Gossip's ability!

If you're a good player, treat players who have "proven themselves" with caution. They may not be the character they "proved" — they could be Tzeentch! For example, a Virgin or Golem who used their ability, or a Nightwatchman whom others learned of.

If you're a good player and want to argue the in-play Demon is Tzeentch, then other Demons' abilities definitely can't be in effect — because no other Demon can be in play alongside Tzeentch! So if you think a "proven" player is Tzeentch, first think: does that make sense without any other Demon ability in play?
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Have him choose one of three bluff characters.
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: After Tzeentch acts at night and chooses a player.
Condition: The player Tzeentch chose is currently alive, can be killed, and Tzeentch is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Tzeentch of the four Chaos Gods, the Lord of Change, themed on ultimate disguise. The first Demon design that interacts with the Demon's bluffs.

Tzeentch's design adds no extra actions — instead, it strengthens the "Demon info" step. Through the simple extra act of "choosing a bluff", it implements the ability while avoiding massive redundant description. And "letting Tzeentch choose" gives the player more decision power, improving the experience. Bluffs are already Storyteller-decided — the Storyteller controls the range of abilities Tzeentch can gain, while giving the player the right to choose "1 of N" — effectively controlling Tzeentch's strength.

characters.name: Titan
characters.ability: On the first night, you turn evil and gain the abilities of all Minions not in play. [The Titan counts as a Minion during setup]
characters.lede: The mighty Outsider Titan joins the game as a Minion.
characters.quote: I once held up the sky; now I only want to tear it down. The gods call me 'evil' — then I shall be evil incarnate, the primordial darkness that devours all light. I have sacrificed my broken body to a will older than the abyss, in exchange for world-shaking power. A snap of my fingers shatters stars; a breath withers all things. This time, there is no salvation — only gods kneeling at my feet in eternal despair.
summaryBullets: Since the Titan simultaneously gains the abilities of all Minion characters on the character list that aren't in play, they do not have the abilities of Minions not on the list.
If any Minion ability the Titan has changes the initial setup, those setup functions do not take effect.
If the Titan is poisoned or drunk, the Titan loses all Minion abilities at once.
If one of the Titan's Minion abilities is kept after death — such as the Spy's — the Titan keeps that ability when dead, but not the others.
If the Titan gains a character ability that has a jinx, that jinx applies to the Titan too.

After the game begins, the Titan is not a Minion, so the Titan does not learn who the Demon or Minions are. Conversely, the Titan player does not appear in the Demon's info either (the Minion players the Demon learns do not include the Titan).
During setup, you must treat the Titan as a Minion. This means adding the Titan requires replacing one of the original Minions. The Titan is never added to the game as an Outsider.
The Titan's ability requires the game's first night, not "your first night." So a player who becomes the Titan mid-game neither turns evil nor gains Minion abilities.
howToRun: When setting up the game, the Titan counts as a Minion. If you include the Titan, the Titan's character token occupies a Minion slot. You cannot add the Titan as an Outsider.

On the game's first night, wake the Titan, tell them they have turned evil, show them all Minion character tokens not in play, then place those Minion character tokens by the Titan's character token — representing that the Titan has gained those Minions' abilities. From now on, run the game as if the Titan has those Minion abilities.
examples: 9-player game. The Titan is in play. Because the Titan replaced the only Minion, no Minion is in play. On the first night, the Demon does not learn who the Minions are, because the Titan is an Outsider, not a Minion. The Titan turns evil and learns they have gained the abilities of the Poisoner, the Spy, the Godfather, and the Devil's Advocate, and is woken that night to use each of them. The Titan gaining the Godfather's ability does not change the Outsider count, because that's a setup-changing ability.

12-player game. The Titan is in play. Only one Minion (the Godfather) is in play, because the Titan replaced one Minion. On the first night, the Demon learns the Godfather player is a Minion; the Godfather learns the Imp player is the Demon. The Titan turns evil and learns they have gained the abilities of the Mastermind, the Pit-Hag, and the Assassin.

15-player game. The Titan is in play. Only 2 Minions (the Godfather, the Assassin) are in play, because the Titan replaced one Minion. On the first night, the Demon learns the Godfather and Assassin players are Minions; the Godfather and Assassin learn the Imp player is the Demon. The Titan turns evil and learns they have gained the abilities of the Mastermind and the Pit-Hag.
On the third night, the Pit-Hag turns the Fortune Teller into the Titan; the Titan neither turns evil nor gains Minion abilities, because the Titan's ability only triggers on the first night.
tips: If you're the Titan, treat yourself as an unusual Minion: you have powerful abilities, but you don't know who your teammates are. Use those abilities cautiously and figure out who your teammates are quickly.
If you're the Titan, you can judge which Minions are in play from your own abilities, helping you find potential teammates.
If you're the Titan, don't reveal that you're the Titan lightly — to the good team, the Titan is even more terrifying than a Minion, and they may rush to execute you.
If you're a good player and you feel the Minion abilities in effect exceed the proper Minion count, the Titan is likely in play!
If you're a good player, the Titan can't mutually confirm with their evil teammates, so the board gets chaotic — evil abilities may attack each other, even kill each other.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake the Titan, tell them they have turned evil, and show them all Minion character tokens not in play.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Minion 1 & 2 & 3 & 4]]
Note: When the Titan is in play alongside Minions that need reminder tokens, use the Titan's "Minion 1" (or "Minion 2," "Minion 3," "Minion 4") token as a substitute for that character's token, used the same way as that Minion character's reminder token.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
An innovative character design: though called an Outsider, the Titan is effectively a fifth Minion card.

Though a "Minion," no mutual recognition. Positioning the Titan as an Outsider cleverly attaches a negative effect matching its powerful abilities.

As an Outsider, the Titan doesn't squeeze out the original Minion slots, guaranteeing that at any player count the Titan gets at least 2 Minion abilities.

Designing the Titan as an Outsider lets it properly enter 13/4/4/4-format scripts, preventing Minion-slot crowding — which in a 3-Minion game would leave the Titan with only 1 Minion ability. It also links with other "abnormal character count" characters as part of systemic design.

characters.name: Druid
characters.ability: If both your alive neighbors are the same alignment, the Demon can only attack them.
characters.lede: If the players on both sides of the Druid share a team, the Demon can only attack them.
characters.quote: Nature has predators and prey. Wolves eat deer, deer eat grass, grass eats the bones in the soil. Every mouth devours another mouth. That is not cruelty — it is balance. But there is one predator for which nature arranged no natural enemy. When it feeds, it is not to live, not from hunger, but only for sport. Since nature prepared no chains for it, I shall become its natural enemy.
summaryBullets: Attack: when a player with a Demon ability, or the Storyteller, selects a player with the Demon's killing ability. Attacks usually kill an alive player; sometimes they don't, such as attacking a player who cannot die or a dead player.

Can only attack X: when a player with a Demon ability is woken for their ability and is told they may only attack specific players. When the Storyteller decides the Demon's target, they may likewise only choose specific players.
While the Druid's ability is in effect, the Demon can only attack the alive players neighboring the Druid — whether that Demon's target is chosen by a player or by the Storyteller.
If the Demon can kill multiple players, update the Druid's condition check only after the Demon has killed all of them.
If the Demon can attack more than 2 players (such as Po), then while the Druid's ability is in effect they may still choose at most 2 players.
The Druid's ability only affects Demon abilities. Deaths caused by non-Demon abilities are not affected by the Druid.

If the Demon has no ability to actively attack players (Yaggababble / Lil' Monsta style), the Demon does not learn the forced targets — i.e., the Druid is not exposed this way. The Storyteller chooses between the two players.
The Druid's condition check ignores Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: If the two alive players neighboring the Druid are both good or both evil (skipping Travellers), place the Druid's "Forced Choice" reminders by those two players' character tokens. If one of the two alive players neighboring the Druid is good and the other evil, remove these reminders. Update these reminders throughout the game whenever this condition changes (for example, a player's team changes or a player dies).

If the two alive players neighboring the Druid are on the same team, at the Demon's point in the night order: if the Demon's ability has a player choose the attack target, wake the Demon, show them the "This character's ability affected you" info token and the Druid's character token, and point at the two alive players neighboring the Druid — the Demon can only attack one of those two players. If the Demon's ability has the Storyteller choose whom to attack, the Storyteller can only choose to kill one of the two alive players neighboring the Druid.
examples: On the second night, the two alive players neighboring the Druid are the Baron (evil) and the Fortune Teller (good); the Demon may attack any target. That night the Demon kills the Saint.

On the second night, the two alive players neighboring the Druid are the Saint (good) and the Fortune Teller (good). When waking the Demon, the Storyteller shows the Demon the Druid's character token and points at the Saint player and the Fortune Teller player; the Demon can only choose one of them. That night the Demon kills the Saint.
tips: If you're the Druid, don't reveal your character before the Demon's first attack — you need that night's deaths to judge whether your ability took effect. If the Demon knows you're the Druid, they may deliberately kill players beside you to muddle your judgment.
If you're the Druid and the two players neighboring you share a team, the Demon cannot kill you, nor any player other than those two.

If you're the Druid and your ability took effect, the Demon definitely already knows you're the Druid. So if a player beside you dies at night, you'd best announce you're the Druid and discuss last night's deaths with everyone.
If you're the Druid and a player beside you died at night because your ability forced the Demon to kill them, then the two players beside you share a team — either both good or both evil.
If you're the Demon and you were woken and told to choose only between two players, the player sitting between them is definitely the Druid.
If you're the Demon and you know who the Druid is, with an evil player beside them, you can deliberately kill the good player to make the evil one look good.
If you're the Demon, the Druid's existence severely disrupts your knife work — deal with them quickly, by execution or by a Minion's killing ability.

If you're the Demon and you notice the Druid is poisoned, their ability won't take effect, and the Druid will usually assume an evil player sits beside them. Exploit this to attack the players beside the Druid as if they were evil.
bluffing: Bluffing as the Druid usually requires close coordination with the Demon, or your story won't hold together.
To bluff as the Druid, plan your strategy. A Druid typically jumps out when the night's dead player isn't one of their living neighbors, since that means an evil player sits beside them.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Forced Choice" ×2]]
Placed when: Whenever the two alive players neighboring the Druid are both good or both evil.
Condition: This token's placement is dynamically checked. Place it while the condition holds; remove it immediately when it doesn't. It is only ever placed by the character tokens of the two alive players neighboring the Druid.
Removed when: The Druid dies or leaves play, or the dynamic check fails.
Special note: the dynamic check examines the Druid's two neighboring alive players and whether their teams match, so it must be re-checked whenever the life status or team of either alive player neighboring the Druid changes.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A Townsfolk design that forcibly controls the Demon's knife, similar to the Ogre — but far more balanced than the Ogre. The ability text also avoids clunky phrasing like "they die, and the Demon can cause no deaths tonight."

The Druid is inherently an exposed character: once the Demon's knife is controlled, the Demon immediately deduces who the Druid is from the position of the forced choices. Yet the Druid's ability text never mentions exposure. The ability is concise and easy to understand while achieving kill-control, exposure, and information output all at once.

In the design of functional, logic-driven Townsfolk, the Druid pushes further with the innovative form of forcibly controlling the Demon's knife work.

characters.name: Myconid
characters.ability: Minions that die by execution keep their ability. You do too.
characters.lede: The Myconid and Minions don't lose their abilities to execution.
characters.quote: Dead mushrooms grow mushrooms. Dead bad people grow mushrooms too.
summaryBullets: A Minion who already keeps their ability doesn't lose it when the Myconid dies by execution — but does lose it when the Myconid dies from anything other than execution.
As long as the Myconid has their ability when a Minion dies by execution (whether the Myconid is alive, or dead but keeping their ability), that Minion keeps their ability.

When a dead Minion who kept their ability becomes a non-Minion character, they no longer keep it, since they're no longer a Minion. But if they change from one Minion to another Minion, they keep their new Minion ability.
If a dead non-Minion player becomes a Minion, they don't keep the Minion ability through the Myconid, because they weren't a Minion when they died by execution.
howToRun: When the Myconid or a Minion dies by execution, place the "Keeps Ability" reminder by their character token. If a Minion keeps their ability, you must keep waking them or using their ability as normal. If the Myconid keeps their ability, Minions who previously kept their abilities through the Myconid still keep them, and Minions who die by execution afterward also keep theirs.
If the Myconid dies from anything other than execution, remove all "Keeps Ability" reminders; from that point on, no player keeps their ability through the Myconid.
examples: On the first day, the Myconid is alive; the Witch dies by execution and keeps her ability. That night, the Myconid is killed by the Demon; the Witch loses her ability.
On the first day, the Myconid dies by execution and keeps their ability. On the second day, the Witch dies by execution and keeps her ability.

On the first day, the Myconid is alive; the Witch dies by execution and keeps her ability. On the second day, the Myconid dies by execution and keeps their ability, so the Witch still keeps her ability. On the third day, the Assassin dies by execution and keeps their ability.
tips: If you're the Myconid, try not to be executed — if you die by execution, executed Minions keep their abilities for the entire game!
If you're the Myconid and you die from anything other than execution — wonderful! No Minion will ever keep their ability because of you!
If you're the Myconid, you can hide yourself as much as possible or bluff as an important Townsfolk, baiting the Demon into killing you at night.
If you're a Minion and you're certain the Myconid is in play, you can boldly get executed — you won't lose your ability even so.
If you're the Demon, carefully avoid attacking the Myconid! Killing the Myconid makes Minions lose already-kept abilities or stops them from keeping abilities through execution.
bluffing: In the early-to-mid game, good players generally won't want to execute a Myconid. But in the mid-to-late game, the Myconid can't escape execution through their ability — because a living Myconid and an execution-dead Myconid both let Minions keep abilities.

In games with obvious traces of Minion abilities, the Myconid is an excellent bluff. You can argue Minion abilities persist because of your ability, and that earlier execution-dead players included a Minion.
To bluff as the Myconid, don't reveal yourself in the early-to-mid game — real Myconids usually try to bluff as other characters early on.
The Myconid is a fine backup bluff, since the ability inherently makes Myconid players hide their true character. If your earlier bluff falls apart, say you're the Myconid!
characters.creator: Taiyi, 星火乐

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Keeps Ability" ×4]]
Placed when: When the Myconid or a Minion dies by execution.
Condition: Place it by the character token of the Myconid or Minion who died by execution.
Removed when: The Myconid leaves play, or dies from anything other than execution.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Myconid's design frees Minions from fearing execution, extending to "any player who dies generously by execution might be a Minion." It nicely breaks the stereotyped logic in traditional scripts that "courting execution means good."

The Myconid's anti-suicide design merges with its core design — simple, crisp, elegant. The Myconid can't avoid their ability's negative effect by courting death, but they can bluff as another character to trick the Demon into killing them, dodging the negative effect that way. This gives players a unique game goal rather than a simple jail sentence.

The Myconid is also an excellent evil bluff: its ability traits mean it never reveals itself early. And Minions can judge whether the Myconid is in play from whether abilities persist after executions.

characters.name: Witness
characters.ability: Each day, visit the Storyteller to learn a true statement about a character type. If that type's count is abnormal, it is false.
characters.lede: The Witness learns daily information about the various character types.
characters.quote: I have seen Townsfolk pray by candlelight, and seen them write curses at the wall's base; I have seen Outsiders knock bearing gifts, and seen them secretly dig up coffins from the graveyard; I have seen Minions grovel at their master's shoes, and seen them kneel in repentance before the idol; I have seen the Demon's hands soaked in blood, and seen them moved to sorrow by a baby's cry. You think I'm telling good from evil? No — I'm merely looking into the same mirror, reflecting two different kinds of light.
summaryBullets: Abnormal player count for a character type: the number of players of some character type differs from the default setup. Characters that change the initial setup (Baron, Fang Gu) or that change players' characters mid-game (Pit-Hag, Imp) can cause a character type's count to become abnormal. In a 12-player game: Townsfolk count not equal to 7 is "abnormal"; Outsider count not equal to 2 is "abnormal"; Minion count not equal to 2 is "abnormal"; Demon count not equal to 1 is "abnormal."
True information: objectively true information; its correctness is not disturbed by any ability effect. Anything not true information is false information.
Whether you must give false information depends on whether, at the moment you give it, the relevant character type's player count differs from the default setup — i.e., is "abnormal."
Which character type the Witness's information relates to is decided by the Storyteller.
The Witness may choose not to get information from the Storyteller, if they wish.

Whether to talk with the Storyteller is up to the Witness, not the Storyteller. Getting information from the Storyteller is not public communication, so other players cannot listen in. The Witness gets information secretly.

The information you give must relate to exactly one character type (Townsfolk, Outsider, Minion, Demon). For Townsfolk-related information, you may give Townsfolk-type information (May and Sean are both Townsfolk) or Townsfolk-character information (May is the Fortune Teller). You may not give information linking multiple character types (e.g., "One of May and Sean is a Demon and the other a Townsfolk," or "Last night a Townsfolk became an Outsider").
Riddles and vague statements are forbidden, e.g., "Last night the blue Ultraman defeated the red-faced little monster."
The Witness does not learn Traveller-related information; Travellers are not treated as a character type (Traveller Exclusion Principle).

Reference information templates: 1) There are 3 Townsfolk among the alive players; 2) Either May or Sean is an Outsider; 3) Either May or Sean is the Baron; 4) The Fortune Teller is in play and the Seamstress is not; 5) The Demon killed multiple players last night; 6) The Demon is a girl; 7) Last night the Demon changed from the Vortox into the Fang Gu.
Information format: a phrase involving only one character type that expresses a clear meaning, as above.

False information format: a phrase involving only one character type that expresses a clear meaning, but whose content is false (e.g., "Either May or Sean is the Demon," when in fact neither is a Demon).
howToRun: Once per day, if the Witness asks for a private chat with you, leave the circle of players together so your conversation cannot be overheard. Then whisper to the Witness one true statement related to one character type (Townsfolk, Outsider, Minion, Demon).

If, at that moment, the number of players of some character type differs from the default number (refer to the player-count setup sheet), then if you give information about that character type, you must give false information.
examples: 12-player game (7/2/2/1), first day. The Witness visits the Storyteller and learns "The Fortune Teller and the Seamstress are both in play." Both are Townsfolk; this game, because of the Fang Gu, there is one more Outsider and one fewer Townsfolk, so the Townsfolk count is 6 — abnormal — and this game the Fortune Teller and the Seamstress are not both in play. "The Fortune Teller and the Seamstress are both in play" is false information.

12-player game (7/2/2/1), third day. The Witness visits the Storyteller and learns "May is the Imp." The Imp is a Demon; this game's Demon is the Imp, and there is one dead Imp and one living Imp in play, so the Demon count is 2 — abnormal — and May is not a Demon. "May is the Imp" is false information.

12-player game (7/2/2/1), second day. The Witness visits the Storyteller and learns "Either May or Sean is the Baron." The Baron is a Minion; the Minion count is 2 — not abnormal — and Sean is the Baron. "Either May or Sean is the Baron" is true information.
tips: If you're the Witness, your information isn't necessarily true. Remember: if the player count of the character type you learned about is abnormal, your information is false! If you've learned a character that adds or removes Outsiders or Townsfolk is in play, you can deduce that your information about Outsiders or Townsfolk is false!

If you're the Witness, false information isn't useless either. If you can confirm a statement is false, the player count for that character type is very likely abnormal, and you can reason backwards from that statement.

If you're the Demon, the flood of information the Witness brings is very bad for evil. Watch which players visit the Storyteller every day, identify the Witness among them, and deal with them quickly.

If you're an evil player, the truth of the Witness's information is tied to abnormal character counts. If some in-play character count is abnormal and good doesn't know it, mislead them as much as possible!
If you're an evil player whose ability can change character types, you can use that to make the Witness produce false information.
bluffing: To bluff as the Witness, remember to visit the Storyteller every day, mimicking the Witness's ability usage!
Be careful: the Witness's information only ever involves one character type! If your report breaks this format, it's practically a confession that you're evil.
If you don't know what information to make up, ask the Storyteller for help! They'll offer suggestions that can help you.
Your information should tie in with "abnormal character counts" and be logically self-consistent, or you may be branded an evil player fabricating information.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
An old topic — comparison with the closest official character is unavoidable. The Savant gets one true and one false statement daily: enormous information volume, with the challenge of telling which is which. The Witness gets one statement daily, drastically shrinking the volume, with correctness instead tied to "abnormal character counts."

"Abnormal character count" is itself a concept extended from common Savant information formats. The Witness directly adopts this already widely understood concept, producing a simpler, easier character with real gameplay depth.

The Witness's information format is strictly bounded to "related to one character type," preventing abstract Storytellers from giving infuriating statements.

The Witness is a systemic character, strongly linked with characters that change the initial setup (such as the Lord of Typhon, Fang Gu, Baron) or change characters (Pit-Hag, Imp). Well-suited for script writers building an overall design around the whole system.

characters.name: Riddler
characters.ability: Each day, you may visit the Storyteller to learn a riddle. The riddle's answer points to a character in play.
characters.lede: The Riddler receives a maddening riddle every day.
characters.quote: No way, no way — don't tell me someone actually can't guess it?
summaryBullets: The Riddler demands strong pacing control and creativity from the Storyteller, or problems like an overpowered Riddler or unhappy players may arise. When running a script with the Riddler, it's best to tell players in advance that the Riddler is a semi-entertainment character, and riddles have no rigorous, unique answer.
Riddles have no fixed format — they can be a phrase, a string of numbers, a symbol, or even a gesture.

Riddles require clever construction by the Storyteller. A good riddle shouldn't be too easy to solve, and when you finally reveal the answer, players should smile knowingly. Unlike other "free-information" Townsfolk who demand clear, unambiguous information, the Riddler is designed for the Storyteller to provide the most mischievous, misleading, funny information possible.
You can control the Riddler's strength via riddle difficulty. When good is weak, give simpler riddles. When evil is weak, give harder or more misleading ones.

The Riddler's ceiling is learning one in-play character per day, but that strength is unfair to evil. So in most cases you should avoid letting the Riddler reach that strength through riddle design. Generally, a riddle that can point to more than one character on the script is relatively balanced.
What riddles the Riddler gets is decided by the Storyteller.
The Riddler may choose not to get a riddle from the Storyteller, if they wish.
Whether to talk with the Storyteller is up to the Riddler, not the Storyteller. Getting a riddle is not public communication, so other players cannot listen in. The Riddler gets riddles secretly.

If you're the Storyteller, your riddles should be well-founded, but players may misunderstand them. Don't worry — patiently discuss and explain with players after the game; the Storyteller is part of the game too.
The Riddler does not get riddles related to Traveller characters (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: a phrase, a string of numbers, a symbol, a gesture, or other innovative riddle forms.
False information format: a riddle whose answer points to no character in play (a phrase, numbers, a symbol, a gesture, or other innovative forms).
howToRun: Once per day, if the Riddler asks for a private chat with you, leave the circle of players together so your conversation cannot be overheard. Then whisper a riddle to the Riddler.
The riddle's answer must point to a character in play.
examples: On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "I heard your icy heartbeat." The answer points to the Engineer, because the Engineer listens to machinery at work.
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "Jinhua ham." The answer points to the Sailor, because the antonym of the Sailor's single-word breakdown is "ham."
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "6." The answer points to the Gambler, because a die has 6 faces.
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "4." The answer points to the Professor, because the Professor's icon contains 4 atoms.
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "5." The answer points to the Balloonist, because "Balloonist" is 5 characters long.
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "Crazy Thursday." The answer points to the Pacifist, because the Pacifist's icon is a bird (alluding to a chicken).
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "Great tonic." The answer points to the Pacifist, because the Pacifist's icon is a bird (alluding to a chicken).
On the first day, the Riddler visits the Storyteller and learns "Born lying in a pair, mouths parting mountains and rivers." The answer points to the Seamstress.
tips: If you're the Riddler, guess as hard as you can which in-play character the riddle points to! If you truly can't, publish your riddle and let everyone help you.
If you're the Riddler and really can't solve it, use elimination: rule out the characters it definitely isn't.
If you're an evil player, the Riddler can be very weak or very strong. Mislead everyone's guesses at the answers as much as possible — make them misjudge which characters are in play.
bluffing: If you're an evil player who doesn't fear death, make up whatever riddle you like! A number, a nonsense sentence, even a gesture! You don't even need to design an answer! Who cares — let the good team puzzle over it slowly!

If you're the Demon bluffing as the Riddler, be more careful with your riddle design. Don't be easily seen as making things up; at least one or two riddles should clearly point to one or two in-play characters, which makes you far more credible.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A salute to Storytellers who love being abstract — your favorite character is here. Craft your riddles well; if you can't, you're dead to me. And stop feeding the Savant random abstract nonsense from now on!

Though the Riddler was designed from an entertainment angle, it strictly follows the design model. Learning one in-play character per day is overpowered; blurring the information on top of that achieves balance.

The Riddler focuses on inspiring the Storyteller's creativity and the players' puzzle-discussing atmosphere, catering to Storytellers with abundant creativity and players with abundant appetite for fun.

characters.name: Shaman
characters.ability: Once per game, at night*, choose 4 characters of different types: for each not in play, a same-type player becomes that character.
characters.lede: The Shaman can change many players' characters in one go.
characters.quote: Crave power? I'll grant it. Crave freedom? I'll grant that too. But the price is losing your human shape. Kneel, and let me stuff your souls into sheepskins. Tremble — you'll find yourselves growing fur, dropping to all fours, your minds left with nothing but chewing and fleeing. Don't worry about getting lost — the pen I've prepared for you lies just ahead.
summaryBullets: After the Shaman makes his choices, first determine which of his chosen characters are not in play. Then, in the order Townsfolk → Outsider → Minion → Demon, choose a player of the same type for each and change their character. It cannot happen that the Shaman chooses an in-play character, that in-play character's player is turned into another character by the Shaman, and the character is then re-judged as not in play, causing another player to become that character.
To use his ability, the Shaman must choose exactly 4 characters, one of each different type (Townsfolk, Outsider, Minion, Demon) — no more, no fewer.
If the Shaman turns himself into another character while the transformations aren't finished yet, the Shaman's ability doesn't stop because of it.
If the Shaman chooses a not-in-play character but no player of that type is in play, no player's character changes.
The Storyteller — not the Shaman — decides which players become the not-in-play characters the Shaman chose.
The Shaman's ability cannot choose Traveller characters (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Shaman. He may shake his head, or choose one character of each of the four different types. Note which of his chosen characters are not in play, then choose a player of the same type for each not-in-play character, wake that player, show them in turn the "You are" info token and their new character token, then put them back to sleep. Continue until every not-in-play character has been transformed. Once the Shaman has used his ability, do not wake the Shaman on later nights.
