examples: On the second night, the Shaman chooses the Vortox, the Poisoner, the Saint, and the Fortune Teller. None of these characters is in play. The Fang Gu becomes the Vortox, the Baron becomes the Poisoner, the Butler becomes the Saint, and the Empath becomes the Fortune Teller.

On the second night, the Shaman chooses the Vortox, the Poisoner, the Saint, and the Fortune Teller. The Vortox is not in play; the Poisoner, Saint, and Fortune Teller are in play. The Fang Gu becomes the Vortox.

On the third night, the Shaman chooses the Vortox, the Poisoner, the Saint, and the Fortune Teller. The Vortox and the Fortune Teller are in play; the Poisoner and the Saint are not. The Shaman becomes the Poisoner, and the Ogre becomes the Saint.
tips: If you're the Shaman, your ability is powerful — you can change the Demon's type, change Minion types, create Outsiders that weren't in play. You can even do all of these at once. But you only get one chance — act with caution.

If you're the Shaman, using your ability early — when you're unfamiliar with which characters are in play — makes it easy to hit Townsfolk or Outsiders, which easily exposes you. Using it in the mid-to-late game, when you know the in-play situation better, gives you more control over which character types change and which don't.

If you're the Shaman and you transform Outsiders or Townsfolk, the changed players will very likely announce their character changed — exposing you. Be mentally prepared for this. But if that was your goal all along, them stepping forward saves you the trouble of finding them.
If you're good and you get turned into a character of the same type, the Shaman is very likely using his ability. Announce it quickly — the Minion and Demon types may well have changed too.
If you're good, don't over-fear the Shaman — his ability is powerful, but he only gets one chance.
If you're good and you think the in-play Minion or Demon characters changed, the Shaman may have used his ability — the Shaman can turn Demons and Minions into not-in-play characters all at once.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a character.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[No Ability]]
Placed when: When the Shaman chooses to use his ability during his night action.
Condition: As long as the Shaman chose characters, place this reminder by the Shaman's character token regardless of whether the Shaman is drunk or poisoned.
Removed when: The Shaman dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
One-shot, large-scale, mass polymorph — thunder! Cool!

The Shaman chooses the characters; the Storyteller decides the players — giving the player room to operate while the Storyteller controls the ability's floor and ceiling.

Self-balancing design. If the Shaman uses his ability early, he easily hits not-in-play Townsfolk or Outsiders, exposing himself. Used late, it's easier to hide — but the death risk grows enormously.

characters.name: Pearl Diver
characters.ability: On your 1st night, you learn how many steps you are from an evil player.
characters.lede: The Pearl Diver learns how far she sits from an evil player.
characters.quote: Everything I take from the sea, the sea takes something from me. At forty, it took my hearing; at fifty, one knee. But what I've earned in return is sight of the undercurrents' direction, and the smell of rust in the water before a storm. Does the sea bully people? No — things at sea are far fairer than things ashore.
summaryBullets: The Pearl Diver learns her distance from any one evil player; the Storyteller decides which evil player. It can be a Minion, a Demon, or another evil player.
The distance the Pearl Diver learns may be measured clockwise or counterclockwise.
When computing distance, the value equals the number of players seated between the Pearl Diver and the player she learns about, plus 1. So the smallest number the Pearl Diver can learn is "1."
When computing distance, dead players still count (if any).
Both players corresponding to the distance the Pearl Diver learns may be evil, or only one of them.
The Pearl Diver's ability ignores Travellers (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: a number (e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4).

False information format: a number at whose distance (in either direction) there is no evil player. For example: if both players at distance 1 from the Pearl Diver are good, then "1" is false information.
howToRun: On the first night, wake the Pearl Diver. Gesture a number to her representing her distance from one evil player (1, 2, 3, etc.). Put the Pearl Diver back to sleep.
examples: The Pearl Diver in seat 1 learns "1," because she sits next to the Minion in seat 2.
12-player game. The Pearl Diver in seat 1 learns "5," because her distance from the Demon in seat 6 is 5 (clockwise).
12-player game. The Pearl Diver in seat 1 learns "7," because her distance from the Demon in seat 6 is 7 (counterclockwise).
Player #1 is the Pearl Diver, player #2 is a Minion, player #3 is an Outsider, player #4 is a Minion. The Pearl Diver learns "3"; the player her information corresponds to is player #4.
tips: If you're the Pearl Diver and you learned 1, at least one of your two neighbors is evil! Go public and try to execute them.
If you're the Pearl Diver, you can simply understand your ability as: you learn about 2 players, at least one of whom is evil.
If you're the Pearl Diver and for some reason you believe your information is false (e.g., the Vortox is in play), then both players at your learned distance are good.
bluffing: Bluffing as the Pearl Diver, you can report information covering 2 good players to attack them as containing an evil player.

Bluffing as the Pearl Diver, if you'd rather survive, you can report information covering an evil player — e.g., a Minion really does sit at that distance. This helps everyone trust you as a genuine Pearl Diver.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Show her a number — her distance from an evil player.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Standard evil-finding model: learn 2 players, 1 of them evil.

The Pearl Diver's ability went through many reworks without a satisfying version. Because of the Odyssey character pack, we finally decided to fill the remaining gaps among official character slots as much as possible, so the ability was reworked into something very simple.

The Pearl Diver's ability is essentially "learn 2 players, one of whom is evil." By current standards this model is slightly weak (compare the similar Investigator: the Investigator only learns Minions, which is slightly weaker than learning evil players, but learns a specific Minion character, greatly raising the information value). It just re-expresses the idea through the concept of distance. This reduces Storyteller control to a degree, since the Storyteller cannot change the distances between players — a subtle buff.

Compared with similar characters like the Investigator and the Noble, the differences are simplicity and better Vortox resistance.

characters.name: Versifier
characters.ability: Each night, learn a word of a famous phrase or poem. The 1st player to recite the whole phrase is executed, even if you are dead.
characters.lede: A player who recites the Versifier's phrase is executed on the spot.
characters.quote: The bright moon startles the crows, restless in their roost; the water-clock runs low, the windlass draws from the golden well.
summaryBullets: The Versifier's phrase can be a famous phrase or line of poetry, usually 5–8 words long. You can decide freely based on player count — generally, the more players, the longer the phrase.
It's not recommended to give the Versifier repeated words, except when the phrase itself contains repeated words.
As long as you fully hear a player recite the Versifier's phrase, you must execute him immediately — even if he's already dead.
After dying, the Versifier loses the ability to get a hint word each night — but doesn't lose the ability to force-execute players who recite the phrase.
If a player recites the Versifier's phrase while the Versifier is drunk or poisoned, the Versifier's ability is not consumed by it.
Once the Versifier's execution ability has triggered, do not wake the Versifier on subsequent nights.
Traveller players cannot trigger the Versifier's ability, even if they recite correctly (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: While preparing for the first night, prepare a famous phrase or line of poetry for the Versifier.
Each night, wake the Versifier and tell him one word of that phrase. Then put him back to sleep.

The first time you hear a player speak the whole phrase, immediately announce that player is executed — even if the Versifier is already dead. Then place the "No Ability" reminder by the Versifier's character token.
examples: The Versifier's phrase is "月落乌啼霜满天". On the first night, the Versifier learns "乌". On the second night, the Versifier learns "天". On the third night, the Versifier learns "月". The next day, the Versifier loudly recites "月落乌啼霜满天" — the Versifier is immediately executed.

The Versifier's phrase is "牧童遥指杏花村". On the first night, the Versifier learns "杏". The next day, the Versifier dies by execution. The Versifier gets no more characters. On the day with 5 players alive, the Versifier loudly recites "一枝红杏出墙来" — nothing happens. The Versifier then recites "杏花零落水痕肥" — nothing happens. The Versifier then recites "牧童遥指杏花村" — the Versifier is immediately executed.
The Versifier's phrase is "烟蒲绿自生". A Townsfolk loudly recites "烟蒲绿自生" during the day — he is immediately executed.
tips: If you're the Versifier, your top priority is figuring out exactly which phrase yours is. To achieve this, survive to the mid-to-late game — with only one or two words, it's hard to pin down the phrase.

If you're the Versifier, even after you're dead, the force-execution part of your ability still works — you can recite the phrase yourself or have your teammates recite it to force an execution. Better still, trick a good player into reciting it.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.tags: Even If Dead, Execution, Information, Loud
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake him and show him a character.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him and show him a character.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[No Ability]]
Placed when: The first time a player speaks the Versifier's phrase and the Storyteller hears it.
Condition: After a player is executed by the Versifier's ability.
Removed when: The Versifier dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Keywords: tempo Minion, mini-puzzle design, claiming evil.

Force-executing a dead player costs half a tempo; force-executing an alive player costs a full tempo — effectively giving the evil team a self-destruct ability.

Granting one character per night encourages the player to survive into the late game.

characters.name: Crosswing
characters.ability: On your Xth night, you may poison the players at distance X from you until dusk.
characters.lede: Crosswing slowly unfurls — every player she touches is poisoned.
characters.quote: People always say wings are a token of flight toward the light — yet they don't know some wings are born to measure the reach of shadows. Touched souls, do not panic, do not pursue. You merely happen to be standing in the gap between me and the light.
summaryBullets: The X value depends on which night of the game it is (note: not Crosswing's Xth night). On the game's first night, X is 1. On the game's second night, X is 2. And so on.
Generally, there are 2 players at distance X from Crosswing. In rare cases, only one.

If Crosswing chooses to use her ability, all players at distance X from Crosswing are poisoned — regardless of whether they're Townsfolk, Minions, Outsiders, or the Demon, and whether they're alive or dead.
Crosswing's ability ignores Travellers (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night, wake Crosswing. He nods, or shakes his head to not use his ability. If Crosswing nods, place "Poisoned" reminders by the character tokens of all players whose distance from Crosswing equals the current night number of the game. Put Crosswing back to sleep.
Each dusk, poisoned players recover — remove their Poisoned reminders.
examples: On the first night, Crosswing at seat #6 is woken and nods to use her ability; that night, the two players at distance 1 from #6 Crosswing — #5 the Fortune Teller and #7 the Saint — are poisoned until the end of the next day. On the second night, #6 Crosswing is woken and nods; the two players at distance 2 — #4 the Pit-Hag and #8 the Gossip — are poisoned until the end of the next day. On the third night, #6 Crosswing is woken and shakes her head; the two players at distance 3 — #3 the Imp and #9 the Banshee — are not poisoned.
tips: If you're Crosswing, carefully judge who will be poisoned by you each night! Try to poison Townsfolk players, and avoid poisoning non-Townsfolk players — that brings many complications, like Outsider abilities failing or the Demon being unable to kill his target.

If you're Crosswing and you find some good players trying to judge whether Crosswing is in play or where Crosswing sits based on whether their abilities fail, you can deliberately skip poisoning them to disrupt their judgment.
If you're Crosswing, note: if you die, nobody gets poisoned by you anymore. Survive into the late game if possible.

If you're a good player, Crosswing's poisoning is always symmetric! If you think a player is poisoned by Crosswing, you can deduce the position of the other poisoned player — and Crosswing's position.
If you're a Townsfolk, generally you'll be poisoned by Crosswing at most one night, because the poison skips past you the next night. Remember this.

If you're a good player, a cunning Crosswing may deliberately not use her ability! If players who should have been poisoned by Crosswing have their abilities work normally, that doesn't prove Crosswing isn't in play!
characters.creator: Taiyi, 洋平 (Yangping)
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake Crosswing; he nods or shakes his head.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake Crosswing; he nods or shakes his head.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Poisoned" ×2]]
Placed when: After Crosswing uses her ability.
Condition: Place it by the character tokens of all players at distance (current night number) from Crosswing. If Crosswing is drunk or poisoned at this time, do not place this reminder.
Removed when: When the day phase ends, or when Crosswing dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: A poisoning Minion — as always, comparison with the Poisoner and the other official poisoning Minions is unavoidable: the Poisoner — always one player poisoned, switches targets without a trace, poisons whoever he wants; the Widow — always one player poisoned, but exposed, and can't move the poison; the Xian — poisons everyone, but only for one night, linked to the Outsider count, slightly exposed. Crosswing — poisons 2 players a night, a heavy dose, can poison every night — but the poison follows a pattern and can't be freely aimed.

characters.name: Paladin
characters.ability: Each night, you learn 2 players: either both are not Minions, or both are not Demons. The 2 clue types alternate each night.
characters.lede: The Paladin learns which players are not Minions or Demons.
characters.quote: Last night I knelt before the holy altar in prayer, and the voice of God fell on my shoulders like flame: 'Go to that town — my lambs are there.' So I came. There is no rust on my armor, for every scratch has been washed in holy water; my blade stays forever warm, for God's power flows within it. Where there is injustice, where there is weeping, there is my battlefield.
summaryBullets: Which clue type the Paladin learns each night is fixed when the Paladin enters play. If, on a night when the Paladin should learn "not Minion" players, he instead learns "not Demon" players due to poison or drunkenness, then the next night — if he is sober and healthy again — he still learns "not Demon" players. It does not switch to "not Minion" just because last night went wrong.
The Paladin does not learn Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: 2 players (e.g., "players #1 and #2" or "May and Sean").

False information format: 2 players not matching the current reminder. For example: while the "Not Minion" token is in play, any 2 players including at least one Minion are false information; while the "Not Demon" token is in play, any 2 players including at least one Demon are false information.
howToRun: When the Paladin enters play, place the "Not Minion" or "Not Demon" reminder by the Paladin's character token.

Each night, wake the Paladin. If the "Not Minion" reminder is by the Paladin's character token, point at two players who are not Minions, then replace the "Not Minion" reminder with "Not Demon." If the "Not Demon" reminder is by the Paladin's character token, point at two players who are not Demons, then replace the "Not Demon" reminder with "Not Minion."
examples: On the first night the Paladin learns May and Sean; May is a Minion, Sean is a Townsfolk. On the second night he learns Zach and Will; Zach is a Demon, Will is an Outsider. On the third night he learns Will and Sean; Will is an Outsider, Sean is a Townsfolk. The Paladin's sequence was not-Demon → not-Minion → not-Demon.

On the first night the Paladin learns May and Sean; May and Sean are both Townsfolk. On the second night he learns Zach and Will; both are Outsiders. On the third night he learns Cole and Wyn; both are Townsfolk. The Paladin's sequence was not-Minion → not-Demon → not-Minion.
tips: If you're the Paladin, work out which nights correspond to not-Minion and which to not-Demon. This is crucial.
If you're the Paladin, a single day of information doesn't help you much — survive as long as you can.

If you're the Paladin, your information may look less useful than directly learning who is good or who is a Townsfolk — but once you figure out what your information corresponds to, it massively aids logic-building.
If you're an evil player, leaving the Paladin alive is an absolute threat to evil — kill him as early as possible.
bluffing: Your information mostly protects certain players. Report players who look good as much as possible — it makes you look more like a real Paladin.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Tell him two players.
characters.otherNightReminder: Tell him two players.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Not Minion]]
Placed when: When the Paladin enters play, or after the Paladin acts.
Condition: When the Paladin enters play, or when the "Not Demon" reminder is removed.
Removed when: After the Paladin acts.

[[Not Demon]]
Placed when: When the Paladin enters play, or after the Paladin acts.
Condition: When the Paladin enters play, or when the "Not Minion" reminder is removed.
Removed when: After the Paladin acts.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A small puzzle design: the Paladin must discern what each night's information corresponds to.

Closest official characters: the Knight, the Fortune Teller, the Town Crier — each with pros and cons.

characters.name: Alewife
characters.ability: When a Minion is executed, they do not die but become drunk.
characters.lede: The Alewife keeps executed Minions from death but leaves them drunk.
characters.quote: This special reserve of mine isn't for just anyone. Only when a great personage like yourself walks through the door do I bear to bring it up from the cellar. Have a taste — it'll put strength in your every limb! But don't rush; sip it slowly. Drink too fast and the kick hits you all at once, and I couldn't lift you back up.
summaryBullets: As long as the Alewife is in play, no matter how many times a Minion is executed, they do not die.
A Minion's drunkenness lasts until the Alewife dies or leaves play.

If the Alewife is poisoned or drunk while a Minion is drunk from her ability, the Minion temporarily sobers up and can die by execution. When the Alewife regains her ability, the Minion returns to being drunk — even if the Minion is already dead by then.
howToRun: When a Minion is executed, cancel that death and place the "Drunk" reminder by that Minion's character token. If that Minion already has the Alewife's "Drunk" reminder, do not place another.
examples: The Alewife is in play. On the first day, the Baron is executed; the Baron does not die, and the Baron becomes drunk.
The Alewife is in play. On the second day, the Devil's Advocate protected themself; the Devil's Advocate is executed, does not die, and becomes drunk.
tips: If you're the Alewife, remember: as long as you stay sober and healthy, no player who dies by execution is a Minion!
If you're the Alewife and a player didn't die by execution, stay alert — they're very likely a Minion protected by your ability!
If you're the Alewife and your ability protected a Minion, that Minion is drunk from now on, meaning they've lost their ability. But if you die, that Minion regains their ability.
If you're the Alewife, don't reveal your identity too early before any player has survived an execution — the Demon can attack you to un-drunk their Minions.
If you're a Minion and you unexpectedly find you didn't die by execution, the Alewife is very likely in play. Deny being a Minion and find any other explanation you can for why you didn't die.
If you're a Minion protected by the Alewife from death, you are drunk from now on. Use your ability cautiously so as not to waste it.
bluffing: If you're another character who can cause execution survival, such as the Devil's Advocate, you can claim to be the Alewife — the player who didn't die by execution is a Minion you protected.
If you go public as the Alewife, it means every player who previously died by execution wasn't a Minion. If people don't accept that, you may not be trusted.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Drunk" ×3]]
Placed when: When a Minion is executed.
Condition: A Minion is executed and the Alewife is not poisoned or drunk; place it by that Minion's character token.
Removed when: The Alewife dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: A bold design, an advanced understanding — no more salt needed; time will tell.

characters.name: Squid Girl
characters.ability: If you are about to die, you might not die, but all Townsfolk are drunk until dusk tomorrow.
characters.lede: Squid Girl makes players drunk when threatened with death.
characters.quote: Pshhh— ah! It's already leaking! Oh no, oh no, it's going out of control! Pshhhhhh—
summaryBullets: Whenever Squid Girl is about to die, you must decide whether to trigger her ability. You may trigger Squid Girl's ability multiple times, or not at all. If you decide not to trigger it, she dies normally.
Any cause that would kill Squid Girl may trigger her ability, including but not limited to execution and character abilities.

Squid Girl only triggers Townsfolk drunkenness when she survives death through her own ability. For example, if Squid Girl survives an execution because of the Devil's Advocate's protection, her ability definitely cannot trigger — because Squid Girl never entered the "about to die" state.
If Squid Girl dies, she loses her ability and all players drunk because of her sober up.
howToRun: When Squid Girl is about to die, if you decide to trigger Squid Girl's ability, Squid Girl does not die and all Townsfolk are drunk — place Squid Girl's "Townsfolk Drunk" reminder.
At dusk the next day, all players made drunk by Squid Girl sober up — remove the "Townsfolk Drunk" reminder.
examples: On the first day, the Psychopath publicly chooses Squid Girl; Squid Girl does not die, and all Townsfolk become drunk.
On the first day, the Golem nominates Squid Girl; Squid Girl does not die, and all Townsfolk become drunk.
On the second night, the Imp chooses Squid Girl; Squid Girl does not die, and all Townsfolk become drunk.
On the first day, Squid Girl is executed; Squid Girl does not die, and all Townsfolk become drunk. On the second day, Squid Girl is executed; Squid Girl dies.
tips: If you're Squid Girl, you have the power to escape death — but unfortunately, your ability can't be guaranteed to trigger. If you should have died but didn't, your ability may have worked.
If you're Squid Girl and you didn't die by execution, or an abnormal safe night occurred, it's best to tell all players you're Squid Girl — otherwise you severely confuse everyone else.
If you're the Demon and you know who Squid Girl is, attack her at the right time to try triggering her ability, disrupting the Townsfolk's abilities.
If you're the Demon and you attacked a player who didn't die, she might be Squid Girl! If she survived through Squid Girl's ability, all Townsfolk are now drunk.
bluffing: If you have an ability that keeps you from dying by execution, such as the Devil's Advocate, you can bluff as Squid Girl. If you're executed but don't die, that helps prove you're Squid Girl.
If a safe night occurs, you can claim to be Squid Girl — reasonably explaining the safe night while implying all Townsfolk are drunk.
characters.creator: Taiyi, 卡布达

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Townsfolk Drunk]]
Placed when: When Squid Girl is about to die.
Condition: Place it when you decide to trigger Squid Girl's ability.
Removed when: At dusk the day after this token was placed. Also remove it when Squid Girl dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Provides more execution-survival logic and safe-night logic, offering more options for Bad-Moon-style scripts.

As an interference Outsider, she combines execution survival, safe nights, and logic interference beautifully. The side effect is huge but the traces are obvious, and those traces can blend with other public phenomena to form systemic design. An excellent design.

characters.name: Tornado
characters.ability: Each night, choose a player: they die. Each dusk, you swap characters with the alive evil player nearest to you clockwise.
characters.lede: The Tornado keeps changing position in a fixed direction.
characters.quote: Your blades? Too dull. Your arrows? Too slow. Your eyes? They can probably only catch my footprints — provided I bother leaving any on the ground. Don't get me wrong, I'm not afraid of you — I just can't be bothered to be touched. A mortal brushing my hem? Filthy.
summaryBullets: The Tornado's night order position only serves as a reference for his attack ability. The character-swapping ability always happens at every dusk except the first.
Each dusk:* every dusk except the first dusk — that is, the moment players close their eyes after each day's execution concludes.
The Tornado swaps characters with the alive evil player nearest to him clockwise — whether that player is a Minion, a Townsfolk, an Outsider, or the Demon.
If there are no other alive evil players, the Tornado doesn't swap characters.
The Tornado's ability ignores Travellers, and the Tornado's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Tornado. Have the Tornado point to a player and kill that player — that player dies; place the "Dead" reminder by their character token. Put the Tornado back to sleep.

After nightfall each day, swap the characters of the Tornado and the alive evil player nearest to him clockwise — wake the Tornado, show him the "You are" info token and his new character token, then put him back to sleep. Wake the new Tornado player, show him the "You are" info token and the Tornado's character token, then put him back to sleep.
examples: On the first day, a player dies by execution. At nightfall, the Tornado player (#1) swaps characters with the Poisoner player (#3); the Tornado player (#1) is woken and learns he's become the Poisoner, and the Poisoner player (#3) is woken and learns he's become the Tornado. That night, the new Poisoner (#1) poisons a player, and the new Tornado (#3) kills a player. After the next day's execution, the Tornado player (#3) swaps characters with the Baron player (#4) — night actions omitted. After yet another day's execution, the Tornado player (#4) swaps characters with the Poisoner player (#1).
tips: If you're the Tornado, the Tornado moves every day — coordinate countermeasures with your teammates to avoid the Demon suddenly dropping dead.
If you're the Tornado, you can play more aggressively over two days, since you'll soon no longer be the Demon — you can play yourself like a Minion.
If you're a Minion and the Demon is the Tornado, you'll soon become the new Tornado — careful! Don't talk yourself out of the game!

If you're a good player, the Tornado moves every day — conventional methods may struggle to pin down the Demon. You must predict where the Demon will move and deal with possible evil players in advance!
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: After the Tornado acts at night and chooses a player.
Condition: The player the Tornado chose is currently alive, can be killed by the Tornado, and the Tornado is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Common survival Demons come in two ability forms: death immunity and position swapping. Common swaps are usually limited-use and leave traces — the Tornado is the opposite: it must swap every day, a forced swap. Limited use is for balance; unlimited use is also for balance. Being able to swap is one kind of restriction; being forced to swap is another.

Due to his ability's peculiarity, the Tornado isn't recommended to share a script with once-per-game Minions — otherwise he may become overpowered.

characters.name: Warlock
characters.ability: If the Demon kills you, each night from now on, choose a player: they die.
characters.lede: The Warlock trades his life for forbidden power.
characters.quote: This contract was never a transaction, but a complete sacrifice. I staked my whole fated death, let my flesh rot back to dust, and let my soul bear the punishment of eternal damnation — all to trade for this demonic power. Do you see the black flames wreathing me? Every leaping dark fire is a rehearsal of the torture I must suffer when I fall into hell in my next life. Do not come provoke me: one who has already lived through the torment of eternal death keeps not a shred of mercy for the mortal world.
summaryBullets: If the Warlock is killed by the Demon, he does not act that night; he acts every night starting from the next night.
After being killed by the Demon, the Warlock acts before all Demons.
If the Warlock dies from anything other than the Demon's ability, his ability does not trigger.
On the night the Warlock is killed, he doesn't know whether his ability triggered; he judges by whether he is woken and uses his ability the following night.
The Warlock cannot choose Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: If the Warlock is killed by the Demon, place the "Has Ability" reminder by the Warlock's character token. Each night from then on, wake the Warlock and let him point at a player; kill that player and place the "Dead" reminder by their character token. Put the Warlock back to sleep.
examples: On the second night, the Imp kills the Warlock. On the third night, the Warlock is woken and kills the Imp. The game ends; good wins.
On the second night, the Fang Gu kills the Warlock. On the third night, the Warlock is woken and kills the Fortune Teller. On the fourth night, the Warlock is woken and kills the Assassin.
On the second night, the Assassin kills the Warlock. On later nights, the Warlock is never woken.
tips: If you're the Warlock, do everything you can to get the Demon to kill you.
If you're the Warlock and the Demon has killed you, you can corroborate that you're truly the Warlock by killing other players.
If you're the Warlock and the Demon has killed you, you can keep hiding your character and hunt suspected Demons every night. Kill the Demon and you win outright.
If you're the Warlock, judge whether your ability triggered by whether you're woken on the night after your death.
If you're the Demon, avoid killing the Warlock at all costs! Triggering his ability has severe consequences — he may turn around and kill you on later nights.
If you're the Demon and you accidentally killed the Warlock, act as much like a good player as possible! If he keeps not attacking you, he ends up helping you reach the final day faster.
bluffing: Bluff as another character first, then — after that bluff fails — admit you're actually the Warlock. That looks like something a Warlock would do.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Let him choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Has Ability]]
Placed when: When the Demon kills the Warlock.
Condition: If the Warlock is sober and healthy at that moment, place it by the Warlock's character token.
Removed when: The Warlock leaves play.

[[Dead]]
Placed when: After the Warlock acts at night and chooses a player.
Condition: The Warlock's chosen player is currently alive, can be killed by the Warlock, and the Warlock is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce the night's dead at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead at dawn, at the Storyteller's convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A landmine slot with a huge gap between floor and ceiling — capable of ending the game outright.

A radical design that hands good players a knife. Faster! Faster!

characters.name: Arbiter
characters.ability: If you nominate & execute another good player, they do not die.
characters.lede: Executions the Arbiter handles never wrongly behead a good player.
characters.quote: Order. I have not come to hear excuses, nor to display mercy. Your sins and merits are already carved into my eyes. I favor no lord and pity no weakling. The innocent, however clumsy of tongue, shall never face the blade; the guilty, however glib, shall never escape judgment. Now — bring them forward.
summaryBullets: If, on some day, the player the Arbiter nominated is executed for another reason (such as the Cerenovus or the Virgin), they are not protected by the Arbiter.
howToRun: If the Arbiter nominates and executes a player, and that player is good, that player does not die from this execution.
examples: On the first day, the Arbiter nominates and executes the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller does not die.
On the second day, the Arbiter nominates and executes the Poisoner; the Poisoner dies.
On the third day, the Arbiter nominates the Mutant. While arguing back, the Mutant carelessly reveals being an Outsider, and the Mutant is executed and dies from their own ability.
tips: If you're the Arbiter, you can go public as the Arbiter and call on everyone to follow your arrangements!
If you're the Arbiter, you can hide your identity but do everything possible to nominate and execute a player.
If you're the Arbiter and the player you nominated and executed didn't die, they're very likely a good player.
If you're the Arbiter and the player you nominated and executed died, they're very likely an evil player.
If you're the Demon and an executed player didn't die with no other reasonable explanation, the nominator is very likely the Arbiter!

If you're the Demon, leaving an Arbiter in play to preside over nominations every day is very dangerous — they'll keep protecting good players, and nobody but your teammates will die by execution! Find a way to kill them quickly.
bluffing: If the player you nominated and executed didn't die — wonderful! It perfectly corroborates you as the Arbiter.
If the player you nominated and executed died, attack them as an evil player!
If you're an evil player bluffing as the Arbiter, good players may repeatedly demand you nominate and execute people. If you fail to protect the executed, you may lose their trust.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A further exploration of execution-survival logic Townsfolk design.

If the Arbiter's nominee dies, nothing is proven; if the Arbiter's nominee doesn't die, it strongly suggests both the Arbiter and the executed player are good — but it exposes who the Arbiter is to the Demon.

Compared to the Tea Lady: the Tea Lady confirms three players and grants night protection; the Arbiter confirms two. Clearly weaker than the Tea Lady.

characters.name: Ninja
characters.ability: Each day, if you are the first or the last player to nominate, and the player you nominated is evil, they die that night.
characters.lede: The Ninja bides his time to assassinate defenseless evil players.
characters.quote: I've been crouching on the rafters for three days. I watched you while you ate; I listened while you whispered. I'm in no hurry. I wait only for that one second when you finally drop your guard — then a gust of wind, a shadow, the softest thud of a body falling. Killing never takes strength, only timing.
summaryBullets: The Ninja is never woken at night, whether or not he caused a death.
If the Ninja was neither the first nor the last player to nominate that day, nobody can die from his ability.

Whether a player dies at night from the Ninja's ability is determined by whether the "Assassinate" reminder is by their character token. If a marked player's team or character changes at night, it doesn't stop the Ninja from killing them.
If the Ninja dies before acting, nobody is killed by the Ninja.
howToRun: After the Ninja nominates, if the nominated player is evil, place the "Assassinate" reminder by that player's character token. If this was not the day's first nomination, and another player nominates afterward, remove the "Assassinate" reminder.
Each night, replace the "Assassinate" reminder with the "Dead" reminder — the marked player dies.
examples: On the first day, the Ninja is the first to nominate and nominates the Poisoner (evil). That night, the Poisoner dies.
On the first day, the Ninja is the first to nominate and nominates the Saint (good). That night, the Saint does not die.
On the second day, the Ninja is the last to nominate and nominates the Imp (evil). That night, the Imp dies.
On the second day, the Ninja is the last to nominate and nominates the Imp (evil). That night, the Imp kills the Ninja first, so the Imp does not die.
tips: If you're the Ninja, your ability directly identifies and kills evil players — extremely powerful! But the trigger conditions are strict: you must nominate first or last, and dodge the Demon's suspicion — otherwise they'll likely just kill you to stop your ability!
If you're the Ninja, don't startle your prey! Don't act too much like a Ninja, rushing to nominate or arranging nominations. The more nonchalant you appear, the more likely you succeed.
If you're the Demon, beware of players who nominate you! If they're the day's first or last nominator and they're the Ninja, you may die outright.
If you're the Demon, the Ninja can't use his ability without nominating — ignore players who didn't nominate.
If you're the Demon, the best way to handle the Ninja is to kill him directly — you're faster.

If you're an evil player, the best way to sabotage the Ninja is disrupting his nominations — nominate first yourself, or deliberately nominate last. But you'd best have a solid reason for doing so, or you'll look like a meddling evil player.
bluffing: Deliberately nominate first, or wait until the last moment to nominate! It makes you look more like a Ninja.
If you have an ability that causes extra deaths, pairing it with a Ninja bluff lets you smear your victims as evil players you assassinated.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Replace the 'Assassinate' reminder with the 'Dead' reminder.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Assassinate]]
Placed when: When the Ninja nominates.
Condition: If the Ninja is sober and healthy at that moment and the nominated player is evil, place it by the nominated player's character token.
Removed when: The Ninja was not the day's first nominator and another player nominates afterward; or when the Ninja acts at night.

[[Dead]]
Placed when: When the Ninja acts at night.
Condition: If the "Assassinate" reminder is in play, and that player can be killed by the Ninja, and the Ninja is not drunk or poisoned, replace that player's "Assassinate" reminder with the "Dead" reminder to remind the Storyteller to announce the night's dead at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead at dawn, at the Storyteller's convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
An interesting design. The Ninja must leave traces while acting after the Demon and Minions — this demands the utmost: don't startle your prey.

Good players who aren't the Ninja can also deliberately pose as one, playing deep mind games with the evil team.

characters.name: Vanguard
characters.ability: Each night* before the final day, choose: either you cannot die tonight, or your 2 alive neighbors cannot die tonight.
characters.lede: The Vanguard must choose between protecting himself and protecting those beside him.
characters.quote: Hey, you look pretty tough. But you have a fatal weakness — you're afraid. Because you've realized that no matter which angle you circle around to, I'm already standing in front of it.
summaryBullets: If the Vanguard chose the players beside him, the two alive players nearest to him on either side cannot die tonight — whether they are good or evil.
The Vanguard keeps players from being killed by the Demon at night. Protected players also cannot die at night from Outsider, Minion, or Townsfolk abilities.
The Vanguard only protects players at night, not during the day.
After the final day arrives, the Vanguard is no longer woken — effectively losing all ability.
The Vanguard's ability ignores Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Vanguard. Let the Vanguard point at himself or the players beside him. Put the Vanguard back to sleep. Place the "Cannot Die" reminder by his character token or by the character tokens of the two alive players neighboring him. Players marked "Cannot Die" cannot die tonight.
At dawn, remove the "Cannot Die" reminders.
After the final day arrives, the Vanguard is no longer woken.
examples: On the second night, the Vanguard chooses himself; that night the Imp attacks the Vanguard, and the Vanguard does not die. On the third night, the Vanguard chooses his neighbors; that night the Imp attacks the Fortune Teller neighboring the Vanguard, and the Fortune Teller does not die. On the fourth night, the Vanguard chooses his neighbors; that night the Imp neighboring the Vanguard kills themself, but the Imp does not die.
On every night after the final day arrives, the Vanguard is not woken.
tips: If you chose to protect the players beside you, the two alive players nearest you definitely won't die at night. If they died, consider that you were poisoned or drunk!
If you think the Demon is more likely to kill you, you can choose to protect yourself!
bluffing: Coordinate with abilities that can cause safe nights, and claim to be the Vanguard!
If you're an evil player, the Vanguard may be a fine choice. You can claim your ability simply didn't trigger because you lost the gamble.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Let him point at himself or the players beside him.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Cannot Die" ×2]]
Placed when: After the Vanguard acts at night and chooses.
Condition: Place one of these tokens by the Vanguard's own character token or by the character tokens of the two alive players nearest to the Vanguard. If the Vanguard is drunk or poisoned at that moment, do not place it.
Removed when: At dawn, or when the Vanguard dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: A shield, a big shield, a shield with no feedback, a cold and merciless shield, a shield that gambles with the Demon.

characters.name: Dawnyx
characters.ability: The good team cannot win while you are alive. A Demon who dies by execution regains their ability at dawn.
characters.lede: Dawnyx lets a dead Demon regain their ability at dawn.
characters.quote: You paint the dawn golden — how tender. The dawn I see is purple: the color of bruised blood, the bruise left when the night is sucked dry alive. The Demon wakes within that bruise, drinking the last drop of darkness before daybreak. You think the demons scatter when the light comes? No. When the light comes, I can finally see your faces. Now, the sky is bright — the game begins anew.
summaryBullets: When the only living Demon dies by execution, the game doesn't end because of Dawnyx's ability — play continues as normal.
Only while Dawnyx is alive is the good team unable to win. If Dawnyx dies but retains her ability, the good team can still win normally.

If no Demon is alive in play and Dawnyx is drunk, poisoned, dead, or loses her ability, immediately end the game and declare a good victory — because nothing is preventing the good team from winning anymore.
If Dawnyx is in play, the good team cannot win — including by all special victory methods, such as the Magician, the Fool, the Mayor, and so on.

Generally, with 3 players left alive and both Dawnyx and the Demon alive, you may declare an evil victory early. But if the script contains ways for good to still win or situations requiring mutual cover, play the final day through to the end per procedure.

Only a Demon who died by execution regains their ability through Dawnyx's ability — not a Demon who died from other causes. Deaths such as suicide or other characters' abilities cannot trigger Dawnyx's ability.
howToRun: As long as Dawnyx is alive and has her ability, the good team cannot win. If only 2 players remain alive and the good team cannot win, declare that the evil team wins.

If the Demon dies by execution, continue playing the game. At dawn, place the "Regain Ability" reminder by the character token of the Demon who died by execution — from now on, that Demon uses their ability normally each day.
examples: On the first day, the Imp dies by execution — because of Dawnyx's ability, the game doesn't end. On the second night, because the Demon is dead, nobody is killed. At dawn, the Imp regains his ability. On every night thereafter, the Imp attacks.
On the first day, the Imp dies by execution — because of Dawnyx's ability, the game doesn't end. On the second day, Dawnyx dies by execution — the game ends. The good team wins.

On the day with 4 players left alive, the Demon dies by execution — because Dawnyx is alive, the game doesn't end. That night, nobody dies. The next day, 3 players remain alive. A good player dies by execution, leaving only Dawnyx and one other alive player. The game ends — the evil team wins.

On the day with 3 players left alive, both the Demon and Dawnyx are alive. The Storyteller declares an evil victory early — because no matter who is executed today, the evil team's win condition is met, while the good team's cannot be.
tips: If you're Dawnyx, survive to the end at all costs — you matter more than the Demon.
If you're Dawnyx, generally, if your ability triggers, that night will be a safe night. Find a way to cover this up.
If you're Dawnyx, you aren't treated as the Demon — that's your advantage. Play as a low-profile good player to survive to the final day.
If you're a good player, Dawnyx's ability triggering usually comes with a safe night. If you believe the Demon is already dead, find and execute Dawnyx as soon as possible.
If you're a good player and you've found a suspected Dawnyx, deal with her first.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Regain Ability]]
Placed when: At dawn.
Condition: Place it by the character token of the Demon who died by execution.
Removed when: Dawnyx dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Greatness needs no extra salt.

The safe-night + safety-net Minion the whole world needs.

Compared with the Scarlet Woman and the Mastermind: like the Mastermind, Dawnyx leaves safe-night traces, but Dawnyx is harder to guard against than the Mastermind. Against the Scarlet Woman, Dawnyx's disadvantage is being traceable; her advantages are that she's not the Demon — easier to hide — and has no final-circle restriction.

characters.name: Kitsune
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a player & an Outsider character: if not in play, they become it. If they are it, they die. [-1 or +1 Outsider]
characters.lede: The Kitsune manipulates all Outsiders.
characters.quote: You kneel too perfectly — that can't be newly learned. Such bone-deep etiquette belongs only to the Shogunate's descendants. But the Shogunate fell fifteen years ago... Intriguing. So are you the Shogunate's orphaned young lady, or the informer who sold out her whole family? Don't tremble, darling — I'm only asking in passing. What do you say?
summaryBullets: Use the Kitsune's ability sensibly to adjust the initial Outsider count — too many Outsiders may be unfair to the good team.
If the Outsider character the Kitsune chose is in play but her chosen player is not that character, nothing happens.
The Kitsune's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: During game setup, before putting character tokens into the bag, either remove one Townsfolk and add one Outsider, or remove one Outsider and add one Townsfolk.
Each night except the first, wake the Kitsune. She points to a player and an Outsider character icon on the character sheet. Put the Kitsune back to sleep.
If the character she chose is in play and is not the player she chose, nothing happens.
If the character she chose is the player she chose, the chosen player dies — place the "Dead" reminder by that player's character token.

If the character she chose is not in play, wake the chosen player. Show them in turn the "You are" info token and their new character token, then put them back to sleep. Replace their old character token with the new one.
examples: Because the Kitsune is in play, there is one more Outsider than default. On the second night, the Kitsune chooses the Baron player and the Saint; the Saint is not in play — the Baron becomes the Saint. On the third night, the Kitsune chooses the Saint player (formerly the Baron) and the Saint — the Saint dies.

Because the Kitsune is in play, there is one fewer Outsider than default. On the second night, the Kitsune chooses the Fortune Teller player and the Saint; the Saint is in play — nothing happens. On the third night, the Kitsune chooses the Fortune Teller player and the Sweetheart; the Sweetheart is not in play — the Fortune Teller player becomes the Sweetheart. On the following night, the Kitsune chooses the Sweetheart player (formerly the Fortune Teller) and the Sweetheart — the Sweetheart dies, and a player starts being drunk because of the Sweetheart.
tips: If you're the Kitsune, turning good players into Outsiders exposes your existence — watch out for this. Of course, you can also ignore the risk: turning important Townsfolk into Outsiders to strip their abilities is a fine approach too.

If you're the Kitsune and you want to kill Outsiders, you need to guess their characters. Some Outsiders may hide or lie about their character to deceive you — but if that Outsider was turned by you, they can't escape your hunt!
If you're the Kitsune, note that your presence changes the default Outsider count in play — find a way to cover this up.
If you're a good player and you were turned into an Outsider, the Kitsune definitely did it! Announce this as soon as possible.

If you're a good player and an Outsider dies abnormally at night, consider whether the Kitsune is in play. If the Kitsune is in play, the initial Outsider count differs from default. Check the Outsider count — see whether the evil team is falsely claiming Outsider!
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have her choose a character and a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: During the Kitsune's night action, when she chose the character matching her chosen player.
Condition: The player the Kitsune chose is currently alive, the Kitsune can kill that player, and the Kitsune is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A hybrid Minion designed around the Outsider system: multi-kill, character change, and Outsider adjustment in one.

A very interesting character with lots of room to operate and imagine. The player must balance disruption, multi-kills, and more to maximize value.

Outsiders can play mind games with the Kitsune — if the Kitsune can't guess the original Outsiders' characters, she can't kill anyone. If the Kitsune has to create an Outsider herself and then kill him, she gets exposed and needs 2 nights.

characters.name: Bellringer
characters.ability: The 1st time you nominate a player, you may ask their character: if they lie, you are immediately executed.
characters.lede: The Bellringer is his own clapper, spending his life to sound the alarm bell of lies.
characters.quote: It is old, and I am old. But it can still ring — ring loud enough for the whole town to hear. People ask me if I'm afraid. I say, a bellringer doesn't fear the sound fading away; he fears that nobody can understand the sound of the bell. Tomorrow's toll, I probably won't come back from. So be it. A lifetime of sound, traded for one instant of truth. Worth it.
summaryBullets: Lying: the asked player gives what they know to be a wrong answer to the Bellringer's question. For example, for a player whose character is the Fortune Teller, answering "no" to "Are you the Fortune Teller?" is lying; "yes" is not. To "Are you X (any character other than the Fortune Teller)?", "yes" is lying; "no" is not.
If the asked player is a misregistration-type character and gives the answer they believe is correct based on the character they think they are, that player is not treated as lying.
Refusing to answer is not lying. Players have the freedom not to cooperate. If the nominated player refuses to cooperate, the Bellringer's ability is wasted.
The Bellringer's ability works only on the first question of his first nomination.

When a player who isn't the Bellringer claims to be the Bellringer and askes someone, you should play along just as you would for a real Bellringer. You may quietly prompt the nominated player to answer promptly.
If a player is turned into the Bellringer or gains the Bellringer's ability, that player's next first nomination triggers the Bellringer's ability normally.
If the Bellringer is not executed by his own ability, the nomination vote proceeds normally.
If the asked player lies, you must immediately declare the Bellringer executed and night falls.
The Bellringer cannot use his ability on himself.
howToRun: If, after nominating for the first time, the Bellringer publicly askes the nominee: "Are you character X?", the other player must answer "yes" or "no," or another answer that clearly conveys the meaning, or refuse to answer. If the asked player lies about the question (see Rule Details), immediately declare the Bellringer executed.
examples: On the first day, the Bellringer nominates for the first time and nominates the Fortune Teller. The Bellringer publicly askes the Fortune Teller player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Fortune Teller player answers "I am not." Nothing happens, and the nomination proceeds normally.

On the first day, the Bellringer nominates for the first time and nominates the Baron. The Bellringer publicly askes the Baron player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Baron player answers "I am." The Bellringer is executed.

On the first day, the Bellringer nominates for the first time and nominates the Drunk, who believes they are the Washerwoman. The Bellringer publicly askes the Drunk player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Drunk player answers "I am." Nothing happens, and the nomination proceeds normally.

On the first day, the Bellringer nominates for the first time and nominates the Baron. The Bellringer publicly askes the Baron player: "Are you the Washerwoman?" The Baron player refuses to answer. Nothing happens, and the nomination proceeds normally.
tips: If you're the Bellringer, talk things through with the player you're about to nominate before nominating! Avoid them refusing to answer or deliberately answering wrong!
If you're the Bellringer and you weren't executed, the other player probably didn't lie to you — or your ability is being interfered with.
If you're the Bellringer and you died by execution, the other player definitely lied!
If you're the Bellringer, you can use your ability on day one to test the players giving early information, verifying their characters.
If you're the Bellringer, you can also save your ability for mid-game to test more critical players. Either way, remember: your ability only works on your first nomination! Don't forget and waste it.
If you're a good player, you can falsely claim to be the Bellringer and aske a player to observe their reaction.

If you're an evil player, watch out for the Bellringer — he can easily tear off your disguise at the cost of his life, leaving you no room to argue! If you're cornered, you can refuse to answer; that makes you look like a guilty evil player, but at least it doesn't let him prove he's the Bellringer. Or you can lie outright! The Bellringer dies by execution immediately — and either way, you definitely won't be executed today!
bluffing: Remember, you don't have the Bellringer's ability, so you can't actually get yourself executed. But you can pretend the other player didn't lie.

Although in most cases a good player you aske probably won't lie, they might lie deliberately to test your ability. Don't panic if so — you can calmly shed the Bellringer bluff, since anyone can claim to be the Bellringer.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[No Ability]]
Placed when: After the Bellringer nominates for the first time.
Condition: Place it by the Bellringer's character token, whether or not the Bellringer is drunk or poisoned.
Removed when: The Bellringer dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Bellringer is a classic BOTC-style reverse-verification functional character. Not triggering → confirms a good player but with no self-proof; triggering → confirms a lie plus strong self-proof, but the good team directly loses an execution round.

Why design it around the first nomination? Why not simply "once per game" or "on the first day"? Limiting it to the nomination phase concentrates everyone's attention on the nominator and the nominee, maximizing theatrical effect. Second, the nominate-and-be-nominated constraint gives the evil team more room for counterplay (self-nomination or a teammate sniping the nomination), so the Bellringer can't do whatever he wants. And "first" nomination encourages the Bellringer to use the ability earlier, providing a logical anchor for the game — fulfilling his role as a "logic anchor" character.

characters.name: FaultBot
characters.ability: Each night, you learn if all other Townsfolk abilities worked normally (since dawn).
characters.lede: The FaultBot learns whether Townsfolk abilities malfunctioned.
characters.quote: Click-clack — error! Error!
summaryBullets: When a Townsfolk player's ability fails to function as intended, the FaultBot learns "no." This includes "interference" within characters' own abilities (such as the Fortune Teller, Ogre, Villager, Snake Charmer) and interference from other characters' abilities on Townsfolk players (including but not limited to poison/drunkenness, interaction interference, and the Vortox's false information).
No matter how many Townsfolk players' abilities malfunctioned, as long as at least one did that day, the FaultBot learns "no."

"Today" means tonight plus the day preceding nightfall. The first night has only a night, with no corresponding day. The FaultBot checks whether all other Townsfolk functioned normally throughout the day (the whole day + the whole night).
In the vast majority of cases, the FaultBot acts at night after all other Townsfolk have acted.
The FaultBot's ability does not check whether the FaultBot's own ability malfunctioned.

The FaultBot doesn't detect the poisoned/drunk states themselves, but abilities that failed to function as intended due to poison/drunkenness. The Spy being registered as good by the Empath, a drunk Noble learning three good players, a poisoned Ogre failing to kill the good player they chose — these are detected. A poisoned or drunk Townsfolk getting correct information is not detected.
Information format: "yes" or "no."

False information format: "yes" or "no," opposite to reality. If all other Townsfolk abilities worked normally today, the FaultBot's false information is "no"; if some other Townsfolk ability malfunctioned today, the FaultBot's false information is "yes."
howToRun: When a Townsfolk player's ability does not work normally, place the "Error" reminder by the FaultBot's character token.
Each night, wake the FaultBot. If the "Error" reminder is in play, shake your head or tell him "no"; if the "Error" reminder is not in play, nod or tell him "yes." Then remove the "Error" reminder.
examples: On the first night, the Fortune Teller chose a good player they registered as the Demon, didn't choose the Demon, and learned "yes." That night, the FaultBot learns "no."
On the first night, the Empath sits between the Spy and the Saint, and because of the Spy's ability learns "0." That night, the FaultBot learns "no."
On the first night, the Poisoner poisons the Dreamer; the Dreamer chooses the Saint and learns "Saint, Poisoner." That night, the FaultBot learns "yes."
On the second night, the Ogre chooses a good player registered as evil by the Ogre's ability; that player is not killed by the Ogre. That night, the FaultBot learns "no."
On the second night, the Poisoner poisons the Nightwatchman; the Nightwatchman chooses a player, and that player does not learn who the Nightwatchman is. That night, the FaultBot learns "no."
On the first day, the poisoned Savant visits the Storyteller and learns two true statements. That night, the FaultBot learns "no."
tips: If you're the FaultBot and you learned "yes," all Townsfolk are functioning normally.
If you're the FaultBot and you learned "no," go public as soon as possible and work with everyone to find whose ability went wrong.
If you're the FaultBot, note that your own ability can also give false information through poison, drunkenness, or the Vortox!

If you're the FaultBot, you're a "secondary information" character — your ability is built on top of other players' abilities. You're more like an alarm bell, so you're not that important; what matters are the Townsfolk who directly function or produce information. Don't fear death too much — you need to give everyone the prompt they deserve as soon as possible.
bluffing: Keep reporting errors! It throws the Townsfolk into chaos — who malfunctioned?
Claim everything is normal when Townsfolk are actually erroring! Cover up the problems!
Don't claim there's no problem when Townsfolk abilities are obviously erroring, or you'll be suspected immediately.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake him and tell him yes or no.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him and tell him yes or no.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Error]]
Placed when: When a Townsfolk player's ability does not work normally; place it by the FaultBot's character token.
Condition: When a Townsfolk player's ability does not work normally.
Removed when: After the FaultBot gets his information.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The first secondary-information slot of the Odyssey pack.

The FaultBot is essentially a simplified Mathematician, in line with the Odyssey pack's keep-everything-simple design style.

Compared to the Mathematician: "numbers" are simplified to "yes/no," and checking "all players" is simplified to checking "Townsfolk players." Why? The Mathematician itself is overly complex; simplifying helps players understand and use the information. Second, checking all players is mostly redundant — Townsfolk abilities should focus on serving Townsfolk themselves, so checking only Townsfolk greatly improves information efficiency, while simplifying the information format lowers its strength. Finally, the simplified information improves Vortox resistance, letting it perform better in scripts containing the Vortox or Vortox-like abilities.

Many simulation-oriented players love the Mathematician and similar designs, but I've always been reserved about them — they add complexity without clearly improving fun or strategy. The FaultBot is the minimalist version of this design, keeping the original "simulation" gameplay while minimizing players' comprehension cost, so this style of play can enter beginner or intermediate scripts without an excessive barrier to entry.

characters.name: Hunter
characters.ability: If a player you nominated dies that night, you are woken to choose a player: they die.
characters.lede: The Hunter sets his trap and quietly awaits the kill.
characters.quote: My traps were laid long ago; dead leaves over the game trails hide the iron teeth. Now I need only lie behind the brush and let my breath merge with the wind. The moment its hind leg steps into the snare and its body lurches off balance — pull the trigger, and the dust settles.
summaryBullets: The Hunter cannot trigger his ability by nominating a dead player, because a dead player cannot die again.
If the Hunter nominated himself and dies that night, he is woken and uses his ability, because nominating himself meets all the conditions of the death trigger.
As long as the player the Hunter nominated dies that night, the Hunter's ability triggers — whether they died from the Demon's ability or another cause.

The Hunter has no night-order slot. He acts immediately after the death of his nominated player resolves — he is woken right after and uses his ability. If several players die simultaneously (e.g., the Demon attacks multiple players), the Hunter acts after all those deaths resolve.
Once woken, the Hunter may choose any player. If he wishes, he may choose a dead player or himself.
If the player the Hunter nominated was about to die but didn't for some reason, the Hunter is not woken.
The Hunter cannot choose Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: When the Hunter nominates a player, place the "Trap" reminder by that player's character token.
If the player marked "Trap" dies at night, wake the Hunter and let him choose a player — place the "Dead" reminder by that player; they die. Put the Hunter back to sleep.
At dawn, remove all "Trap" reminders.
examples: On the first day, the Hunter nominates the Fortune Teller. That night, the Fortune Teller is killed by the Imp. The Hunter is woken and chooses the Imp; the Imp dies, and the game ends.
On the first day, the Hunter nominates the Fortune Teller. That night, the Fortune Teller does not die, and the Hunter is not woken.
On the second day, the Hunter nominates the Imp. That night, the Imp kills themself. The Hunter is woken and chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller dies.
tips: If you're the Hunter, nominate players you think might die at night! Trigger your ability as often as possible.
If you're the Hunter and you think you'll likely die at night, you can nominate yourself to try to trigger your ability.
If you're the Hunter and you were woken at night, your nominated player is dead. Choose players who look evil as much as possible!
If you're the Hunter, don't reveal you're the Hunter. If the Demon knows, they can avoid your nominated players to prevent triggering your ability.
If you're the Demon, beware — the Hunter is very dangerous. If he triggers frequently, he can both prove himself by killing players and possibly kill you outright!
If you're the Demon, killing players who weren't nominated today is a very safe option — or kill players nominated by people who don't look like the Hunter.

If you're the Demon, once you know who the Hunter is, his ability is no longer scary. You can avoid attacking his nominated players. But sometimes, if you notice the Hunter is convinced some good players are evil, you can deliberately trigger his ability and let him kill players for you to speed up the game.
bluffing: The Hunter can only kill if his nominated player dies that night — remember this.
If your nominated player died that night but no extra death appeared, your Hunter bluff may be hanging by a thread.
If you have an ability that causes extra night deaths, the Hunter is a great bluff. Nominate a player, kill them at night, and at dawn claim the other player who died that night was killed by you.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Trap]]
Placed when: When the Hunter nominates a player.
Condition: After the Hunter nominates, place it by the nominated player's character token.
Removed when: At dawn.

[[Dead]]
Placed when: When the Hunter chooses a player at night.
Condition: The Hunter's chosen player is currently alive, can be killed by the Hunter, and the Hunter is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce the night's dead at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead at dawn, at the Storyteller's convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
An evil-hunting Townsfolk, a new Townsfolk niche debuting in Odyssey, including the Witcher, Lunar Knight, Assassin, Ranger, Warlock, Hunter, and other differently-shaped Townsfolk. Evil-hunting Townsfolk fill a niche left empty by official design — TPI is very cautious about giving good players "knives." Evil-hunting Townsfolk have a huge gap between floor and ceiling and can give the evil team a poor experience, so they test design skill.

In my view, evil-hunting Townsfolk should replace "camping" and protection Townsfolk. "Camping" ones like the Soldier and the Mayor are neither traditional landmine slots nor have room for subjective play — they're life-sentence campers who mostly can't make their ability matter, or don't even know when it did. Protection Townsfolk are unusable in scripts that don't need safe-night logic. Evil-hunting Townsfolk, while similar in form (gambling with the Demon), produce extra deaths instead of safe nights — better fitting certain scripts' actual needs.

As long as the Demon makes an effort to avoid the Hunter's ability, it's fairly easy to dodge. Most of the time, the Hunter — like the Soldier and the Mayor — rarely fires his ability. But by design, the Hunter gives players a higher skill ceiling and a motive to act, giving them a goal to pursue — at least they're not bored senseless in a cell.

Even if the Hunter is never woken all game, he still functions somewhat like a Monk's protection: the Demon can only avoid killing his nominated player, or the Hunter's ability triggers.

The Hunter's existence gives other good players room to bluff as the Hunter and somewhat "protects" nominated players. The Demon must guess who is the Hunter and who isn't, possibly leading to misjudged kill choices.

characters.name: Echo
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a character: they die. If that character is not in play, next night you choose an additional character (stackable).
characters.lede: The Echo has the ability to accumulate attack counts — he directly attacks specific characters.
characters.quote: Time is not linear, and neither is death. Every unanswered cry, after echoing, converges into a deafening shriek. The Echo never forgets; the Echo never forgives. The Echo is the net fate has laid — the more you struggle, the tighter you're bound.
summaryBullets: Unlike other Demons, the Echo chooses a character when attacking — not a player. The Storyteller may need to remind players of this special aspect of the Echo's ability.
If the Echo wishes, he can attack evil characters.
If multiple players of a character are in play and the Echo chooses that character, the Storyteller decides which of them dies.

Every time the Echo chooses a not-in-play character, the number of characters he must choose next time increases by 1. If the Echo keeps choosing not-in-play characters, the required number keeps stacking. If he chooses multiple in-play characters at once, all those players die.

If the Echo is drunk or poisoned when choosing a not-in-play character, he still must choose an additional character the next night. If the Echo is drunk or poisoned when choosing an in-play character, he doesn't need to choose an additional character the next night.
If the Echo isn't woken by his own ability at night for some reason, he can only choose one character the next night.
The Echo's ability cannot choose Traveller characters (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Echo. Have the Echo point to a character on the character sheet; if there are "Dead" reminders from the Echo in the center of the Grimoire, have the Echo choose that many additional characters. Remove all "Dead" reminders from the center of the Grimoire. For each chosen character that is in play, place a "Dead" reminder by the corresponding player. If multiple players are that character, the Storyteller chooses one of them to die. For each chosen character that is not in play, place a "Dead" reminder in the center of the Grimoire, to remind you that the Echo can make more choices tomorrow night.
examples: On the second night, the Echo chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller is in play — the Fortune Teller dies. On the third night, the Echo chooses the Saint; the Saint is in play — the Saint dies.

On the second night, the Echo chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller is not in play — nobody dies. On the third night, the Echo chooses the Saint and the Fortune Teller; neither is in play — nobody dies. On the fourth night, the Echo chooses the Baron, the Empath, and the Washerwoman — all are in play, and those players die.
tips: If you're the Echo, send the characters you find most troublesome straight to their graves — don't hesitate!

If you're the Echo and you're not sure whether a player is really playing a certain character, choose that character at night to test it. If they die, they really were that character. If not — no harm done; you haven't wasted your attack.
If you're the Echo, watch for players who "died unexpectedly". Maybe they swapped claims with someone — and they're actually the one you're really looking for.
If you're the Echo, don't repeatedly choose the same not-in-play character — unless you want to build up power!

If you're the Echo and the script has Demons who can attack multiple players in one night, you can deliberately choose a not-in-play character (such as one of your bluffs) so you cause no deaths — but the night after next, you gain the ability to attack multiple players!
If you're a good player and important Townsfolk are dying in the first few nights, consider the possibility that the Demon is the Echo!
If you're a good player and a safe night occurs, the Echo may be urgently building power! Beware of him ending the game early!
characters.creator: Taiyi, 阿尔伯特 (Albert — homage to the designer of the colliding design)
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a character.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead" ×5]]
Placed when: After the Echo acts at night and chooses characters.
Condition: If at least one player of the character the Echo chose is currently alive, can be killed by the Echo, and the Echo is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead players at dawn. For each character the Echo chose that is not in play, place one in the center of the Grimoire.
Removed when: After announcing the dead players at dawn, the Storyteller may remove the Dead reminders by those players' character tokens at their convenience. Whenever you wake the Echo to tell him the total number of choices he may make, or when the Echo isn't woken for some reason, remove all reminders from the center of the Grimoire.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
It started as a flash of inspiration — a special mechanic (wrong choices are deferred) — but on reflection, this actually solves some of Ajo's pain points.

Coincidentally, someone had designed an almost identical character before; credited in Concept.

The Echo and Ajo look one sentence apart in ability text, but in application they're worlds apart. The Echo slots seamlessly into all kinds of multi-kill and safe-night scripts, providing great cover for other safe-night and multi-death logic. Unlike Ajo, who depends heavily on the Storyteller, the Echo is a character the Storyteller cannot "manipulate".

What if he keeps deliberately choosing not-in-play characters, saving up to attack everyone on the final day? Not a problem — first, never attacking exposes the Demon type. Second, it gives every information role plenty of time to gather information, which is wonderful for the good team. The total kill count doesn't increase — it's just deferred, and deferred kills aren't necessarily good for evil.

characters.name: Kraken
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a player: they die. The 1st time you die, you live but register as dead & may only choose your living neighbors.
characters.lede: The Kraken lives on among the crowd, registering as dead.
characters.quote: I rise from an abyss where even the corpses of gods cannot sink. I have heard the first cry of the tearing crust; in the cleft between magma and absolute zero, I forged my heart into an undying molten core. Vitality is the only luggage I brought back from the deep dive. I am the Kraken — immortality walking the abyss.
summaryBullets: Living but registering as dead (a concept from the official character "Zombuul"): a player is treated as dead by other players and character abilities and appears dead in the town square, but is actually still alive. They cannot nominate and can only vote using a vote token. They act at night as if alive. This state exists independently of character abilities — it is not drunkenness or poisoning, and it does not end if the source ability disappears.
