A player already registering as dead cannot register as dead again: if they receive this effect again, or die again, they truly die.

"The final day": the first day of the game with fewer than 5 alive players (not counting Travellers). On the final day, the Storyteller publicly announces at the earliest opportunity that today is the final day. A game has at most one "final day" — if the game doesn't end on the final day, later days with fewer than 5 alive players are not treated as the final day. If the game ends early (e.g. special victory or the Demon's death), that game may have no "final day". Before the final day: the game period before the final day comes. When the final day arrives: the moment the final day comes (usually the first dawn with fewer than 5 alive non-Traveller players). After the final day arrives: the final day and the game period after it.
A Kraken registering as dead looks dead, but he is woken at night and uses his ability.

A Kraken registering as dead looks dead, but he still counts toward the evil team's win condition. For example, when only 2 seemingly alive players remain plus the Kraken registering as dead, the game doesn't end — because 3 players are actually alive.
The Kraken may choose no player and forgo his attack, whether or not he registers as dead.
If a Kraken registering as dead chooses a player who doesn't meet the requirement, shake your head and have him choose again.
The Kraken's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: If the Kraken dies before the Storyteller announces the final day has arrived, and he isn't already alive but registering as dead, he lives but registers as dead (see Rule Details). Announce that the Kraken has died and place the "Registers as Dead" reminder by the Kraken's character token. From now on, the Kraken is treated as dead by other players and character abilities, and like a dead player, he can only vote using a vote token and cannot nominate.

Each night except the first, wake the Kraken. Have the Kraken point to a player, or shake his head to choose nobody. If he chose a player, that player dies — place the "Dead" reminder by their character token. Put the Kraken back to sleep. If the Kraken is alive but registering as dead, he can only choose an alive player neighboring him, or shake his head to choose nobody. If his chosen target doesn't meet the ability's requirement, shake your head and have him choose again.
examples: On the first day, the Kraken is executed. He's still alive, but to the other players he appears dead. That night, he kills the Fortune Teller neighboring him. On the second day, the Kraken — registering as dead — is executed again; the Kraken truly dies, and the good team wins.

On the second night, the Kraken kills himself (living but registering as dead). After dawn, the Storyteller announces his death. Every night thereafter, the Kraken kills an alive player neighboring him.
The Storyteller announces the final day has arrived; that day the Kraken is executed and dies — the good team wins.
tips: If there aren't enough dead players near you, best not to kill yourself rashly. While registering as dead you can only kill alive players neighboring you — if the night deaths are all players next to you, it very obviously points to you being a Kraken registering as dead.
Even without registering as dead in the early game, you're very powerful. You don't have to register as dead — treat it as your last resort.

If you're a good player and you find the players dying at night always cluster around a specific dead player, don't hesitate — point out he may be a Kraken registering as dead, and try to execute him again.

If you're a good player: although the Kraken has mighty vitality, once registering as dead he can only kill alive players beside him. So if a player you suspect of being the Kraken dies, and that night a player not neighboring him dies — he definitely isn't the Kraken.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: After the Kraken acts at night and chooses a player.
Condition: The player the Kraken chose is currently alive, can be killed by the Kraken, and the Kraken is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

[[Registers as Dead]]
Placed when: When the Kraken dies.
Condition: If the final day hasn't arrived yet, the Kraken isn't already registering as dead, and he's not drunk or poisoned, place it by the Kraken's character token.
Removed when: The Kraken dies again or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Odyssey's first — and probably only — registering-as-dead design.

Registering as dead is hard to design, because the keyword has almost no "payoff point" for character types other than Demons.

A registering-as-dead Demon can't avoid comparison with the Zombuul. The Zombuul is a highly specialized Demon, surviving on massive execution-survival and safe-night logic. The Kraken replaces the Zombuul's kill-condition restriction with a kill-position restriction, letting the Kraken fit normally into most ordinary scripts.

Why "you may kill a player" rather than "choose a player: they die"? In a 4-player circle with a registering-as-dead Kraken, if the Kraken had to kill an alive player, a weird 2-player finale would arise, inevitably exposing the Kraken. Giving the Kraken the option not to kill lets him skip his attack and enter a 3-player finale through a safe night — and lets him provide mutual cover with other safe-night-logic characters in the script, such as the Mastermind, protection characters, Dawnyx, etc.

Why "registering as dead" instead of "the 1st time you die, you live but register as dead"? It's simple, easy to understand, and players already broadly recognize the concept from the Zombuul — no redundant description needed.

characters.name: Centaur
characters.ability: Each night*, choose another player (different to last night): if their type matches last night's player, they die.
characters.lede: The Centaur kills players of matching character types.
characters.quote: If justice arrives too late, my iron hooves will deliver it personally. Don't fear the fate of being trampled — my hooves, at least, are merciful: they don't disguise themselves as hope, nor drag out into despair. They are the most honest pity I can give you.
summaryBullets: The Centaur may choose any player except himself and the player he chose last night. If he wishes, he may choose a dead player.

If the Centaur is poisoned or drunk, he cannot kill any player. If the Centaur was poisoned or drunk last night but is sober and healthy now, and the two players he chose on those nights share a character type, the player he chose tonight is killed by him.

If the player the Centaur chose last night has become a player of another character type, compare their newest character type with the player the Centaur chose tonight — if they match, the Centaur's ability triggers.
The Centaur cannot choose Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night, wake the Centaur. Let him point at any player. If the Centaur chooses the player he chose last night or himself, remind him to change targets. Put the Centaur back to sleep. If the chosen player's character type matches the player marked with the "Chosen" reminder, the chosen player dies — place the "Dead" reminder by that player's character token. If the character types differ, or the "Chosen" reminder hasn't been placed yet, nothing happens. Finally, whether or not the character types matched, place or move the "Chosen" reminder to the character token of the player the Centaur most recently chose.
examples: On the first night, the Centaur chooses the Fortune Teller. On the second night, the Centaur chooses the Empath; the Empath dies. On the third night, the Centaur chooses the Saint. On the fourth night, the Centaur chooses the Butler; the Butler dies.

On the first night, the Centaur chooses the Scarlet Woman. On the second night, the Centaur chooses the Baron; the Baron dies. On the third night, the Centaur chooses the Imp. On the fourth night, the Centaur chooses the Fortune Teller.
On the fourth night, the Centaur chooses the dead Imp. On the fifth night, the Centaur chooses the living Imp; the Imp dies. The game ends; good wins.
tips: If you're the Centaur and you killed a player, that player shares a character type with the player you chose last night. Usually they're both Townsfolk; occasionally they're both Outsiders or both Minions.

If you're the Centaur and you chose two players both claiming to be Townsfolk, yet they're unharmed — you'd best go public: one of them is hiding a non-Townsfolk character, very likely an evil player.
If you're the Centaur, choose a player who looks like a Minion! Then next night, choose another player who looks like a Minion! If they really are both Minions, you've killed one.
If you're the Demon, the Centaur may keep killing players. If he isn't hitting you or your teammates, leaving him alone may be the better idea.

If you're the Demon and the Centaur chose you or your teammate without killing you, you can defend yourself by claiming an Outsider or a different character type. If necessary, deal with the Centaur at night.
bluffing: The Centaur is a highly aggressive bluff. Claim to be the Centaur, attack two players both claiming Townsfolk, and accuse them of not dying to your ability — this creates enormous focus.
If you can cause extra deaths, that's strong evidence supporting your Centaur bluff.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake him and let him choose a player.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him and let him choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Chosen]]
Placed when: After the Centaur chooses a player.
Condition: As long as the Centaur chose a player, place this token — whether or not it killed them, and whether or not the Centaur is poisoned or drunk.
Removed when: After the Centaur chooses a player, the token moves to that player's character token.

[[Dead]]
Placed when: When the Centaur chooses a player.
Condition: The Centaur's chosen player is currently alive, meets the Centaur's ability condition, can be killed by the Centaur, and the Centaur is not drunk or poisoned — place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce the night's dead at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead at dawn, at the Storyteller's convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A knife-wielding Townsfolk. Builds logic by continually creating deaths.

Landing a kill → proves two players share a character type, a degree of self-proof. Not landing one → no self-proof, but highly aggressive.

The Centaur can kill not only Townsfolk but also Outsiders and Minions — though very rarely the Demon — preventing the game from ending too quickly.

characters.name: Bug Catcher
characters.ability: If you nominated another player, that night you are woken & learn if they are the Demon.
characters.lede: The Bug Catcher catches the Demon through nominations.
characters.quote: Crickets, katydids, rhinoceros beetles! Dragonflies, mantises, fireflies! Butterflies, grasshoppers, scarabs! All of you, into my net! ...Ha! Got you!
summaryBullets: If the Bug Catcher didn't nominate or nominated himself, he is not woken that night.
Whether or not the player the Bug Catcher nominated died by execution that day, the Bug Catcher is woken that night and learns whether they are the Demon.
Information format: "yes" or "no."
False information format: "yes" or "no," opposite to reality. If the player the Bug Catcher nominated today is the Demon, the Bug Catcher learns "no"; if not, he learns "yes."
howToRun: When the Bug Catcher nominates a player other than himself, place the Bug Catcher's "What Bug?" reminder by the nominated player's character token.

That night, wake the Bug Catcher. If the player marked "What Bug?" is a Demon character, nod or tell the Bug Catcher "yes." If that player is not a Demon character, shake your head or tell the Bug Catcher "no." Remove the "What Bug?" reminder.
examples: On the first day, the Bug Catcher does not nominate. That night the Bug Catcher is not woken.
On the first day, the Bug Catcher nominates himself. That night the Bug Catcher is not woken.
On the first day, the Bug Catcher nominates the Baron. That night the Bug Catcher is woken and learns "no."
On the first day, the Bug Catcher nominates the Fang Gu. That night the Bug Catcher is woken and learns "yes."
tips: If you're the Bug Catcher, nominate often! Especially players suspected of being the Demon! Catch them!
If you're the Bug Catcher, you can also nominate suspicious players only at key moments — this helps you hide that you're the Bug Catcher.
If you're the Bug Catcher and you learn a player is the Demon, announce it quickly! Call on everyone to deal with them at once.
If you're a good player, nominate as much as possible to help the Bug Catcher stay hidden!
If you're the Demon and you find a suspected Bug Catcher has nominated you, you can kill them at night to avoid exposure! Careful — some "landmine" characters may pose as the Bug Catcher!
bluffing: Bug Catchers tend to nominate a lot. To bluff as one, remember to nominate often!

If you're the Demon bluffing as the Bug Catcher, a good plan is to nominate a Minion in the mid-to-late game and claim the Minion is the Demon. Whether or not people believe you, you look less like the Demon — because if they do believe you, they'll execute the Minion.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: If the Bug Catcher nominated another player today, wake him and tell him yes or no.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[What Bug]]
Placed when: When the Bug Catcher nominates a player other than himself.
Condition: When the Bug Catcher nominates a player other than himself, place it by the nominated player's character token, whether or not the Bug Catcher is poisoned or drunk.
Removed when: After the Bug Catcher is woken at night, or when the Bug Catcher dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: The Bug Catcher works well as a Demon-focused information slot in ordinary scripts, and also fits into the nomination-play character group in nomination-themed scripts.

characters.name: Scalebearer
characters.ability: On your 1st night, you learn a player: 2 players of the opposing alignment are equidistant from them.
characters.lede: The Scalebearer learns a player equidistant from two opponents.
characters.quote: Seventy percent of this town's precious trades pass over my scale. Gold, silver, jewels, musk, ginseng — all through my hands. I've made many enemies. Short-changers hate me, cheats curse me, someone once splashed filthy water on my doorstep. I won't move. Where the scale is, there I am. Only when the scale runs false should I move.
summaryBullets: The Scalebearer may learn either a good player or an evil player. Either way, at some distance from the learned player, there must be two players on a different team to them.
The Scalebearer's ability ignores Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: one player, e.g., "May" or "player #3."
False information format: one player (who in the vast majority of cases can only be good), but at no distance from them are there two players on a different team.
howToRun: On the Scalebearer's first night, wake the Scalebearer. Point at a player. Then put the Scalebearer back to sleep. That player must satisfy: at some distance from them, there are two players on a different team to them.
examples: On the first night, the Scalebearer learns player #3 (good). Players #1 and #5 are both evil, and both sit at distance 2 from player #3.
On the first night, the Scalebearer learns player #3 (evil). Players #2 and #4 are both good, and both sit at distance 1 from player #3.
On the first night, the Scalebearer learns player #6 (good). Players #1 and #11 are both evil, and both sit at distance 5 from player #6.
tips: If you're the Scalebearer, what you learned is either a good player or an evil player. If you think you learned a good player, then two evil players sit at equal distances from them — use elimination to find those two evil players. If you can't find two equally distant evil players, then what you learned is an evil player!
bluffing: Make up any player you like — you can attack the pair equidistant from them, or attack that player as evil outright.
If you're the Demon, inventing a player seated between two Minions may be a fine choice.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake him and tell him one player.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A first-night information slot. Simple format, plenty to reason about.

Some say the Scalebearer has too many possible outcomes. Really? Let's argue with data. The table below enumerates the information possibilities of 4 similar characters in a standard 12-player game. The Cultivator has 5 possibilities, the Scalebearer likewise 5, the Clockmaker 8, the Chef 10. So the "too many possibilities" argument doesn't hold water at all.

The above only addresses "too many possibilities," not probability or strength (identity-deduction games don't deal in probability — don't bring it up. If in doubt, open any AI and ask "Is 'wolves always spawn at the edges' correct in Werewolf?" — the AI will answer you. No further discussion here). Admittedly, in information strength the Scalebearer is far below the Clockmaker and company. The Scalebearer's design intent is exactly what TPI calls a "somewhat helpful but not too strong" first-night information slot.

Some note that in single-Minion games the Scalebearer may be unable to point to a good player and can only point to an evil one. True — but it's not a bug. Characters fluctuating in strength across different player counts is normal; official characters are no different.

characters.name: Dame
characters.ability: Each night, you learn a character that is in play. When an evil player dies, you become drunk.
characters.lede: The Dame learns in-play characters each night, but begins to drink at some point.
characters.quote: There are two kinds of drunk in this world. The first comes from drinking too much of the same wine; the second from hearing too many different lies. The first kind passes after a night's sleep. The second kind seeps into your bones. I drink with different people almost every day; I know the first kind can't hurt me — but I also know that after the second kind happens too many times, you never wake up again. So tell me: am I drunk right now, or sober?
summaryBullets: The Dame only learns Townsfolk, Outsider, Minion, and Demon characters.
You may tell the Dame the same character more than once, if you think it necessary.

It's recommended to alternate good and evil characters for the Dame. Try not to give good characters constantly — especially Townsfolk — while the Dame is not drunk, because her information strength would exceed expectations. The rough strength ranking of what she learns is Townsfolk > Demon > Outsider > Minion.
If the Dame is drunk, she may learn a character in play or a character not in play.

If an evil player dies while the Dame is poisoned or drunk from another character's ability, still place the Dame's "Drunk" reminder. Once the Dame is sober and healthy again, she immediately becomes drunk from her own ability.
If the Dame is created mid-game, she doesn't become drunk from evil players who died earlier. But she starts being drunk when the next evil player dies.
The Dame does not learn Traveller characters (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: a character in play (e.g., the Fortune Teller or the Baron).
False information format: a character not in play (e.g., the Fortune Teller or the Baron).
howToRun: Each night, wake the Dame and tell her one character in play (it may be a Townsfolk, Outsider, Minion, or Demon). Then put the Dame back to sleep.
When an evil player dies, place the "Drunk" reminder by the Dame's character token — she is drunk from now on. If the Dame is already drunk from her own ability, do not place it again.
examples: On the first night, the Dame learns the Baron. On the second night, the Dame learns the Chef. On the third night, the Dame learns the Imp. No evil player has died; the Baron, the Chef, and the Imp are all in play.

On the first night, the Dame learns the Baron. On the second night, the Baron dies; the Dame starts being drunk and learns the Fortune Teller. On the third night, the Dame learns the Saint. The Baron is in play; the Fortune Teller and the Saint are not.

On the first night, the Dame learns the Fortune Teller. On the second night, the Baron dies; the Dame starts being drunk and learns the Imp. On the third night, the Dame learns the Saint. The Fortune Teller and the Imp are in play; the Saint is not.
tips: If you're the Dame, the character you learned on the first night is definitely in play. If it's a good character, the player claiming that character should be good.
If you're the Dame, the later the game goes, the less credible your information — because the chance an evil player has died grows with time.
If you're the Dame and you clearly know an evil player has died, your information has no value from that point on.
If you're an evil player and you know the Dame is in play, dying early may not be a bad idea — it corrupts the Dame's information and misleads the good team.
If you're the Demon and you know the Dame is in play, don't fear her. You can attack her, or try attacking your own teammates to make the Dame drunk — corrupting her information is a fine option too.
bluffing: If you're a Minion, the Dame is an excellent bluff. Deliberately reporting characters that seem not in play lets you attack earlier deaths as containing evil players.

If you're the Demon, the key to bluffing as the Dame is reporting relatively credible in-play characters in the early-to-mid game, then switching to characters that seem not in play in the mid-to-late game. This helps everyone trust you more.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake her and tell her a character in play.
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake her and tell her a character in play.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Drunk]]
Placed when: When an evil player dies.
Condition: When an evil player dies, place it by the Dame's character token, whether or not the Dame is poisoned or drunk.
Removed when: The Dame dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Dame looks like an ongoing-information slot, but her role is closer to a first-night/limited information slot, because her information value declines over time. Only the first night's information is fully reliable.

The rough strength ranking of learning different character kinds is Townsfolk > Demon > Outsider > Minion. Learning a good character confirms a good player, while learning an evil character can't do that. But fixing the Demon's species matters greatly for building logic.

The Dame is designed partly as a counterpart to the King. The King powers up in the mid-to-late game; the Dame is the reverse, powering up early-to-mid.

characters.name: Notary
characters.ability: Each night*, you learn if today's executee & their nominator are the same alignment.
characters.lede: The Notary verifies whether the executed and their nominator share a team.
characters.quote: I threw this register away once, then picked it back up. That day's record — I raised my seal three times and never brought it down. The two names on that page were too alike; alike not like enemies, but like brothers.
summaryBullets: Optional rule: if the script contains the Vortox, you may forbid players from nominating themselves, whether or not the Notary is in play.
If no player died by execution during the day, or the player who died by execution was never nominated that day (e.g., Cerenovus or Virgin executions), the Notary is not woken that night.
If more than one player died by execution during the day: if every pair (executed player + their nominator) shares a team, tell the Notary "yes." Otherwise tell him "no."
If a player nominated someone and the nominee was executed that day for any reason (e.g., Cerenovus or Virgin), the Notary's ability condition is satisfied.
If only one player was executed that day and their nominator was a Traveller, the Notary is not woken that night (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: "yes" or "no."
False information format: "yes" or "no," opposite to reality. For example, if the executed player and their nominator share a team, then "no" is false information, and vice versa.
howToRun: When a player dies by execution, if the player who nominated them today is on the same team as them, place the "Same" reminder by the Notary's character token. If they're on different teams, place the "Different" reminder by the Notary's character token.

Each night except the first, if a player died by execution today and was nominated today, wake the Notary. If the "Same" reminder is in play, tell him "yes" or nod. If the "Different" reminder is in play, tell him "no" or shake your head. Then put the Notary back to sleep and remove all "Same" and "Different" reminders. If no player died by execution today, do not wake the Notary.
examples: On the first day, the Baron dies from a nomination started by the Fortune Teller. That night, the Notary learns "no."
On the second day, the Poisoner dies from a nomination started by the Imp. That night, the Notary learns "yes."
On the third day, the Chef dies from a nomination started by a good Bureaucrat (a Traveller). That night, the Notary learns "yes."
On the fourth day, the Chef nominates the Imp; the Imp is executed but does not die. That night, the Notary is not woken.
On the fifth day, nobody nominates. That night, the Notary is not woken.
tips: If you're the Notary, you only get information when players die by execution — encourage everyone to execute!

If you're the Notary and you learned "yes," the executed player and their nominator are very likely two good players, and only slightly likely two evil players. If you learned "no," exactly one of them is evil!

If you're a Minion, you can nominate and execute other players, then use the Notary's information to attack them as evil! Or let them nominate and execute you, then likewise use the Notary's information to attack them as evil — that's more credible, since people generally trust dead players more.
If you're a Minion, have the Demon nominate and execute you — this easily makes the Notary think you're both good.
If you're the Demon, nominate carefully! If you nominate and execute a good player, the Notary will very likely attack you directly as evil!
If you're the Demon and you know for certain the Notary is in play, nominating and executing evil players easily builds the town's trust in you.
bluffing: If you're a Minion bluffing as the Notary, you can be more aggressive! Report lots of "no" results to keep creating opposition!
If you're the Demon, reporting "yes" when the executed player and their nominator both look good helps you win the other players' trust!
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him and tell him yes or no.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Same]]
Placed when: When a player dies by execution.
Condition: The player who died by execution and the player who nominated them are on the same team.
Removed when: After the Notary goes back to sleep.

[[Different]]
Placed when: When a player dies by execution.
Condition: The player who died by execution and the player who nominated them are on different teams.
Removed when: After the Notary goes back to sleep.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A simple, handy ongoing information slot. An ongoing information slot that checks the dead — more precisely, half dead players and half alive players. This kind of character's information is generally stronger than alive-player-checking information, because checking the dead and checking the living differ in information value.

Suited for scripts without many team-checking information slots, joining as the core ongoing information slot to play a logic-building role.

characters.name: Scarecrow
characters.ability: You think you are a Townsfolk character, but you are not. If you die, no-one dies at the next execution.
characters.lede: The Scarecrow thinks they're a Townsfolk; after death, the Scarecrow protects the next executed player.
characters.quote: Crows are clever. Before they peck me, they stand on me for a while, testing whether I'm alive. Once they're sure I'm straw, they peck away at ease. Before you push the next person up there, couldn't you do a test too — first see what this scarecrow looks like when it burns. Then decide whether to burn the next one.
summaryBullets: Even if the Scarecrow is drunk, poisoned, or dead, they still think they're the Townsfolk they believe they are. Once a player becomes the Scarecrow, they always think they're a Townsfolk unless they become another character.
If the Scarecrow dies, the next execution causes no death. But if that player wouldn't have died anyway, the Scarecrow's ability does not carry over to the execution after that.
Neither the Scarecrow nor any other player knows whether a player who survived execution was protected by the Scarecrow — players must deduce this themselves.
The character the Scarecrow believes they are never duplicates another Townsfolk in the initial setup.

If a player becomes the Scarecrow mid-game, they think they've become a Townsfolk character. If that player was already a Townsfolk character, they may keep believing they're their original character without learning of the change — or they may believe they've become a different Townsfolk character. This is up to the Storyteller.
howToRun: During game setup, before putting character tokens into the bag, remove the Scarecrow token and add one extra Townsfolk character token. Place the Scarecrow's "Scarecrow" reminder in the Grimoire. Put the replacement Townsfolk character token into the bag instead of the Scarecrow's character token.

While preparing for the first night, place the Scarecrow's "Scarecrow" reminder by the replacement Townsfolk's character token to remind you that player is actually the Scarecrow. That player is now an Outsider and no longer has that Townsfolk's ability, but they still think they're a Townsfolk.
During the game, treat the Scarecrow as the Townsfolk they think they are. If that character would act at night, wake the Scarecrow and let them act.
If the Scarecrow dies, place the "Protect" reminder by the Scarecrow's character token. The next time an execution occurs, the executed player does not die. Remove the "Protect" reminder.
examples: The Scarecrow thinks they're the Noble. On the first day, the Scarecrow dies by execution. On the second day, the Baron is executed but does not die.
The Scarecrow thinks they're the Fortune Teller. On the third night, the Scarecrow dies. The next day, the Butler is executed but does not die.
tips: The Scarecrow doesn't know they're the Scarecrow. As long as the Scarecrow is on the script, if your character is a Townsfolk, you might be the Scarecrow!
If an execution caused a death, no Townsfolk who died before it was the Scarecrow. If an execution caused no death, the player who died last night or was executed yesterday might be the Scarecrow.

If you're the Demon, you can generally locate the Scarecrow quickly, since the Scarecrow always reports false information or has a malfunctioning ability. Killing them at the right time protects you or your teammates. In some cases, it can also get a good player who was about to be executed executed again — wasting the good team's execution chance.
bluffing: Bluffing as the Scarecrow is very difficult. First you must bluff as a Townsfolk, then reveal your ability isn't working properly — which looks exactly like an evil player. You may be executed as a lying evil player.
A player bluffing as the Scarecrow doesn't have the Scarecrow's ability, so after your death nobody survives execution — making you look even more like an evil player.
The Scarecrow works as a last-resort excuse: if your claimed character is questioned about a malfunctioning ability, you can argue you might be the Scarecrow.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Scarecrow]]
Placed when: While preparing for the first night.
Condition: After collecting all players' character tokens into the Grimoire, place it by one Townsfolk character token.
Removed when: The Scarecrow leaves play.

[[Protect]]
Placed when: When the Scarecrow dies.
Condition: When the Scarecrow dies, place it by the Scarecrow's character token.
Removed when: After the Scarecrow's ability triggers, or when the Scarecrow loses their ability or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Scarecrow is like a somewhat-exposed Drunk. Compared to the Drunk, the Scarecrow interferes far less with logic-building, but fits scripts with built-in execution-survival logic much better — think of it as the dedicated Drunk for execution-survival scripts.

Even in non-execution-survival scripts, you can try adding the Scarecrow. Even when an execution-survival occurs, players can't necessarily tell who's the Scarecrow — and the survival can be exploited by the evil team.

characters.name: Rascal
characters.ability: On your 1st night & 1st day, Townsfolk abilities yield false info.
characters.lede: On the day the Rascal appears, every Townsfolk makes errors.
characters.quote: The fisherman said he's taking his fish to market tomorrow morning; the seamstress said she can't be bothered to lock her door at noon; the artist is out drinking at the brothel tonight. I overheard it all! Tomorrow morning, the fisherman opens his creel to find only three toads. The seamstress can't pry apart her glue-stuck scissors. And, and! Best of all — the artist will wake up and fall flat on his face, because I tied his shoelaces together!
summaryBullets: False information: objectively wrong, untrue information. Whether information is false is not affected by any ability.
While the Rascal's ability is in effect, any information a Townsfolk player gains through an ability is false — even if they're drunk or poisoned, the information is guaranteed false.
The Rascal's ability doesn't affect information gained by other means, such as rules the Storyteller explains or changes to a player's character or team.
If the Rascal dies, the Rascal's ability stops working immediately.
If the Rascal is created mid-game, the Rascal's ability takes effect immediately until the end of the next day.
The Rascal's ability doesn't "double-negative" with other interference effects. For example, when the Vortox and the Rascal are both in effect, Townsfolk still only get false information.
howToRun: When the Rascal enters play, place the "Mischief" reminder on the Grimoire.
While the "Mischief" reminder is on the Grimoire, whenever a Townsfolk's ability requires you to give them information, the Storyteller must give false information.
After the Rascal has passed his first night and his first day, remove the "Mischief" reminder.
examples: The Rascal is in play. On the first night, the Chef, the Empath, the Seamstress, and every other information-gathering Townsfolk gets false information.
The Rascal is in play. On the first day, the Savant gets two false statements.
tips: If you're the Rascal, you'd best announce your character as soon as possible! Your ability causes massive interference.

If you're the Rascal, after talking with a player of an important character you trust, you can each claim the other's character. This both promptly announces the Rascal is in play and covers for them, helping them survive to the mid-to-late game.
If you're the Rascal, being executed usually doesn't remove your negative effect — even if you're not executed on day one, your ability's effect ends at nightfall anyway.
bluffing: If you're a Minion and you're sure the Rascal isn't in play, announce you're the Rascal! It causes enormous confusion for the good team.
If you're the Demon, bluff as the Rascal with caution — once the good team finds the first night's information wasn't wrong, they may execute you immediately.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Mischief]]
Placed when: When the Rascal enters play.
Condition: On the game's first night or when the Rascal is created, place it in the center of the Grimoire or by the Rascal's character token.
Removed when: After the Rascal has passed his first night and his first day.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The rough model of an interference Outsider is one player (unknown) being drunk for a limited time. The Puzzle Master and the Truelove both fit this model. The Drunk is different — he doesn't make a Townsfolk drunk, but any Townsfolk could be the Drunk, functioning similarly to one player being drunk.

The Rascal has a definite time point — one day, clearly shorter than the model; an enormous scope — all Townsfolk, clearly wider than the model; guaranteed-false information — clearly weaker interference than drunkenness. Balancing the trade-offs, the Rascal is a roughly on-model interference Outsider.

characters.name: Loverbound
characters.ability: On your 1st night, choose another player: after you or they die, the other might die at any time.
characters.lede: The Loverbound and their beloved may die at any time after the other dies.
characters.quote: They say dying for love means leaving together. Wrong. Dying for love is when you're gone and I'm still here, but every step I take lands on the road you walked. You walked too fast — I couldn't keep up. But it's all right; every road has an end. When that day comes, I won't say goodbye. I'll say: wait for me — this time, let me walk in front. I've finally understood: dying for love was never two people's deaths, but one person's life being too long — so long it can only be ended another way.
summaryBullets: The Storyteller might kill the other player at any point after the Loverbound or the "Lover" dies — or never kill the other one for the entire game.

If the Loverbound or the "Lover" is currently under a death-protection effect, that player doesn't die. If that death-protection effect is a limited-use effect (such as the Fool), both the Loverbound's ability and the protection ability are consumed.
The Loverbound cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: On the first night, wake the Loverbound. Have the Loverbound point to another player. Place the "Lover" reminder by that player's character token. Put the Loverbound back to sleep.

At any time after the Loverbound or the "Lover" dies, you may kill the other one. If it's during the day, immediately announce that player is dead. If it's at night, place the "Dead" reminder by that player's character token and wait until dawn to announce which players died that night.
examples: On the first night, the Loverbound chooses the Fortune Teller. On the second night, the Loverbound dies. On the fifth night, the Fortune Teller dies.
On the first night, the Loverbound chooses the Baron. On the third day, the Baron dies by execution. That night, the Loverbound dies.
tips: If you're the Loverbound, best have a chat with your "Lover" — protect each other to avoid chain deaths.
If you're the Loverbound, be careful about revealing who your "Lover" is — the Demon may deliberately kill you both.
If you're the Demon, figuring out who the Loverbound chose matters — you can kill one of them at the right time, hoping the other follows.
bluffing: Bluffing as the Loverbound can explain some strange deaths — provided you're already dead.
The Loverbound works as a backup bluff. After your other bluffs all fail, you can reveal that you're actually a Loverbound.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Have them choose a player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Lover]]
Placed when: After the Loverbound acts at night and chooses a player.
Condition: Place it by the player the Loverbound chose.
Removed when: The Loverbound leaves play.

[[Dead]]
Placed when: After the Loverbound or the "Lover" dies, during the night, when the Storyteller decides to kill the Loverbound or the "Lover".
Condition: If the Storyteller decides to kill the Loverbound or the "Lover", place it by the Loverbound's or "Lover's" character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn. If the Storyteller chooses to kill the Loverbound or the "Lover" during the day, no reminder is needed — place the shroud marker directly and prompt the player to flip their life token.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: An extra-death Outsider. Simple, easy to understand, gives the player room to operate, and encourages private chats.

characters.name: Viking
characters.ability: When you vote with your vote token, the nominee is executed immediately.
characters.lede: After death, the Viking can force an execution.
characters.quote: I smell the fear on you, stinking like rotting meat. The death you dread is merely a threshold in my eyes. Step across it, and the Valkyries will lead me to Valhalla. You, though — you'll just rot in the ground after death, too foul even for the maggots. So when I personally send you on your way, that's not an execution; it's a purification. Kneel properly — don't make me say it twice.
summaryBullets: Vote token: the voting indicator a player gains upon death. A dead player gains one vote token and may only vote by using it. Whether each player has vote tokens, and how many, is public knowledge.

Using a vote token: the act of a dead player voting by spending their vote token. Losing a vote token through non-voting means does not count as using it. This act is public and visible to all players.
The Viking's votes while alive have no other effect. Only the single vote after death (the vote token) has the forced-execution effect.
The Viking loses his vote token after using it. Generally, the Viking can use his ability only once per game.
The Viking can only use his ability normally after death (he has no vote token while alive). The Viking does not lose his ability by dying.
howToRun: When the Viking votes with his vote token, after calling through all players' votes, collect the Viking's vote token. Then immediately declare the currently nominated player executed.
examples: On the second day, the dead Viking votes for the Imp with his vote token. The Imp gets only 1 vote, but the Imp is immediately executed and dies. The game ends.

On the fifth day, the dead Viking votes for the Fortune Teller with his vote token. The Imp previously got 10 votes, the Fortune Teller only gets 1 — but the Fortune Teller is immediately executed and dies.
tips: If you're the Viking, your ability only works after death — find a way to die, by execution or at night. Dying by execution is usually a poor trade, since you waste a chance to execute the Demon; if your ability then doesn't execute the Demon either, you've wasted two execution chances.
If you're the Viking, you can use your ability early-to-mid game to prove you're really a Viking. You can also save it for the final day to force-execute a player who lacks the votes.
If you're the Demon, it's best to keep the Viking alive — while he lives, he can't use his ability.

If you're a Minion, you can deliberately enrage the Viking and taunt him to execute you. If the Viking asks to be executed that day and uses his ability to execute you the next, the Demon has won at least two extra execution rounds.
bluffing: Bluffing as the Viking is fairly risky, because Vikings generally seek death — it's hard to explain why you're a Viking who's been alive and well the whole game.
Remember, you don't have the Viking's ability: even after death, you can't force-execute anyone. Be mentally prepared for that.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
Vote-token characters are always strongly tied to death; the Viking is another attempt at vote-token design.

If the Viking uses his ability early-to-mid game, he can self-prove — but a dead player's self-proof is very limited. If the Viking uses it on the final day, he directly decides the final executed player. The self-proof value is minimal, but he can overrule everyone and win outright (or lose).

characters.name: Visagiste
characters.ability: If you nominate or are nominated by a Minion or Demon, they may become a not-in-play same-type character tonight, even if you are dead.
characters.lede: The Visagiste lets Minions and Demons change character through nominations.
characters.quote: The same touch of rouge — on the cheek it's shyness, at the corner of the eye it's allure, at the lips it's spite. One face, three places, three faces. My clients always say 'just do whatever,' but I never do whatever. I have to look at her bone structure first, then her features, and only then decide who she'll become tonight.
summaryBullets: The Visagiste does not lose her ability from death — even if the Visagiste dies after nominating or being nominated, or a Minion or Demon nominates the dead Visagiste, her ability still triggers normally that night.
The Visagiste's ability can only create characters that are not in play.
A Minion can only become another Minion; a Demon can only become another Demon.
If, on the same day, multiple Minions and Demons nominated the Visagiste or were nominated by the Visagiste, each of them may choose to become another character of the same type that night.
howToRun: If the Visagiste nominated a Minion or Demon, or a Demon or Minion nominated the Visagiste, place the "Makeover" reminder by that Demon's or Minion's character token.

That night, wake all players with a "Makeover" reminder by them. Show them the "This character's ability applies to you" info token, then show the Visagiste character token. Each player woken this way may either shake their head or point to a character on the character sheet of the same character type as their current character. If a player's choice would make their character the same as another player's character, shake your head at them and have them choose again. Once they've chosen, put them back to sleep. Remove all "Makeover" reminders. Perform the corresponding character changes in the Grimoire according to those players' choices.
examples: On the first day, the Visagiste nominates the Vortox. That night, the Vortox chooses to become the Fang Gu.
On the second day, the Fang Gu nominates the Visagiste. That night, the Fang Gu chooses to become the No Dashii.
On the third day, the Baron nominates the dead Visagiste. That night, the Baron chooses to become the Poisoner.
tips: If you're the Visagiste, best not to reveal your character carelessly — your ability could easily be exploited.
If you're the Visagiste, as long as no player nominates you and you don't nominate other players, your ability definitely can't trigger. Remember this.
If you're the Visagiste and a player suddenly nominates you for no reason — especially after you've announced you're the Visagiste — you have reason to believe they're a Minion or the Demon.
If you're a Minion, you can use the Visagiste's ability to change your character — provided you know who the Visagiste is.
If you're the Demon, don't expose yourself just to use the Visagiste's ability. Find sufficient justification for your nominations, or find a way to get the Visagiste to nominate you.
bluffing: The Visagiste is very sensitive about her own nominations. If you want to bluff as the Visagiste, best not to nominate other players carelessly — this makes you look more credible.

Use the Visagiste as a backup bluff. The Visagiste always tends to hide her character; after your first bluff fails, you can reveal that you're actually a Visagiste — and even attack the players who nominated you as Minions or the Demon.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake the players with a "Makeover" reminder by them.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Makeover]]
Placed when: When the Visagiste nominates or is nominated, and she is sober and healthy.
Condition: Place it by the nominating or nominated Minion or Demon player.
Removed when: After that player's character-selection step is complete.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
There are very few evil character-change designs among the official characters. Evil character change is one of the most important parts of the evil team's advantage, and the official Pit-Hag alone is too powerful, leaving players with a mistaken understanding of character-change abilities.

The Visagiste is a strategic Outsider that leaves traces and can be proactively used by the evil team. Whether or not the Visagiste is in play, both teams can build bluffs and mind games around this character. Especially in nomination-themed scripts, both teams can find reasonable explanations for nominating or not nominating.

characters.name: Geisha
characters.ability: On your 1st night alive & your 1st night dead, learn an alive player: the 2 are on opposing alignments.
characters.lede: After death, the Geisha fully learns two players on different teams.
characters.quote: The girl next door threw herself into the river over a man. When they fished her out, the smile was still on her lips. Everyone called her foolish, called her mad. I said nothing. I knew she wasn't mad — she'd simply done the math. Mama taught us: for a girl of the house, true feelings mean giving more than you get. But that girl said — never feeling anything is the real bad bargain; you pay with your whole life. 'Living' and 'having lived' differ by one word, and by a whole lifetime. She had lived, and that made it worth it.
summaryBullets: If the Geisha's first night alive is also her first night dead, she learns two alive players on different teams at once.
The player the Geisha learns must be alive at the moment she acts.
Whether the Geisha died by execution or another cause, whether by day or by night, at the Geisha's point in the night order on the night of the day she died, she is woken and learns a player.
The Geisha may learn a good player first and then an evil player, or an evil player first and then a good player — this is up to the Storyteller.
If a dead player becomes the Geisha, they only learn one player that night (meaningless information).
The Geisha does not learn Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: one player, e.g., "May" or "player #3."
False information format: one player; the player learned on the first night dead must be on the same team as the player learned on the first night alive.
howToRun: On the Geisha's first night alive, wake the Geisha and point at an alive player, placing the "Learned" reminder by that player's character token. Then put the Geisha back to sleep.
On the Geisha's first night after death, wake the Geisha and point at an alive player. Then put the Geisha back to sleep. This player must be on a different team to the player marked "Learned."
If the Geisha's first night alive is also her first night dead, wake the Geisha and point at two alive players on different teams.
examples: On the first night, the Geisha learns player #1 (the Fortune Teller). On the second night, the Geisha dies; the Geisha learns player #2 (the living Baron).
On the first night, the Geisha learns player #3 (the Poisoner). On the second day, the Geisha dies by execution; that night, the Geisha learns player #4 (the living Saint).
On the first night, the Geisha learns player #1 (the Saint). On the fourth day, the Geisha dies by execution; that night, the Geisha learns player #2 (the living Imp).
tips: If you're the Geisha and you stay alive the whole game, you provide no value. Seek death. But if you believe every other player is evil, don't seek death lightly — you might lose the game outright.

If you're the Geisha, dying early and dying late mean different things. Dying early, you learn two players on different teams you can use as a logical anchor for the whole game. Dying mid-to-late game, the other alive player you learn has a high chance of being the Demon.
If you're the Geisha, sometimes there's no rush to die — most players will be dead before the game ends anyway.

If you're the Demon, either deal with the Geisha early or keep her alive until the game ends. If the Geisha dies mid-to-late game and you're the only evil player left, the situation becomes very dangerous for you.
bluffing: Geishas are always seeking death. Playing a player who wants to die makes you look more like a Geisha.
The Geisha works as a backup bluff: when your first bluff fails, you can explain you're actually a Geisha.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.tags: Information, On Death, You Start Knowing
characters.firstNightReminder: Wake her and tell her one player.
characters.otherNightReminder: If she died today, wake her and tell her one player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Learned]]
Placed when: On the Geisha's first night alive.
Condition: Place it by the character token of the player the Geisha learned.
Removed when: The Geisha dies or leaves play.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
The Geisha looks like a delayed Seamstress, seemingly weaker — after all, the Seamstress gets all her information on the first night. Is that so? Read on.

The Geisha is neither first-night information nor a landmine. She's more a flexible "information filler." Early on, lacking a logical anchor, the Geisha can accept death and provide opposing-team information. In the mid-to-late game, when the Geisha dies, she can find the opposing player among the few survivors — perhaps even the Demon.

The Geisha learns alive players — this is crucial, because dead players' information value is far lower than alive players'. The word "alive" weighs heavier the later the game goes. So the Geisha is not "the earlier the death, the better."

Comparing again with the Seamstress: probabilistically, the Seamstress is more likely to learn same-team players than different-team ones. Learning two players on different teams is far stronger information than learning two on the same team. The Seamstress triggers simply but has lower information value, while the Geisha — though her trigger is harsher — always learns opposing players, steadily gaining higher-value information.

Why isn't the Geisha designed as "after death, learn two players," instead of learning one alive and one dead? Getting one player first helps the Geisha predict that player's team and evaluate the best time to die.

In summary: characters that look extremely similar are completely different in practice. A clear understanding of the game's mechanics and the flexibility to apply them is the key to making simple yet practical characters.

characters.name: Mermaid
characters.ability: Each day, you may publicly accept a player's compliment: evil abilities cannot affect them until you accept another player's compliment.
characters.lede: The Mermaid protects the players who praise her.
characters.quote: Little darlings on the shore, do your ears itch? That's because my singing has burrowed into your hearts! Everyone in town knows — the moment I open my mouth, even the seagulls can't bear to fly away~ I'm in a wonderful mood today, so each of you may make one wish — but you have to compliment me first! Starting with you, yes, the one in the hat. 'Mermaid sister is the fairest'? Hmm... barely passing. Come here and high-five me!
summaryBullets: Evil characters' abilities include all Minion and Demon abilities — including but not limited to death, poison, false information, and so on.

If a protected player would be poisoned, made drunk, or subjected to another ongoing effect by an evil character's ability, that effect is temporarily suppressed (you may flip the poison reminder face-down) rather than removed outright. If the Mermaid dies or becomes poisoned or drunk mid-effect, ending the protection, those players are immediately affected again (e.g., re-poisoned).
Each day, the Mermaid can accept only one player's compliment, and you should respond to her acceptance — e.g., publicly acknowledging it — so players clearly know which player might be protected.
The Mermaid cannot accept her own compliment to herself.
If the Mermaid doesn't respond to or rejects a player's compliment, she may still accept another player's compliment afterward.
For players who aren't the Mermaid: if they also accept another player's compliment, you should play along and respond just as you would for the Mermaid.

If the Mermaid and other players are being too perfunctory about the "compliment," appropriately prompt them that they must interact sincerely to earn the Mermaid's protection — you can have them compliment again. The Mermaid was designed to encourage socializing and interaction; use her ability sensibly to liven up the atmosphere.
The Mermaid cannot accept Traveller players' compliments (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each day, the first player whose compliment the Mermaid publicly accepts: place the "Immune to Evil" reminder by their character token, and remove all other "Immune to Evil" reminders.
A player marked "Immune to Evil" is not affected by evil characters' abilities.
examples: On the first day, the Saint publicly compliments the Mermaid player: "Sister, you look lovely today," and the Mermaid player publicly responds, "Well said — I accept your compliment." That night, the Imp attacks the Saint; the Saint is protected by the Mermaid and does not die.

On the second day, the Fortune Teller publicly compliments the Mermaid player: "Your understanding of the game is really good; I should learn from you," and the Mermaid player publicly responds, "I love hearing that — I'll protect you, baby." That night the Poisoner chooses the Fortune Teller, but because the Fortune Teller is protected by the Mermaid, the Fortune Teller still gets correct information.

The Fortune Teller is protected by the Mermaid. That night the Poisoner chooses the Fortune Teller; the Fortune Teller is not poisoned. Later, the Mermaid is attacked by the Demon and dies; the Fortune Teller immediately returns to being poisoned.
tips: If you're the Mermaid, hiding your identity is mostly pointless. You need to interact with other players to use your ability, and interaction exposes you as the Mermaid.
If you're the Mermaid, accept compliments from more important players! Or accept whichever compliments you enjoy most! Play however you like! Protect whomever you like!

If you're an important Townsfolk and you're protected by the real Mermaid, your ability definitely can't be affected by the Demon or Minions — usually you won't die and won't be poisoned. Your information becomes highly credible!
If you're a good player, bluffing as the Mermaid appropriately helps the real Mermaid stay hidden.

If you're the Demon, several players may claim to be the Mermaid — quickly figure out who's real. Or you can try complimenting the Mermaid yourself to win her protection, so no other important Townsfolk gets it.
bluffing: Bluff as the Mermaid and deceive the players you "protect" into thinking their information is highly credible.
Mermaids always choose to protect the more important-looking Townsfolk, so choose the more important players — it makes you more credible.
Players the Mermaid protects usually don't die at night. Don't attack the player you're "protecting," or you'll have no way to explain it.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Immune to Evil]]
Placed when: When the Mermaid publicly accepts another player's compliment.
Condition: The Mermaid is not poisoned or drunk; place it by the character token of the player who complimented the Mermaid.
Removed when: The Mermaid dies, leaves play, or accepts a new player's compliment.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A social character.

Whether or not the Mermaid is really in play, other players will claim to be her to cover for her — making for a lively scene where everyone compliments each other, quickly warming up the atmosphere.

Essentially a publicly triggered protection ability: it leaves traces for evil, but it's also stronger — immunity to all evil abilities.

characters.name: Psychic
characters.ability: Each night*, choose a player: if they are dead, you learn their team.
characters.lede: The Psychic can check dead players' teams.
characters.quote: My gift lets me smell the scent of souls. A good soul smells like grass after rain, sweet with morning dew; an evil soul smells like scorched leather, mingled with blood and sulfur. The one who passed last night — his scent is spreading through my nostrils right now... Would the lady wearing perfume and the gentleman who hasn't bathed please step back, so I can tell you accurately whether he was a lamb or a jackal.
summaryBullets: If the Psychic chooses an alive player, he learns nothing.
If the Psychic chooses a player who died that night, he learns that player's team.
The Psychic cannot choose Traveller players (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
Information format: "good" or "evil" — or thumbs up for good, thumbs down for evil.
False information format: "good" or "evil" — or thumbs up for good, thumbs down for evil — opposite to the truth.
howToRun: Each night, wake the Psychic. Let him point at a player. If his chosen player is dead, give him a thumbs-up or thumbs-down gesture. Put him back to sleep. If his chosen player is alive, give no information. Put him back to sleep.
examples: On the first day, the Noble dies by execution. That night, the Psychic chooses the Noble and learns "good."
On the first day, nobody died. That night, the Psychic chooses the Noble; the Noble is alive, and the Psychic learns nothing.
On the first day, nobody died. That night, the Psychic chooses the Imp; the Imp chooses themself that night and dies, and the Psychic learns "evil."
tips: If you're the Psychic, prefer choosing dead players who seem evil.

If you're the Psychic, after the first execution you'll usually face having only one confirmed dead player to choose — sometimes none at all. Then you may need to guess who will die that night and choose them.

If you're the Psychic, the more recently a player died, the higher the information value. If you don't want to check earlier dead players, you can gamble on guessing tonight's deaths — but if you guess wrong, you get nothing.
bluffing: The Psychic can only learn dead players' teams — be careful not to talk yourself into a corner.
Generally, the Psychic prefers choosing players who died by execution.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Wake him and tell him good or evil.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A benchmark-template character. Single check, but only of the dead.

If we wrote the ability in the most basic, common way — "Each night*, choose a dead player: you learn their team" — you'd immediately experience the power of this game's legacy spaghetti code: can you choose a player who died that very night? If so, how would they know who died that night? Try them one by one? If not, how do you explain it to players? The text says choose a dead player, so why single out tonight's dead? Wouldn't new players constantly slip up? The fix is simple: change "precondition filtering" to "postcondition checking." You choose whoever you like — but whether you get information afterward is on you. Handing the problem to the players solves everything.

characters.name: Yasha
characters.ability: Each night*, you may choose a player you nominated today, or who nominated you: they die, even if you are dead.
characters.lede: The Yasha takes revenge at night on those who crossed him.
characters.quote: My belly has been hollow for a thousand years, never filled. This emptiness is not lust of the flesh — it is the fear you've forgotten. By day you laugh and chat at ease, but when you turn over in the deep night, whose breath is that chill on your back? It is I, standing by your pillow, counting your breaths one by one. I am in no hurry, for hunger is the finest seasoning. The moment you unconsciously speak my name — that is when my feast begins.
summaryBullets: If the Yasha was neither nominated nor made a nomination today, the Yasha is not woken.
The Yasha can kill at most one player per night.
If the Yasha chooses a player who doesn't meet the condition, shake your head and signal him to choose again.
If the Yasha nominates himself, he can kill himself that night.
The Yasha doesn't lose his ability from death. If a player nominates the dead Yasha, the Yasha is woken that night and can kill the player who nominated him.
The Yasha's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Whenever the Yasha nominates or is nominated, place the "Grudge" reminder by the character token of the player he nominated or who nominated him.

Each night except the first, if a "Grudge" reminder is on the Grimoire, wake the Yasha. He chooses a player with a "Grudge" reminder, or chooses nothing. Put the Yasha back to sleep. If the Yasha chose a player with a "Grudge" reminder, place the "Dead" reminder by that player's character token. After the Yasha finishes acting, remove all "Grudge" reminders.
examples: On the first day, the Yasha nominates the Fortune Teller. That night, the Yasha is woken and chooses the Fortune Teller — the Fortune Teller dies.
On the second day, the Saint nominates the Yasha; the Yasha dies by execution that day. That night, the Yasha is woken and chooses the Saint — the Saint dies.
On the third day, the Baron nominates the already-dead Yasha. That night, the Yasha is woken and chooses the Baron — the Baron dies.
On the first day, the Yasha makes no nomination and no player nominates the Yasha. That night, the Yasha is not woken.
tips: If you're the Yasha, participate in nominations or get nominated by other players as much as possible — that's how you use your ability.
If you're the Yasha, don't cause deaths every day — that's too obvious. Attack other players intermittently so you look less like a Yasha.
If you're the Yasha, it doesn't matter if everyone already thinks you're the Yasha — to kill you they still must nominate you, and you can kill the players who nominate you.
If you're the Yasha and already dead, you can still be effective. Have other evil players nominate you and attack them at night — this can end the game early in the late game.
If you're a good player, watch the nominations of players who died abnormally at night — do they all point to the same player? If so, that player is very likely the Yasha.

If you're a good player and you've identified a player as the Yasha, think carefully about how to deal with him. Executing him means sacrificing another player; not executing him means he may nominate and attack other players every day.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose a player with a "Grudge" reminder.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Grudge" ×2]]
Placed when: When the Yasha nominates or is nominated.
Condition: When the Yasha nominates a player or is nominated by a player, place it by the character token of the player he nominated or who nominated him.
Removed when: After the Yasha finishes acting.

[[Dead]]
Placed when: When the Yasha chooses a player during his night action.
Condition: If the player the Yasha chose has a "Grudge" reminder and the Yasha is sober and healthy, place it by that player's character token to remind the Storyteller to announce that night's dead player at dawn.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A multi-death Minion with strong initiative, controllable.

Suited for nomination-themed scripts — deterring good players' nominations and providing more death logic for abnormal deaths.

characters.name: MarMonk
characters.ability: When the Demon attacks you, an evil player is attacked instead.
characters.lede: The MarMonk redirects the Demon's attack.
characters.quote: Bamboo meets the frost with heaven-high pride; the fiercer the wind snaps its boughs, the stronger its spirit grows. A hollow heart takes in the force of storm and cloud; one inch of gentle bosom embraces all eight wilds.
summaryBullets: Attack: when a player with a Demon ability, or the Storyteller, selects a player with the Demon's killing ability. Attacks usually kill an alive player; sometimes they don't, such as attacking a player who cannot die or a dead player.

In the vast majority of cases, a living evil player — not a dead one — should be attacked instead of the MarMonk. If the Demon is the only living evil player in play, the Demon should be attacked instead of the MarMonk.
The MarMonk's ability changes the Demon's attack target; it is not death immunity.

Whether the Demon attacks by day or by night, and whether the target is chosen by a player or by the Storyteller, an evil player takes the attack for the MarMonk. This also means the Demon cannot kill the MarMonk.
Traveller players never substitute as attack targets (Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Whenever the Demon player chooses to attack the MarMonk, or the Storyteller decides to attack the MarMonk with the Demon's ability, an evil player is attacked instead of the MarMonk.
examples: On the second night, the Imp attacks the MarMonk; the Baron is attacked instead of the MarMonk, and the Baron dies.
On the fourth night, the Fang Gu attacks the MarMonk; the only living evil player is the Fang Gu, so the Fang Gu is attacked instead of the MarMonk, and the Fang Gu dies. The game ends.
tips: If you're the MarMonk, present yourself as an important death-fearing character as much as possible, baiting the Demon into attacking you.
If you're the MarMonk, you can swap claimed characters with some important players, making the Demon mistake you for the more important character and attack you.

If you're the MarMonk, you can't know whether your ability triggered. If the player who died at night seems suspicious and you were extremely likely to be attacked that night, the dead player may be an evil player who died in your place.
If you're the Demon, beware the MarMonk — avoid attacking him.
If you're the Demon, you can't deal with the MarMonk yourself — have a Minion handle him or find a way to get him executed.
bluffing: The MarMonk works as your backup bluff, especially after failing to bluff an important character.
Generally, the MarMonk doesn't die at night — you can use this to explain why the Demon never attacked you.
characters.creator: Taiyi

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: A benchmark-template character with sensible landmine strength.

characters.name: Tanner
characters.ability: On your 1st night, you learn the evil character nearest to you.
characters.lede: The Tanner learns the closest evil character.
characters.quote: The inside of this boot shaft is badly worn — that's from rubbing on a stirrup. Coming to my shop, you must be a courier? I've no ready-made military gear here, only freshly soaked cowhide for making belly-bands for the town's donkeys. Well then — your sole's about to fall off. Half-sole repair, or a whole new piece?
summaryBullets: If two evil characters are equally close to the Tanner, the Tanner learns one of them; the Storyteller decides which.
Evil characters means Minion characters and Demon characters. The Tanner's ability looks for the nearest Demon or Minion, ignoring Townsfolk and Outsiders even if they are evil.
The Tanner only learns one evil character — not a distance or a player.
Information format: one evil character, e.g., the Baron or the Fang Gu.
False information format: one evil character, but not the evil character nearest to the Tanner.
howToRun: On the first night, wake the Tanner. Tell him one evil character — it must be the character of the evil player nearest to him. Put the Tanner back to sleep.
examples: On the first night, the Tanner learns the Goblin. The Goblin is the evil character nearest to the Tanner.
On the first night, the Tanner learns the Fang Gu. The Fang Gu and the Goblin are both at distance 1 from the Tanner.
tips: If you're the Tanner, the evil character you learned is definitely in play — that's important information in itself. Second, it's the evil character nearest to you; if you can pin down which player is that character, everyone closer to you than them is good.
If you're the Tanner and you learned a Demon character, the Demon is near you — pay more attention to the players around you.
If you're the Tanner and you learned a Minion character, a Minion is nearer to you than the Demon — there may be no Demon among the players beside you.
bluffing: Bluff as the Tanner and report false information to disrupt the good team's judgment of how evil characters are distributed.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.firstNightReminder: Tell him one evil character.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content: A benchmark first-night information slot.

characters.name: Minotaur
characters.ability: Each night*, choose an alive player: they die. Before the final day, if all evil players have died by execution, your team wins.
characters.lede: The Minotaur feigns defeat — in truth, luring the good team into the trap of failure.
characters.quote: Do you know the labyrinth's true brilliance? It isn't making people lost — it's making people believe every step lands in the right direction. For a thousand years, I've fled on wounded hooves, looking spent and finished. They chased me through stone gate after stone gate, thinking it a shortcut to victory. But there is no guiding thread here, no marks for turning back. Those seemingly open passages — every turn leads to a trapdoor or a spike pit. Every approach, every 'almost got him', is nothing but an illusion I tailored for them. When they excitedly greet their 'victory', what awaits them is only the boundless darkness in the labyrinth's depths.
summaryBullets: "The final day": the first day of the game with fewer than 5 alive players (not counting Travellers). On the final day, the Storyteller publicly announces at the earliest opportunity that today is the final day. A game has at most one "final day" — if the game doesn't end on the final day, later days with fewer than 5 alive players are not treated as the "final day". If the game ends early (e.g. special victory or the Demon's death), that game may have no "final day". Before the final day arrives: the game period before the final day comes. When the final day arrives: the moment the final day comes (usually the first dawn with fewer than 5 alive non-Traveller players). After the final day arrives: the final day and the game period after it.
The Minotaur cannot choose dead players. If the Minotaur chooses an already-dead player (whether they died earlier or that night), have him choose again.

The Minotaur's special victory only triggers when all evil players have died by execution — meaning if even one evil player dies from a cause other than execution, the Minotaur's special victory cannot trigger.
Evil Travellers are not counted as evil players by the Minotaur's ability, and the Minotaur's ability cannot choose Traveller players (the Traveller Exclusion Principle).
howToRun: Each night except the first, wake the Minotaur. Have the Minotaur point to any alive player. Put the Minotaur back to sleep. The chosen player dies — place the Minotaur's "Dead" reminder by that player's character token.
When an evil player dies by execution, if the final day hasn't arrived yet and all other evil players have died by execution, declare that the evil team wins.
examples: 12-player game. On the first day, the Baron dies by execution. On the second day, the Poisoner dies by execution. On the third day, the Minotaur dies by execution — the evil team wins.

15-player game. On the first day, the Baron dies by execution. On the second day, the Fortune Teller dies by execution. On the third day, the Poisoner dies by execution. On the fourth day, the Spy dies by execution. On the fifth day, the Minotaur dies by execution — the evil team wins.

10-player game. On the first day, the Baron dies by execution. On the second day, the Fortune Teller dies by execution. On the third day, the Poisoner dies by execution. On the fourth day — the final day — the Minotaur dies by execution; the good team wins.
tips: If you're the Minotaur, plan your win method from the very start of the game. If you want the special victory, all Minions must die heroically — and you need to deliver the die-for-the-cause order to every Minion.

If you're the Minotaur and your special-victory plan gets interrupted — e.g., a Minion dies from a non-execution cause, or the executions remaining before the final day are no longer enough to execute the remaining evil players — immediately change strategy and survive to the game's final moment the traditional way.

If you're another Demon: even if you're not the Minotaur, you can have Minions die at key moments. This makes the good team believe the in-play Demon is the Minotaur, changing their execution strategy and winning you more survival room.

If you're a good player and you think the good team is on a roll, executing one suspected evil player after another — watch out! The in-play Demon is very possibly the Minotaur. If the Minotaur is in play and gets executed as the last evil player, you lose. If you sense the Demon might be the Minotaur, change your execution strategy — execute the most Demon-like players early, or save suspected Demons for execution on the final day.
characters.creator: Taiyi
characters.otherNightReminder: Have him choose an alive player.

customBoxes.title: Reminder Tokens
customBoxes.content:
[[Dead]]
Placed when: After the Minotaur chooses a player.
Condition: If the player the Minotaur chose is currently alive and can be killed by the Minotaur, place it by that player's character token.
Removed when: After announcing the dead player at dawn; the Storyteller may remove it at their convenience.

customBoxes.title: Design Notes
customBoxes.content:
A special-victory Demon. Execution deterrence. Forces the good team to think harder about execution order and the characters of executed players.

Can only choose alive players — cutting off the Minotaur's stall tactic of deliberately killing dead players to force the good team into consecutive executions.

characters.name: Kappa
characters.ability: On the final day, you may learn from the Storyteller how many Outsider players there are. [Any number of Outsiders]
characters.lede: The Kappa may change the number of Outsider players.
